The Only Living Pickpocket in New York is an entertaining dramedy with some tributes to New York City. It’s also a very interesting take on heist movies. It isn’t the typical version of this movie, but it definitely incorporates elements of the best ones.

Additionally, John Turturro gives a fantastic performance. It may put him at the forefront of some Best Actor awards this year. He is one of the best things about The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, and that’s what helps this one important scene stand out so much.

Warning: The Only Living Pickpocket in New York spoilers are ahead. Proceed with caution.

Tatiana Maslany plays Kelly, Harry’s (John Turturro) long-neglected daughter. Before facing his death, Harry takes a detour to see Kelly one last time. In this scene, she pours out all her anger and frustration about her father for abandoning her all these years. Harry mostly allows his daughter to express her anger because this is the last time they will ever see each other.

However, he remains somewhat hopeful that this can end meaningfully and peacefully. He doesn’t really get that, but makes some amends before dying.

Maslany is one of my favorite actors. Therefore, I was once again mesmerized by one of her performances. Turturro truly is transcendent in this scene. He emotes so much with his facial expressions and the unspoken words. It’s always a privilege to watch two masters at their craft work and play off one another. I now wish they were a duo who appeared in more projects together. They’re so breathtaking together.

The first half of The Only Living Pickpocket in New York tells us a lot about Harry’s current life and career. However, we don’t learn much about his backstory. The full picture of how he developed this life and these relationships doesn’t come together until this pivotal scene. The confrontation between Harry and Kelly reveals so much backstory. We learn how he neglected his first family and a little bit of the story with his current wife.

Harry picks pockets for a living, but this is the first time you see how much of a deadbeat he used to be. It’s a stunning scene because it reminds us that he’s nefarious in many ways. However, it also shows his layers. He’s done bad things, but he’s not a terrible person, just a typical complicated human.

The Only Living Pickpocket in New York is about a man who is going to die. Unlike many movies with a similar concept, the main character doesn't discover they have a terminal illness; Harry will be murdered at the end of the movie. We know he’s going to die from early in it. Therefore, most of the movie is him trying to make amends and save those he cares about before it's over.

The scene between Harry and Kelly gets to the heart of that. This is a complex man trying to say goodbye before it's too late. It’s about doing something worthy of your legacy before you meet your end. There are many reasons to watch The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, but that scene is one of them. Add it to your must-watch 2026 movies list.

When I'm not writing about pop culture, I can be found channeling Gordon Ramsay by kicking people out the kitchen.

#3464. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3463. Presley Gerber's Hollywood Home Reportedly Listed for $3.6M After His Death

The late model Presley Gerber‘s 3,000 square-foot Hollywood Hills home is reportedly for sale following his shocking September death at age 27.

Real estate records reportedly indicate that the mid-century dwelling has been listed for $3.595 million, featuring four bedrooms and three baths in addition to outdoor and indoor living spaces, per TMZ.

With an impressive canyon view of the Hollywood Hills, the residence’s reported amenities include a jacuzzi, a cold plunge, a heated pool and a sauna. The property also features a separate guest house.

Gerber reportedly purchased the Los Angeles area home in March 2023 for $3.4 million.

News broke on September 21 that Presley — son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and Casamigos co-founder Rande Gerber — died one day earlier from a suspected overdose while staying in a Santa Monica rehab center. (The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner confirmed to Us on September 21 that Presley’s cause of death was listed as “deferred” initially because its staff was in the “early stages of investigating” and that “limited information is currently available.”)

Us subsequently learned that officers from the Santa Monica Police Department responded to a call regarding a possible overdose at an address matching the rehab facility on the day of Presley’s death.

“The Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner has identified the individual as Presley Gerber, 27,” a September 21 statement read. “SMPD detectives are investigating the death as a suspected overdose. At this time, there is no indication of foul play. The official cause and manner of death will be determined by the Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner.”

Presley had been open about his struggles with addiction and mental health, including speaking to reporters on a red carpet about his journey of self-acceptance just two months before his untimely death.

“The most free I felt was when I was finally honest with myself,” Presley said at a June We Are ENOUGH x Aviator Nation launch event. “Move your body regardless of how you’re feeling. Get outside. Get some sun. If you don’t feel like moving, lay on the grass.”

During a 2023 “Studio 22” podcast appearance, the Dolce & Gabbana and Ralph Lauren model stated his desire to help people struggling with addiction by sharing his story.

“Whether I help one person or a 100 people get out of that place that I was in at one point in my life, that’s all I need to do,” Presley told podcast listeners at the time. “I’ve had a lot of time to look into myself and learn about myself with therapists. I’ve seen a lot of stuff, and I’ve learned a lot of things, and what I hope I can do is have made the mistakes for some other people so they don’t have to make the same mistakes that I made.”

His parents, Crawford and Randy, 60 and 64 respectively, broke their silence about Presley’s death in October by sharing a new statement reflecting on their son’s life.

“Presley Walker Gerber. July 2, 1999-September 20, 2026. We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother. We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years. He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever,” the couple wrote in a joint statement shared on October 18. “We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability. We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain. Til we meet again our sweet boy.”

The same month, Presley’s sister, model and actress Kaia Gerber, penned her own poignant memorial post about the ongoing process of grieving.

“Prez, I don’t have the words, and maybe the tiny mercy is that we didn’t need them all along. Words fail and words subtract and words summarize and words always lack truth. And how naive of me to believe that language could transcend grief,” Kaia, 25, wrote via an October 18 Instagram post. “I’ve read all of the books and I have none of the answers. My articulation is no match against this, the magnitude of losing you. I am, quite literally, down on my f***ing knees.”

The Shards star described her late brother as “inherently good,” adding that she considered herself to be Presley’s “lucky eternal witness” throughout their lives.

“My best buddy, my great protector, the hardest I’ve ever laughed and the one true love of my life — you lit all of my candles and took all of my monsters away. And I love you. And I love you. And I love you. Only you know how much. Thank you for being here,” she concluded.

#3462. Democrats Plot (and Party) in Washington After Midterms Rout

This is the November 12, 2026 edition of Party Animals, a letter from the back rooms, barstools, and bacchanals of Washington, DC—with exclusive reporting, interviews, and analysis.

Good evening from Washington, where Party Animals is coming to grips with how the social scene in the capital will change amidst a dramatic transfer of power. Gone will be the heady days of President Donald Trump’s total control of the US government. The next two years will be defined by how his administration handles a muscular Democratic opposition.

At Crooked Con, a conference put on the weekend after the midterm elections by the media company founded by former Obama staffers and Pod Save America hosts Jon Favreau, Tommy Vietor, and Jon Lovett, I got a sense of just how confident the party is after almost two years in the wilderness.

Read Party Animals: A letter from the back rooms, barstools, and bacchanals of Washington, DC—with exclusive reporting, interviews, and analysis.

Befitting the sensibilities of the incoming Congress, Crooked week kicked off with a surprise appearance from Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who wore keffiyeh-patterned Air Force 1s to the live taping of his Pod Save America episode. The crowd went ballistic.

In this edition of Party Animals, the view from Washington’s new libbed-up social scene; what a Newsmax show says about Trump’s tumbling popularity among young Americans; and my colleague Joe Hagan’s interview with Beto O’Rourke, the original Democrat-who-might-win-Texas, about how the party finally pulled it off in the Lone Star State.

Also mentioned in this issue: Barrett Adair, Matthew Foldi, Robert Garcia, Katie Miller, Felicia Schwartz, Keith Edwards, Vaughn Hillyard, Marc Beckman, Marco Rubio, Michael Scherer, Chi Ossé, and more.

Got tips? Hit the Party Animals hotline: aidan_mclaughlin@condenast.com. Or text me—my number is 917-817-8266. Complaints will be aired on Newsmax. Praise will be debated and affirmed by a Crooked Con panel.

I doubt there were many places on earth more buoyant than Crooked Con in DC last weekend. The conference brought together a legion of newly elected Democrats, veteran members of Congress, journalists, and liberal content creators for a day of live plotting that culminated in a party at City Tap House, where Robert Garcia, the incoming emperor of Oversight, worked the room. “I was pretty optimistic going into the election, but this is beyond anything I imagined,” Favreau tells Party Animals. “The majority of the country is clearly ready to move on from the Trump show and give Democrats another chance.”

The creators were ecstatic. At an after-after-party nearby, Barrett Adair, a platinum blonde progressive with more than 200,000 TikTok followers, bounced around in a hot-pink latex dress. Pints were passed about so generously that once I had acquired three, I stopped bothering to tell which was which. Keith Edwards and Chi Ossé chatted intently in the corner. The night felt like a portent of what was to come: After nearly two years of the MAGA Huns marauding freely throughout the capital, the libs were soon to be back in charge—of Congress, at least. They celebrated accordingly.

“There's a lot to feel good about,” said Favreau. “Now we have to make it count.”

As the country grapples with the sheer magnitude of the blue wave that crashed down last week, our nation’s besuited analysts are seeking to identify the warning signs, like a postdisaster reconnaissance team examining the swell of a tsunami after it has decimated a Southeast Asian beach town. How did Trump lose the key voting blocs, like young men, that vaulted him back to power in 2024?

I’d like to propose a bellwether: The Big Beautiful Trump Show, an unsubtle program that debuted on conservative network Newsmax in October. It’s unclear whose brilliant idea it was to launch a North Korea–style propaganda show in support of a historically unpopular president weeks before he led his party into a generational election wipeout, but the show was hosted for three episodes by a DC-based influencer named Matthew Foldi. A source shared the ratings: The show debuted to 1,000 viewers in the younger demographic, the 25–54 age group coveted by advertisers. “Insanely low,” the source explained. A Newsmax spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

Pour one out (a pint of raw milk, perhaps) for Katie Miller’s podcast, which is going on hiatus. I was a loyal listener—she booked pretty much every Trump Cabinet member, even the shy ones, and the friendly setting elicited more insight than you’d typically get out of a guarded pol like Marco Rubio. In a post on X, Miller said she would be pausing the show due to her husband’s new role as Trump’s chief of staff, writing that “the time commitment is too great and now is the time to step away.” The next day, The Atlantic’s Michael Scherer reported that Miller had signed a contract with Paramount for a future podcast deal, but that she had ended that as well. Paramount spokesperson Melissa Zukerman told Party Animals, “I don’t see she has anything with us.” When asked if Miller ever had a contract with Paramount, Zukerman did not respond.

Huang Out: The Economist does the important math and estimates that Jensen Huang’s Chinese affair “could go down as the most expensive shag in history.”

The Mayflower Millers: Read Kevin D. Williamson, of The Dispatch, on Stephen Miller and the incomprehensible case of the “heritage American.”

Dems in Vogue: Model Caroline Trentini reflects on her photo shoot with Iowa governor-elect Rob Sand, shot by Steven Meisel for a 2004 issue of Vogue Italia. I’m reliably told that these photos went quadruple platinum on Tumblr.

Cyberyuck: Read my colleague Nate Freeman’s soaring eulogy for the Cybertruck, Elon Musk’s grand experiment in bad taste.

Rogan unchained: CNN’s Brian Stelter explores how Joe Rogan went from boosting Trump to the White House to exposing his administration’s deepening rifts. The latest: Rogan’s interview with former Robert F. Kennedy Jr. adviser Calley Means, who accused Trump’s inner circle of corruption.

The next two years: Vanity Fair’s Chris Whipple examines how Stephen Miller—who once told him Trump’s powers “will not be questioned”—will operate as chief of staff. In a previously unreported part of a past interview, Whipple asked Miller: “Would you agree, though, that it’s also the chief of staff’s job to tell the president what he doesn’t want to hear?” Miller replied: “No, I wouldn’t say that.”

The Shadow First Lady: MS NOW reporters Felicia Schwartz and Vaughn Hillyard profile Marc Beckman, the curious “exclusive senior adviser” to Melania Trump who has no diplomatic experience—or even security clearance—but wields mighty power over US policy in Ukraine and Russia.

#3461. I’d Love To Know If Michael Weatherly Will Return To NCIS Full Time, And Wilmer Valderrama Shared His Take

After the cancellation of NCIS: Tony & Ziva last year, Michael Weatherly is back on the Mothership as Tony DiNozzo for Season 24 on the 2026 TV schedule. While Tony was initially in D.C. to expand his security company, he wound up becoming the newest NCIS director following Vance’s death last season. Even though it seems like this could be a permanent ordeal, nothing on NCIS is predictable. So, I would love to know if he’d ever go back to being on the show full time. Now, Wilmer Valderrama has shared his take.

Since Tony is now the director of NCIS, and he’s actually doing a pretty decent job so far, I can’t help but wonder if this could turn into a more permanent role for him. While speaking with USA Today, Valderrama, who joined NCIS right after Weatherly left, weighed in on his potential to return next season, saying:

I mean, I don’t have any information on that. It really, truly is up to the fans. The fans dictate so much of what NCIS does. And that’s one thing that I think the fans should always know that we’re always listening, and that whatever they want, we’re going to do our best to bring it to life. If it works for people and people like the dynamic, I have no doubt he will be here beyond it. Why wouldn’t you?

It’s hard to predict how things will go next season when we don’t even know if there is going to be a next season. However, while NCIS has not been renewed for Season 25 yet, considering the show and franchise’s popularity, it feels highly likely. Plus, Tony has been a fan-favorite character since the very beginning, and his return seemed to have helped put NCIS on top in the ratings. So, keeping him around would make perfect sense.

For now, though, Valderrama is just excited about what's happening in the current season. In fact, he reflected on working with Weatherly and how special it's been, considering his entrance on the show happened because his now-co-star had departed:

Every time that someone iconic from the show [returns] 10 years later, having the opportunity to share the screen with Michael, who was obviously such a massive, fundamental part of NCIS, was kind of like a really great full-circle [moment] for us to be on the same screen together and do scenes together, considering that his departure opened the door for my arrival, and now we can share the screen and co-lead the show together is pretty great.

It’s been fun to not only see Weatherly back on NCIS but to see him interact with cast members he’s never crossed paths with before, including Valderrama. Of course, I’ve loved seeing Tony’s reunion with McGee and Jimmy, too.

I also love that because Tony is in charge of NCIS now, he has the chance to have so many different relationships with everyone at the organization. Now, I just hope we'll get to continue to see his relationships develop over the course of multiple seasons.

For now, though, NCIS is still early in its 24th season, and I'm sure they have lots of surprises planned. The series took its time in finding the right replacement for director after Vance’s death, and since NCIS has now set up McGee’s future as SECNAV, I can’t think of anyone other than Tony who would be a good fit.

So, here's hoping he sticks around long-term. While we wait to see if that happens, you can catch new episodes of NCIS on Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET on CBS, streaming the next day with a Paramount+ subscription.

#3460. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3459. Russell Brand's Ex-GF Claims Star Married Katy Perry for 'Fame' in New Doc

Russell Brand‘s ex Jordan Martin has alleged that the disgraced comedian once told her he “always wanted” to marry someone famous before dating his future wife Katy Perry.

“[Russell was] doing exactly what he always wanted to do [with Perry] and be married to someone famous, which he always said he would be,” Martin claimed in the new Netflix documentary Russell Brand: Open Secret.

Martin reportedly dated Brand, 51, for several months in 2007 while he was filming his breakthrough movie, Forgetting Sarah Marshall. In the documentary, Martin recalled that Brand summoned her to the movie’s set in Hawaii because he “wanted someone there to stop him from ‘trying it on’ with people on set,” per Page Six.

“He said to me I should be dating somebody more famous than you,” Martin recalled.

She accused Brand of turning their Hawaiian vacation into a traumatic experience by complaining that she was “dressing like an attention-seeking tart” and insisting he “didn’t feel comfortable” with her sunbathing.

Us has reached out to Brand and Perry’s representatives for comment.

Brand tied the knot with Perry, 42, in India in October 2010. Their marriage proved to be short-lived as he allegedly texted Perry a mere 14 months later in late 2011 to announce he was filing for divorce.

The “Watch It Burn” singer’s raw reaction to Brand’s devastating text message was caught on camera as she was filming her 2012 documentary Katy Perry: Part of Me at the time.

“In the very beginning of me getting into the industry, I would be out and about and I would hear girls, or actresses or musicians or whatever, they would say, ‘Oh no, I don’t want to be in a relationship because I don’t want to have to choose between being in a relationship and having a career,’” Perry explained in Part of Me. “I thought to myself, ‘Pfft, when I find that person that’s going to be my life partner, I will never have to choose because they’ll be accepting of me completely. … They won’t be threatened or have weird motives.’”

She continued, “[My partner] will be accepting of me, the things I love, the ambition, what I aspire to, what I want to create. They’ll be accepting and supportive. I started to realize, ‘Oh my God, that’s not true. That fairytale I had for me is not true for me right now.’”

In another unguarded moment, Perry insisted that she’d done “everything it takes to not fail” in her marriage to Brand.

“[The marriage] still failed,” she lamented. “The bad that comes along with the good is a journey and I learned so much from that journey.”

In a 2013 Vogue interview, Perry alleged that Brand struggled to see her as an “equal” when they were together.

“I felt a lot of responsibility for [the marriage] ending, but then I found out the real truth, which I can’t necessarily disclose because I keep it locked in my safe for a rainy day,” she teased at the time. “I let go and I was like: This isn’t because of me; this is beyond me.’ So I have moved on from that.”

Brand has also spoken publicly about his marriage breakdown over the years, including claiming on his “Stay Free With Russell Brand” podcast in 2025 that Perry was “not entirely normal.”

“She’s an extraordinary, massive star­ — but she’s not weird or off key,” he said at the time. “And wasn’t involved in anything nefarious, as far as I could tell. … The reasons that a marriage didn’t work are the normal human reasons [why] marriages don’t work, and I have nothing but respect for her.”

However, the Get Him to the Greek actor reacted harshly to Perry’s newfound romance with former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, calling the politician a “globalist stooge.”

“I was OK with Orlando Bloom, but Justin Trudeau? Come on, man! Don’t put me in a category with that guy,” he sniped at a December 2025 Turning Point USA event.

Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison on Monday, November 9, after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He is being held in HMP Wandsworth in South London. (The comedian was accused of multiple instances of sexual abuse between 2004 and 2009 by four women.)

In the wake of the verdict, London’s Metropolitan Police confirmed to Us that its officers were investigating additional rape allegations made by two unidentified women.

“The suspect has previously been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations,” a Met spokesperson stated. “Files have been submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service in relation to both complainants.”

Brand has always maintained his innocence and has denied ever having nonconsensual sex.

#3458. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

We’re just a week away from seeing one of our most anticipated book-to-screen adaptations, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, and in the lead-up to it, the book’s author Suzanne Collins has finally weighed in on the movie. She had a lot to say, but I was especially touched by her shout-out to original Haymitch actor, Woody Harrelson.

Suzanne Collins is not a producer on the new prequel, but she’s seen the film, and now she’s “singing its praises”. In a letter shared by Lionsgate, the bestselling author called Sunrise on the Reaping “an extraordinary film” that “maintains the book’s narrative and themes, while bursting with his own distinctive style.” Along with complimenting the whole filmmaking team for bringing her story to life, she also took the time to say this:

I can’t say enough about [Woody Harrelson’s] masterful depiction of Haymitch in the original films. Knowing only scant details of his backstory, he intuitively filled in the emotional journey of the character with a pitch perfect performance. Being free of any conflict between page and screen made the job of writing his youthful trials much easier.

Harrelson’s Haymitch has long been an unforgettable part of The Hunger Games movies, and it’s great to see the book’s author giving the actor his flowers. Haymitch only had about 30 minutes of screen time in the first four films, and yet he made a huge impact with his performance. Even when I’ve gone back to the books, it’s been impossible to think about the character without picturing Harrelson. It sounds like the same can be said for Collins when she decided to write Haymitch's own Hunger Games story with Sunrise on the Reaping.

The Sunrise on the Reaping movie certainly wouldn’t have been possible without the kind of impression Woody Harrelson made with Haymitch, and I love to see Collins recognizing this. Here’s how she continued:

Woody’s return to reprise his character, along with our amazing original stars, Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson, adds such poignancy to the film. It’s such a gift to watch them bridge Haymitch’s Hunger Games to Katniss’s tale.

Now, if you’ve read the book, you know that Haymitch, Katniss and Peeta from the timeline after The Hunger Games ends are part of the story. Last year, it was reported that Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson would be back before Lawrence confirmed she’d reunited with both Hutcherson and Harrelson in the new movie. Collins added a big thank you to the actors for returning to Panem to help tell the story of her novel. We can’t wait to see it take place on the big screen.

While Woody Harrelson gets to briefly reprise his role, the movie is carried by a new actor, Joseph Zada, who stars as a young Haymitch. The 21-year-old has spoken about how he got into character, and it sounds like it's paid off given all the early praise Zada has received already.

Sunrise on the Reaping is Joseph Zada’s movie, but I appreciate the attention Collins gave to Woody Harrelson and his excellent performance as the original version of the character. Now, to see Haymitch's story, you can catch Sunrise on the Reaping in theaters on November 20.

#3456. ‘La Bola Negra’ Defied Hollywood’s Expectations—and Made Movie Stars out of Miguel Bernardeau and Guitarricadelafuente

In 1936, Federico García Lorca, the Spanish poet and playwright, was working on a new play, La Bola Negra, which was never completed. Only four pages of it were found. Later that year, the 38-year-old homosexual anti-fascist sympathizer was executed during the Spanish Civil War on the orders of right-wing military authorities. Ninety years later, Spanish directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi have crafted a new, ambitious film named after these scant remnants. Their glamorous but gritty film stars Spaniards Miguel Bernardeau, of Elite fame, along with Álvaro Lafuente Calvo, the singer known as Guitarricadelafuente, in his first major acting role. La Bola Negra is an epic that spans close to a century; it follows several gay men whose lives are bound together by their identities, love and loss, and the looming presence of the Spanish Civil War, all under the shadow of García Lorca’s work.

There are works of art that escape definitions, pieces of media that transcend. La Bola Negra, both the film and the play, is a biography and a document of war; a love story and a tale of generational trauma; an examination of queerness in Spanish history. The film contains stories that speak of fear, of desire, of guilt, and of shame. And it is a work that defies the easy summary of a logline.

“So you would like us to craft that sentence for you,” Bernardeau, 29, says, laughing while sitting next to Guitarricadelafuente at a restaurant in Manhattan. He’s athletic and handsome. He comes across as a classic macho onscreen, perhaps a residue of the characters he’s been cast as, but in person he is softer and warm, thoughtful. His hair is cut in a shaggy semi-mullet, and he’s wearing a Dolce & Gabbana black T-shirt featuring a young Monica Bellucci, a vintage find.

“It’s a movie that when you finish it, it makes you want to live,” Guitarricadelafuente, 29, says. His curly hair spills over his forehead onto his wire-frame eyeglasses. As Guitarrica—a diminutive for guitar in Aragonese (his family has roots in Aragon) and his stage-name shorthand—he sings about romance and sex, mixing the sounds of Spanish tradition with the synths and reverberations of pop. Like Bernardeau, he’s disarmingly attractive, but his persona is more open. Not unlike their characters, Bernardeau appears more stoic, as if he’s standing on firmer ground; Guitarrica is lighter on his feet and bashful, perhaps settling into the newness of being a movie star.

“Not to be dramatic,” Guitarrica continues, “but people, friends that have seen the movie with us, it takes them a moment to compose themselves after,” he says. “Like, fuck, it’s an intense film. I think it makes you want to live and not do anything half-hearted.” Bernardeau looks at his costar with admiration and utters a line from the film: “Nadie desaparece del todo” (No one disappears completely). “It’s a phrase that Rafael says that keeps coming back to me,” he says.

With the enormity of approaching García Lorca, an idol for Spaniards, a paragon for writers, and a hero for queer men, Calvo and Ambrossi (both modern versions of all these things) were not bold enough to attempt to complete La Bola Negra. Instead they built an affecting universe around it, drawing inspiration from it and other works by García Lorca, as well as co-writer Alberto Conejero’s La Piedra Oscura. The latter was itself loosely inspired by Rafael Rodríguez Rapún, a companion of García Lorca and a member of his theater troupe, who died as a soldier during the civil war.

The film tells three stories: that of Sebastián (Guitarrica) in 1937, a young trumpeter taken into the Nationalist army who encounters Rafael (Bernardeau) as a new prisoner put under his watch; of Carlos (Milo Quifes) in 1932, the lead character in García Lorca’s original play and a young gay man who is denied membership to a casino club because of his sexuality; and in 2017, of Alberto (Carlos González), a modern-day historian who, following the death of his grandfather and an excavation into his past, finds himself indelibly connected to the other men. In Carlos’s vignette, club members vote on his admission using black and white balls, where a black ball (la bola negra) signifies a negative. When Carlos receives several, he has to confront his father. The tension between shame and confession becomes the heart of the film.

Sebastián is a character who is, as Guitarrica puts it, “like a custom-made suit” for him. He ran into Ambrossi and Calvo after performing at the Primavera Sound festival in Barcelona two years ago. “It was one of those nights where, after a few drinks, you kind of forget what was said,” he says with a laugh. But he heard from Calvo after that, and soon he was in Madrid meeting with the directors. “I thought they’d ask me to make a song for the soundtrack,” he says. Instead they told him they were writing a film with Conejero, and offered him the role of Sebastián. “I wasn’t confident at all, nothing was clear,” Guitarrica says, “but I saw the faith they had in me.”

Bernardeau, who was invited to audition for Rafael, also had his doubts. “I didn’t think I did well,” Bernardeau says of his audition. “I was like damn, I missed the opportunity of a lifetime.” But after a week and a half of self-inflicted torture, he was asked to read with Guitarrica and was then offered the role. He was sure about his costar: “The choice of Álvaro made perfect sense,” he says.

Bernardeau and Guitarrica were familiar with each other’s work. “But we met as Sebastián and Rafael,” Bernardeau says. These days they appear to have the kind of friendship, of reverence for each other, of two men who’ve gone to war together—even if just on camera.

Despite its hefty emotional punch and astonishing staging, La Bola Negra is a film about war. Human stories are its spoils, and the unrealized potential of lost lives is buried on the battlefields. The Spanish Civil War still looms darkly over the country. Their dead, from unknown soldiers to acclaimed names like García Lorca, have become Spain’s ghosts.

“I felt a ton of responsibility,” Bernardeau says of playing Rafael, with his connection to a real person. “There is a responsibility in telling the story of someone who is no longer here,” he says. “By making this film, I found that he is important to many people, and I didn’t know that.” Bernardeau knew of García Lorca much like anyone who learns about their home country’s foremost literary giants in school, but the life of Rafael perhaps eluded the textbooks. (Ambrossi and Calvo gave him a reading list, and Bernardeau got to work.)

For Guitarrica, the process was more internal. The character of Sebastián was crafted for him, which afforded him the license to find himself in the role, he says, and consider history by imagining what it would have been like to have lived it.

“There was a lot of introspection,” he says. Guitarrica was also learning how to arrive at certain emotions “and unearth my own experiences to be able to give nuance to my character,” he says. Back in Madrid, during that first meeting with the directors, they asked him if he had any emotional traumas. “I said no, and they said, we’ll see,” he says, laughing. Acting, Guitarrica has found, means excavating old wounds. Did he encounter any turmoil? “Well, yes,” he laughs, “but I’m not telling you about that.”

Since the film premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in May and received a 20-minute standing ovation, with Ambrossi and Calvo winning the award for best direction (alongside Fatherland director Pawel Pawlikowski), Bernardeau and Guitarrica have covered magazines in Spain and beyond and become two of the internet’s latest fixations. La Bola Negra will also represent Spain in the best international feature film category at the Academy Awards, should it be nominated.

“I love that it’s a story that we feel is so ours, that is such a fundamental part of our society and our collective imagination,” Bernardeau says. “The war has impacted us through generations, and it is part of us in different ways.”

He says he doesn’t want to romanticize, but the global reception of such a regional story has given him some faith in humanity. “Because, in the end, it shows that we’re all different, but all the same; that the most personal is also the most creative,” he says, making sure I know that he’s quoting a phrase attributed to Martin Scorsese.

“I think that this film is largely about an idea that is pretty straightforward,” Guitarrica says. “Simply, it’s about the drive to live. Of not leaving anything on the table or unfinished. And that is a very universal story.”

#3455. Virgin River's Shocking Exits Over the Years: Biggest Cast Changes

Virgin River has gone through a surprising amount of cast exits through the years.

Based on Robyn Carr’s book series, Virgin River follows the lives of residents living in a small town in Northern California, including Mel (Alexandra Breckenridge) and Jack (Martin Henderson). The hit series, which premiered in 2019, also stars Colin Lawrence, Annette O’Toole, Tim Matheson, Benjamin Hollingsworth, Sarah Dugdale, Zibby Allen and Kai Bradbury.

After seven seasons, there have been some major departures from the Netflix show. Grayson Gurnsey left as Ricky after season 4, and Mark Ghanimé, who played Cameron, had a surprising exit once season 6 was released.

“I think this season saw a little bit of a sendoff for Cameron,” showrunner Patrick Sean Smith exclusively told Us Weekly in December 2024. “In terms of Mark, the actor who I adore, he unfortunately won’t be coming back for season 7.”

Smith didn’t rule out a potential return for the character in the future. “But that’s not to say that Cameron’s not a part of our world forever,” he added. “I would love to bring him back, and bring his character back when the story presents itself.”

In March 2026, Virgin River returned for season 7, and it was later confirmed that Marco Grazzini will not reprise his role as Mike. In another twist, Lauren Hammersley, who has played Charmaine since the show premiered, is also not expected to come back for season 8.

“For me, I’m just trying to look [at] the longevity of the show and making sure that the characters that we’re keeping have enough story engine in them to keep going,” Smith told Deadline at the time. “So I can’t say there are any specific cast shakeups planned, but I think we will have to start to — as characters run their course — make some decisions and bring in some new blood.”

The show was renewed for season 9 before season 8 premiered on Netflix.

Keep scrolling for the biggest Virgin River cast exits through the years:

Paige played a central role in the first season, but Lexa Doig’s role decreased and the character was ultimately written off by season 4.

Lynda Boyd left the show in season 3 when Lilly was killed.

After playing Ricky since Virgin River debuted in 2019, Grayson Gurnsey exited in season 4 as his character joined the Marines. He briefly returned, but Ricky hasn’t been mentioned since season 6.

Cameron was introduced in season 4 and appeared in two seasons before being written off the show.

Season 7 solved the mystery of Charmaine’s kidnapping. It was later confirmed that Lauren Hammersley wouldn’t be reprising her role going forward.

#3454. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

Since Henry Cavill hasn’t been part of the upcoming DC release slate in a few years, I thought we’d finally put to rest his infamous mustache-gate. However, I just learned the actor isn’t only back in a mustache for Movember; he’s also bringing attention to the Justice League controversy-turned-meme for a new brand partnership. Color me surprised.

Cavill has been quiet lately as he works on the Voltron and Highlander movies, along with being hard at work on the Warhammer 40K series he’s passionate about getting right. Last week, though, he launched a collaboration with Googlebook where he talks about his storied history with his mustache directly, saying “What I know is mustache injustice!” in a series of commercials promoting the laptop. So, what’s going on? Per the actor:

When Google approached me to start conversations about this, they had a concept in mind. And then, obviously, the important thing is to showcase the features of Googlebook, but we also wanted to have a lot of fun with it as well. I wanted to lean as much as possible into poking fun at me.

If you’re somehow unfamiliar with Henry Cavill’s mustache-gate, let me give you a history lesson. So, the actor decided to grow a glorious mustache for his role in Mission: Impossible - Fallout. But then, suddenly, he was called back to work on Justice League for reshoots while he was still obligated to do work on the MI movie.

This caused conflict between the two productions because the Fallout director didn’t want Cavill wearing a fake mustache to complete the film. Ultimately, it was decided he’d play Superman with his mustache on, and it was removed in post-production with CGI. The Witcher actor has said he wouldn’t have grown the mustache if he’d known the reshoots were going to happen. Anyways, check out the commercial where he makes fun of the viral Hollywood story:

Yeah… this is hilarious. In the commercial, Cavill creates his own '80s-inspired video game on his Googlebook called Mustache Protocol using Google Antigravity. The concept of the video game is that you play as a mustachioed Henry Cavill on a mission to stop rogue CGI artists from erasing all the mustaches in the world. In an interview with Inverse, the former Superman actor also said this:

During the Justice League release, the theatrical release, there was obviously that very strong meme going around of me, both mustachioed and mustache-less. And we thought that was a great idea to just have a good giggle. It hasn't really ever gone away, that joke. And so we thought, let's lean into it and let's have some fun while we showcase the incredible features of Googlebook.

The memes were certainly strong around Henry Cavill’s mustache for a while. Someone even added the stache back to Justice League. The whole thing has never left the mainstream, and the actor has even kept the jokes going in recent years with his subsequent projects.

And, still, I’m surprised this happened. I applaud Henry Cavill for this hilarious brand partnership, because it’s kind of genius. Oh, and it’s for a good cause, too. Google is donating $11 to support awareness and funding for men's mental health, suicide prevention, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer in honor of Movember for all who play Mustache Protocol. Just another reason he’ll always be Superman to us.

#3452. Why Batman: The Animated Series Chose Man-Bat As Its First Villain

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Batman: The Animated Series" is darker than most superhero cartoons before and since — literally darker. Drawn on black paper, "Batman: The Animated Series" presents Gotham City like an art deco painting mixed with an old Hollywood crime movie. But it wasn't only gangsters that went bump in the night. The very first episode, "On Leather Wings," uses one of the most out-there Batman villains: Man-Bat, aka zoologist Kirk Langstrom (Marc Singer), transformed by a potion into a half-man/half-bat creature like a winged werewolf.

Debuting in 1970's "Detective Comics" #400 by Frank Robbins and Neal Adams, Man-Bat had 20+ years of comics history behind him when "On Leather Wings" was made. But for non-comic fans, that episode would be the first time they'd seen him. According to "Batman: The Animated Series" co-creator Bruce Timm, that's exactly why he was the pilot's villain. In "Modern Masters Volume 3: Bruce Timm," he recounted:

"Man-Bat was chosen specifically [for the first episode] because he wasn't familiar to very many people outside of comic book fans. Nobody had any preconceived notions about him. It wasn't like the Joker, where you had to deal with people expecting him to be Jack Nicholson or Cesar Romero."

"On Leather Wings" was written by Mitch Brian, who had also developed the "Batman" series bible. What became "On Leather Wings" originated as an episode premise in that bible, though with the gruesome detail that Man-Bat was killing tourists, which isn't in the episode as made. Brian has said he pushed for Man-Bat to give the series a dash of the fantastical right off the bat (no pun intended) — "Batman: The Animated Series" could do not just film noir, but also Universal Horror-esque mad science and monsters.

Man-Bat as Batman's first villain also carries narrative symmetry. His moniker is a twist on Batman's own and he takes Batman's mission to "become a bat" one step further. "Man-Bat kind of works because he's literally the reverse of Batman and he's also got the obsessive interest in bats," said Bruce Timm in "Modern Masters."

Now, technically, Catwoman's debut episode "The Cat and the Claw" premiered first on September 5, 1992, one day earlier than "On Leather Wings" did. "Batman Returns," starring Michelle Pfeiffer as Catwoman, had hit theaters that past summer. (Currently, "The Cat and the Claw" is also listed as the first episode of "Batman: The Animated Series" on HBO Max.) But, functionally, "On Leather Wings" is a much better pilot episode — because that's what it was made to be.

It also demonstrated that "Batman: The Animated Series" was more than just a movie tie-in, down to the choice of villain. In "I Am The Night: The Ultimate Unauthorized History of Batman Series," author Daniel Dockery notes a villain like Man-Bat would've been "nigh impossible to pull off in live-action." Remember, this was 1992, a year before "Jurassic Park" unlocked the potential of CGI. A human-sized bat monster? And an action scene where it flies through Gotham with Batman towed behind it on a rope? Yeah, in the 1990s, a live-action "Batman" movie that even attempted any of that would look ridiculous. But in a cartoon, it was thrilling, and proved "Batman: The Animated Series" was a canvas for unique Batman stories.

Starting with "On Leather Wings" also highlights another tenet from the aforementioned "Batman" series bible: no origin story episodes, because the audience already knew Batman's origin from decades of prior "Batman" comics, movies, and cartoons.

During "On Leather Wings," the police mistake Man-Bat for Batman (Kevin Conroy) and hunt the Dark Knight instead. This premise rests on Gotham City already knowing Batman, which is only possible because the series starts in media res with Batman as an experienced crimefighter. The first time we see Batman is deliberately unspectacular; he's sitting in the Batcave, in costume, reading a newspaper article about the Man-Bat attacks.

The "Batman is framed" subplot also demonstrates that this isn't the Adam West show where Batman is literally deputized by the police and trusted by all of Gotham as a paragon of justice. Many people are already scared of Batman, so it's not a huge leap to blame him for Man-Bat's attacks. (The series' movie spin-off, "Batman: Mask of the Phantasm," even used a nigh-identical story, with Batman being mistaken for the film's eponymous villain.)

Turning Man-Bat's identity into a mystery differs from his first appearance in the comics. There, we meet Man-Bat as Langstrom first and see his gradual and tragic transformation. Mitch Brian compared Man-Bat to "The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde," and by making "On Leather Wings" a mystery, it brings Man-Bat closer to that book. It also, crucially, allows Batman to act as a detective. The twist of Man-Bat being Langstrom works because, again, he's not a villain most of the audience already knew inside-and-out.

Artist Kevin Nowlan, who had drawn a Man-Bat story in DC's "Secret Origins" #39, was initially recruited to design the villain. (See his concept art above.) Bruce Timm's finalized design includes his characters' standard broad upper chest, which fits well with Man-Bat's arms growing out into wings. In form and function, Man-Bat was the perfect pilot villain for "Batman: The Animated Series."

#3450. 'Chicago Fire' Actress Robyn Coffin Announces Breast Cancer Diagnosis

Chicago Fire actress Robyn Coffin is expected to undergo surgery after being diagnosed with breast cancer.

“Robyn has been diagnosed with breast cancer. Terrible news,” a statement on her GoFundMe page read. “The good news – she has a crack team at the hospital organizing and planning her surgery and aftercare and recovery.”

Coffin set up the fundraising page with friend Gianine DeFrancesco in hopes of supporting the actress through her upcoming operation and recovery. An initial fundraising goal has been set at $75,000, with more than $15,000 already raised as of publication.

“When Robyn doesn’t work, she doesn’t get paid,” DeFrancesco clarfied via GoFundMe. “So, this go fund me is not only to fill in the gaps that insurance will surely leave, but also to help sustain Robyn and [her husband] Grant while Robyn is off work. Thank goodness they have insurance, but let’s not get cocky – let’s give them a nest egg because we know there will be surprises.”

Coffin is expected to have a right partial mastectomy with magseed localization on December 3, followed by a course of radiation. First, she will meet with her care team on November 24 to make a final decision on whether a partial or full mastectomy will be the best treatment option.

“If that visit results in affirming the right partial mastectomy, Robyn is expecting to be out of work for 3 weeks,” DeFrancesco explained. “If a full mastectomy is required, Robyn’s time off work will increase quite a bit, as the surgery is much more extensive.”

Fans were assured in the fundraising appeal that Coffin will be able to count on her “husband Grant and supportive friends [as] wonderful caregivers.”

“We know that with insurance the surgery and hospital bill will amount to $40k. Because the surgery is hard upon, this amount is most urgent. The balance is for said surprises: a longer recovery period (see not working), medicine off the plan or not fully covered, or whatever is thrown at them,” DeFrancesco noted. “So, Village – thank you in advance for embracing Robyn with love and support. We’ve got her!”

Coffin’s Chicago Fire costar Miranda Rae Mayo shared a link via Instagram to the GoFundMe page to encourage donations, writing, “This beautiful and wonderful woman is in need of support. You may know her as Cindy Herrmann on our show. Any and everything helps.”

Mayo, 36, and fellow Chicago Fire cast member Hanako Greensmith — who play Stella Kidd and Violet Mikami, respectively — personally donated to help fund Coffin’s treatment.

Coffin is best known for playing Captain Christopher Herrmann‘s (David Eigenberg) wife Cindy Hermann on NBC’s long-running procedural hit Chicago Fire, having recurred or guest starred in each of the show’s 15 seasons. (The character also crossed over to Chicago Med for a 2016 episode.)

Having appeared in more than 60 episodes of Chicago Fire, Cindy’s most memorable story line involved her being diagnosed with lung cancer in season 11. Cindy underwent a grueling regimen of chemotherapy and radiation treatments before being declared cancer-free at the end of the season.

Coffin has also made supporting appearances on many hit shows throughout her career, including Empire and Under Covers.

#3449. Mads Mikkelsen Delivered His Best Performance In This Unforgettable 2012 Movie

Few European actors have found the blend of native and international success that Mads Mikkelsen has. Born in Denmark, he became a star in his home country during the 1990s and 2000s, his career kicking off with Nicolas Winding Refn's 1996 crime thriller "Pusher." He's since become a favorite of Hollywood productions, too, starting with his role as the Bond villain Le Chiffre in "Casino Royale."

Since then, Mikkelsen has remained a go-to Hollywood bad guy, appearing in blockbusters like Marvel Studios' "Doctor Strange." He's also one of the privileged few to have played arguably the most famous screen villain ever, Hannibal Lecter. More than a few would argue Mikkelsen's Lecter in the 2013 TV series "Hannibal" is even better than Anthony Hopkins in "The Silence of the Lambs."

Mikkelsen's razor-sharp cheekbones, intense stare, and European accent instantly code him as "villain" in Hollywood language. When "Rogue One: A Star Wars Story" cast him as Galen Erso, a sympathetic scientist conscripted into building the Death Star, it read as casting against type to American audiences. But look at Mikkelsen's Danish resume and you'll find he's a much more diverse actor than the box that Hollywood has stuck him inside. Amusingly, one of those movies — Thomas Vinterberg's "The Hunt" — stars Mikkelsen as a good man mistakenly persecuted as a villain.

Lucas (Mikkelsen) is a Danish kindergarten teacher. One of his students, his best friend Theo's (Thomas Bo Larsen) daughter Klara (Annika Wedderkopp), has a puppy love crush on him. Obviously, he gently turns her down. Klara then vengefully suggests to the school principal that Lucas exposed himself to or molested her. (In reality, as the movie shows, her crude older brother shoved an iPad displaying porn in her face.) The ugly rumor grows out of control, and Lucas' reputation pays the price.

In "The Hunt," the town rushes to the worst possible conclusion about Lucas. All but a few loved ones like his son, Marcus (Lasse Fogelstrøm), believe the worst from hearsay. But they don't actually know it for a fact (indeed, what ultimately helps clear Lucas is the facts pointing in his favor). The movie is never ambiguous, though; we know from the very beginning that Lucas is innocent and this is all just a terrible tragedy of miscommunication. "The Hunt" also avoids reactionary narratives about scorned women peddling false rape allegations because Klara is a young child. She simply doesn't grasp the consequences of what she did, as is the case with the other preschoolers who echo her claims.

Compare a similar recent film, "Fjord," inspired by a real-life story about a Norwegian evangelical couple whose children were taken from them after suspicions of abuse. Like in "The Hunt," the allegations are implied to stem from leading questions and miscommunication from the kids. But "Fjord" counterintuitively stacks the deck in the parents' favor while trying to present objectivity, perhaps because it knows many left-leaning audiences are inclined to side against the conservative couple and takes perverse enjoyment in testing those sympathies.

A film like "The Hunt" could choose not to reveal Lucas' innocence either way or cast doubt, inviting you to sympathize with a possible monster as an endurance test. But the reality of "The Hunt," seeing an innocent man be branded with a scarlet letter, is also agonizing to watch in its own way. It's a modern iteration on the parable of the feathers in the wind, and how once spoken, even untruthful gossip can't be erased.

As Lucas, Mikkelsen sheds any of the power or menace he projects as a villain in those aforementioned Hollywood movies. "The Hunt" is also a Danish-language film, and Mikkelsen's comfort with his native tongue also makes for an even more seamless performance.

To this day, I've never forgotten the catharsis of a scene where Lucas stands up for himself. After being assaulted in a grocery store, he walks in again, headbutts the hostile clerk, and demands his groceries back. The first time I watched "The Hunt," I rewound the movie to see the scene a second time.

That relatively late-in-the-movie scene is a well-earned respite from Lucas' victimhood. Even in a story like this, too much passivity from a protagonist turns into a chore. Lucas similarly takes matters into his own hands at the movie's emotional climax. Again, Klara's father Theo is Lucas' best friend; while Theo takes Klara's side, he claims to know Lucas so well he can tell when he's lying or truthful by just looking into his eyes. Lucas goes to Christmas Mass, putting himself dead center in the community that has exiled him, and looks at Theo across the pews.

The power of this lynchpin scene is in Mikkelsen's silent, icy stare (Lucas pointedly ditches his glasses during this scene). But it's not the aloof stare of Le Chiffre or the predatory one of Hannibal Lecter. In his sad eyes and slight frown, Lucas is begging Theo to read the truth on his face. When that's not enough, he storms over to Theo, sobbing, and refuses to let him look away from his eyes.

Mads Mikkelsen is an extraordinary actor, and yet the greatest proof of that is him playing a normal man in "The Hunt."

#3448. I Avoided 'It's A Small World' For Over A Decade Because Of That Song, But Disneyland's Holiday Version Won Me Over

Disneyland will always be a magical place, but there is something particularly magical during the holiday season. The lights, the fake snow (because this is Southern California), the trees, the food, and the music all make it extra special this time of year. I have been to Disneyland more times than I can count, but there is one ride I have avoided for over a decade: It's a Small World.

It's not that I don't like the ride. It's just that if I hear that earworm-inducing song, even just the first note, I will have it stuck in my head for days, maybe even weeks. However, this was my first time experiencing the ride during the holiday season, and it had me singing a different tune.

First of all, the ride has definitely had a glow-up since the last time I stepped onto the boat. From adding inclusive dolls in wheelchairs and new characters like Coco's Miguel and his alebrije dog, Dante, to adding a third and final verse to the song, there was a lot for me to see and hear. However, the holiday version takes things a whole step further.

If you have never been on this attraction, let me tell you, you are in for a treat. And yes, there is another song that may be just as hard to get out of your head as the original. The holiday version of this ride incorporates none other than "Jingle Bells." Disney knew what they were doing, and surprisingly, I am here for it.

As I took that first bend into the tunnel, with rain coming down on my head, I was greeted by a bright "Happy Holidays" sign before entering the magical, doll-filled world, complete with all the twinkling lights of the season. There are garlands hanging everywhere, toys, presents, floating Christmas trees, and signs in all different languages wishing you happy holidays and a merry Christmas.

I had a chance to chat with one of Disneyland's cast members, Alexa Garcia, about why she loves It's a Small World this time of year. She told us:

Inside, you've got the beautiful music heard in different languages, and it's just such a beautiful message during this time of the year.

I found myself connecting with the music in a way I haven't in quite some time, and I even got a little choked up. Honestly, I think having "Jingle Bells" mixed in with the iconic song throughout really helps.

And then there is the final room, which is truly a showstopper. As the boat takes its final turn, you enter a white winter wonderland with everyone singing "Deck the Halls." It is elaborate, decadent, beautiful, and above all, just really, really cute.

This ride really won me over, and I am so glad I gave it another chance. Otherwise, I would have missed out on all the holiday joy this little boat ride gave me. And with the combination of songs, you actually end up leaving without either of them stuck in your head. At least, that is what happened to me.

While I may not be in a hurry to ride It's A Small World again without its holiday makeover, I encourage everyone visiting Disneyland for the holidays to give it a chance. The holiday celebration runs through January 6, 2027. I guess I'll just have to wait until next Christmas to willingly get back on board.
