#3446. Everything You Should Know About Black Friday 2026 Sales: Early Deals, Dates, and Retailers

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales appear to be becoming a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already put out their plans and even started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this upcoming Black Friday sale a great one. Here is everything you need to know to prepare you for the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers doing sales are the usual: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always vet all of our deals for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

#3445. Nearly a Decade Ago My Friend’s Private Plane Fell Out of the Sky. Then, in Florida This Month, It Happened to Another Friend.

When I was in my late 20s, I lived in the worst building in the best part of SoHo. My apartment above the French restaurant Raoul’s had been created by merging two units, so it was quite spacious. When I decided to move in with my boyfriend in Los Angeles, I still planned to spend a quarter of my time in New York and wasn’t about to give up this gem. But I figured I could find a roommate who would be psyched I wouldn’t be there a ton, and keep the smaller bedroom for myself.

The writer Deborah Schoeneman introduced me to her best friend from Cornell University, who she said would be the perfect roommate. Jen Blumin was a Sex and the City character come to life: a tall, gorgeous blonde who managed a high-end event space with a private pool a few blocks away, mostly for corporate sponsors. I figured she wouldn’t be home much while I was, and told her if she had $1,800 a month, she had a deal. The day she moved in, she gingerly walked up the four flights of stairs carrying a large wrought-iron cage containing a shrieking bird. “Did I not tell you I had a cockatoo?” she asked with such insouciant camp, such mock innocence, that I just had to laugh.

Schoeneman, Grigoriadis, and Blumin in 2010 at Round Hill Resort.

Thus began one of my life’s great friendships, proceeding through many more ripostes, a decade of shared living space, and the birth of two kids each. Jen became wildly successful by turning vacant institutional buildings into heart-stopping event spaces, and even landed the contract for New York Fashion Week at the old post office across from Pennsylvania Station. The love of her life and father of her children, the architect James Ramsey, conceived of an idea with Dan Barasch, another Cornell chum, to create a “low line” under the old Delancy Street trolley terminal, and for a while it seemed like that was going to happen. But the relationship fell apart, and then things move very fast in my memory: Jen started to say she disliked New York City and wanted to live full time in the North Fork, a new boyfriend showed up, now she was moving to Puerto Rico for the climate and tax breaks, then she and the boyfriend were buying a private plane to fly direct from Puerto Rico to Islip, NY.

When I heard about this new acquisition by my far-more successful friend, I have to admit I thought it sounded rad. Private planes occupy an almost mystical place in our culture. You’re up in the skies, free of seatmates chomping tuna sandwiches or annoyances like last-minute checked bags. You’re watching the clouds drift by, close enough to touch God. So what if her plane wasn’t the fanciest! It was still glamorous. As former Vanity Fair editor Tina Brown wrote on her Substack, everyone wants to be your friend when you have a plane: “The late TV legend Barbara Walters used to lament the necessity to vacation every year with the crass termagant CEO of a bra company just because said termagant happened to own her own plane.”

For the wealthy, private planes, which have become increasingly popular as a mode of transportation in recent years, aren’t only the ultimate in seclusion, but also the ultimate in spontaneity. You’re in a power position that’s completely the reverse of commercial flights, which reduce you to helpless nose-boned chattel. If you’re paying the bill, most decisions are controlled by you: You decide when you leave, who to invite, what to eat (certainly not pretzels and ginger ale), and whether there’s space for your three bulldogs.

But the day after Mother’s Day in 2017—which Jen memorialized by sending a group text to myself and the core girlfriends with a snapshot of her two toddlers on a big rock in Puerto Rico—Jen’s private plane fell out of the sky. She was flying with her children about 15 miles east of Eleuthera, an island in the Bahamas, in the Bermuda Triangle. None of them were found.

I think a lot about Jen, but rarely more than now, nearly a decade after her death. That’s because this month, the same set of New York friends—loosely—are mourning another person who died with his family, including two more children under five years old. Adam Robinson, who chartered the Learjet that dove into a Florida road on November 1, leaving hypersurreal audio and video recordings that are now seared into the nation’s collective memory, arrived in New York a little later than Jen. I met him in the mid-2000s, but he seemed to be cut from the same cloth as she was: a tall, gregarious Lehman Brothers trader who had inherited a loft on lower Broadway from our mutual friends, the founders of the website College Humor (there was a lot of apartment swapping in lower Manhattan back then).

Adam was the definition of a “good guy”: smart, kind, and wry at the right moments. He had the open-hearted self-possession of someone who had traveled widely, but now he was in New York City to start his career, which, like so many of us, involved being hyper-social. He was not a close friend, but I was always happy to see him, and would usually spend 10 minutes at a crowded party chatting before moving on (this means a lot if you, like me, ascribe to the Fitzgeraldian notion that large parties provide intimacy, and prefer not to waste your breath in this rarefied milieu on dolts). A few guys in the crowd were into email marketing, and I heard that Adam had started a business in that industry but didn’t know much about his life after he moved to Austin, nor that he, too, had become quite successful.

It’s eerie that Adam’s private plane was headed to Eleuthra, the same area where Jen disappeared. But beyond that coincidence, what I keep returning to is how Jen and Adam’s stage in life had so many similarities: both in their 40s, too early to retire, they had nevertheless entered what you could call the “second phase” of success. They weren’t only trying to make money but to enjoy the money they’d made, and for them, that meant devising a new kind of life. Adam had moved from Austin to Aspen and wanted to pursue more outdoor adventures, some of which involved destinations hard to reach by commercial flights. Jen didn’t need to take her fatal private journey—JetBlue flies direct from San Juan to JFK—but having her own plane definitely came with bragging rights, though neither was the type to post a “flashing a peace sign on a PJ” semi-candid shot on Instagram.

And yet the private plane, so much a symbol of freedom and success for both Jen and Adam, led to their demise. This type of aviation is far less regulated than commercial planes, which hew to “strict government regulations enumerated in hundreds of pages of fine print…everything from the stowing of tray tables to announcements concerning lavatory smoke detectors,” as Jeff Wise wrote in Vanity Fair in 2025. That may be okay when you’re traveling in a $75 million G800, or as a guest of Drake in his $185 million plane, or with Kylie Jenner in her $73 million Bombardier, but when you’re on a small plane, it matters. Wise notes in his story that since 2020, almost half of the private plane crashes in the US have been Citations, which are on the smaller side.

And when traveling in a plane that lacks the sophistication of a commercial jet, whether you’re JFK Jr., Aaliyah, or just two people that everyone in a certain downtown Manhattan set knew in the mid-aughts, weather happens. Bad decisions in the cockpit compound, if the pilots even have time to make them. And then everything you’ve worked so hard for is lost, with the wreckage extending to family members and best friends left behind. “If I was Adam, I would rather be on the plane than on the ground” is the refrain I keep hearing from my friends this week, meaning that they’d rather perish with their families than live without them. Success and its luxuries are wonderful things. But they don’t guarantee you’ll get to come home.

#3444. Is The Rings Of Power Connected To Peter Jackson's Lord Of The Rings Trilogy?

The canon of the "Lord of the Rings" movie and TV franchise has become a little complicated in recent years. Sauron's war finally arrives in "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, and with the show's return, it's worth asking: Is this series canonical to Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" films? We finally have a firm answer, and it's ... sort of (if we read between the lines).

In a recent interview with Screen Rant, "The Rings of Power" co-showrunner Patrick McKay addressed the canon question head-on without giving a simple "yes" or "no" answer. Still he made it pretty clear where things stand, explaining, "There is room in Middle-earth for everybody, and we're fans of those films, and we hope it's great." (He was referring to the already controversial upcoming film "The Hunt for Gollum" with that last bit.)

In terms of the "Lord of the Rings" timeline, "The Rings of Power" is set thousands of years before the "Lord of the Rings" movies. So, in theory, they could work together. Speaking further though, McKay established that the show exists alongside the many interpretations of J.R.R. Tolkien's Middle-earth books over the years and not necessarily as part of any other adaptation (including Jackson's):

"So many talented artists in so many mediums over 75 years have interpreted this material, painted or drawn it, or put it in a song or made it into a film or an animated film. I think to sit on a shelf with all those other works, we are only too delighted for that to be our fate."

He added that the movies and the show are "in conversation with one another." Put simply, then, "The Rings of Power" is not strictly canon within the universe of Jackson's films.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" brings the fabled Second Age of Middle-earth's history to life on-screen for the first time. Therefore, it's centuries removed from both the events of J.R.R. Tolkien's "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings" books and Peter Jackson's film adaptations alike.

Even so, it initially looked like Jackson was going to be involved with "The Rings of Power," only for Amazon to ghost him while developing the Prime Video series. Why? In essence, it was apparently a contractual matter. In a statement issued in 2022, Amazon claimed, "In pursuing the rights for our show, we were obligated to keep the series distinct and separate from the films." So, basically, "The Rings of Power" can't, for legal reasons, be officially canonical to Jackson's movies. Of course, Patrick McKay couldn't just come out and say that, so he found a more diplomatic way to go about it.

Jackson, obviously, is the man that turned "The Lord of the Rings" into the one fantasy franchise to rule them all, as his adaptations of J.R.R. Tolkien's books became massive, beloved hits that have endured for decades. Still, while it makes sense that Amazon would, in theory, want him to work on "The Rings of Power," it seems securing the rights for the show meant sacrifices had to be made.

Nevertheless, Jackson is producing (but not directing) "The Hunt for Gollum," with Gollum actor Andy Serkis helming the movie himself. Warner Bros. is also developing another "LOTR" movie co-written by superfan Stephen Colbert, so this franchise has a future on the big screen as well.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" is streaming now on Prime Video.

Wicker might not get any Oscar recognition (although that would be a pleasant surprise), but I'd argue it's one of the best theater-going experiences of any film released on the 2026 movie schedule. Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård’s unconventional rom-com turned out to be much more than a smutty romance about a perfect man built of wicker. Audiences were won over not only by Skarsgård’s wicker abs, but also his character’s pure heart, leaving many hungry for more, Skarsgård included. And I laughed out loud when I heard the “sequel” he’s been pitching.

Alexander Skarsgård has never been one to take himself too seriously, especially while doing press tours. I can’t say I blame him, doing the same interviews over and over would get pretty old otherwise. However, his effortless deadpan and jesting tendencies make it difficult to sometimes tell if he’s being serious or not, like with this recent pitch to Entertainment Weekly about a Wicker follow-up:

It’s called Corduroy. We tried to find financing for it, but, for some reason, it’s been hard, but we’re pitching it around Hollywood this week.

At this point, I can’t tell if this is a serious pitch or not, but the idea is genuinely hilarious. Skarsgård added that this corduroy character would be “delicate and soft,” as well as an “attentive lover.” I’ve got to be honest, that doesn’t sound as sexy as a sturdily built wicker man, but I get the sense this concept is in very early stages of development. Forget splinters, we’d be wondering about carpet burn.

Seriously, I’m going to need someone to ask the A-lister about this again, because I really need some clarification. Skarsgård is known to joke with the media, even tot he point of teasing a “smear” campaign against his father, Stellan Skarsgård (Sentimental Value) during awards season. However, I wouldn’t put it past him to actually try and get this wild sequel made.

I’m just not fully sold on “Corduroy” for another reason. If your mind went to the same place as mine upon hearing this pitch, you understand why. Yes, I’m talking about the children’s story “Corduroy,” in which a corduroy teddy bear comes to life in a department store. Given Wicker’s salacious content and marketing, it feels really weird to relate the two, and therefore I fear it might be difficult to get that sequel pitch off the ground. However, the Legend of Tarzan actor has been persistent in the idea of a Wicker sequel, and I’m curious to see what that might look like.

This isn’t the first time the Northman actor has pitched a sequel to his latest movie. During the press tour, Skarsgård expressed interest in continuing the Wicker Husband’s story, following questions about what happens at the end of Wicker when the unconventional family of three leaves their village behind.

Clearly, Skarsgård enjoyed playing the wicker sex symbol that has taken the internet by storm, but that’s not surprising. If 2025’s kinky Pillion taught us anything, it’s that Skarsgård isn’t afraid to get a lil freaky (in the best ways) and Wicker seems to have opened a whole new realm of possibilities in his mind.

However, between the wicker husband’s kind heart and the fairytale-like setting that allows this somewhat raunchy, yet overall heartwarming love story to take place, I’m just not sure the same effect would work with a “corduroy husband” or any other textile husband for that matter. I’ll be quite surprised if something along these lines pops up on the 2027 movie schedule, but you can bet I’ll still buy a ticket. In the meantime, check out Wicker in theaters now.

#3442. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.

#3441. Journey Drummer Deen Castronovo Exits Band Mid-Tour Due to 'Health Matters'

Journey is pushing ahead with its Final Frontier Tour following the departure of the band’s longtime drummer, Deen Castronovo.

“After careful consideration and an extensive year of touring, our talented, longtime drummer Deen Castronovo has decided to step away to focus on personal health matters that require his attention,” the “Open Arms” band revealed via a Friday, November 13, statement. “He has our full support during this time and extends his heartfelt thanks to the fans for the love, encouragement, and kindness he has received.”

The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductees have enlisted fill-in drummer Steve Murphy for the remainder of this year’s dates on Journey’s farewell tour.

“Native New Yorker Steve Murphy who comes to us from working with bands such as Alan Parsons Project, Trans Siberian Orchestra, Christopher Cross and Jack Bruce will be joining us for the remainder of November,” the band confirmed via Instagram. “We look forward to continuing to share unforgettable nights of music with all of you.”

Castronovo’s shocking departure from Journey follows two recent incidents where he had to exit the stage mid-performance, forcing his bandmates to rearrange their show on the fly, with drum tech Steve Toomey ultimately filling in on both occasions.

Viral footage captured Journey announcing from the stage at the BOK Center in Tulsa on October 8 that Castronovo was being rushed to the hospital due to a “medical emergency” after performing only 2 songs in a planned 28-song setlist.

“We’re going to see what happens as this progresses,” Journey keyboardist and rhythm guitarist Jonathan Cain explained to fans that night. “It’s an unfortunate situation. We’re very sorry. We’re hoping it’s only a delay, but please — I’m sorry. Don’t worry. Have your prayers ready. Have your prayers ready for Deen Castronovo, everybody. Thank you.”

Journey frontman Arnel Pineda assured fans after an extended break that the drummer was “going to be fine.” Later in the show, lead guitarist Neal Schon dedicated the rest of the Tulsa show to Castronovo.

“This concert’s for Deen tonight,” he told the audience. “I’d love you all to pray for him. Everybody’s been going through a lot. I think he’s going to be fine.”

Castronovo was back on stage with Journey on October 10 at the Frost Bank Center in San Antonio, though he was again rushed from the stage in Boston after performing 12 songs on Tuesday, November 10.

Journey has not disclosed exactly what medical issues Castronovo is dealing with.

Prior to joining Journey in 1998, Castronovo played with singer John Waite and future Journey bandmates Schon, 72, and Cain, 76, in rock supergroup Bad English from 1987 to 1991. He later joined Ozzy Osbourne‘s backing band in 1995.

Journey’s Final Frontier Tour is set to wrap up for the year at the Honda Center in Anaheim on November 24.

#3440. 15 Best Hard Sci-Fi Movies Of All Time, Ranked

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

While science fiction includes everything from space opera to cyberpunk, one sub-genre that we have a special place for is hard sci-fi. These movies place a stronger emphasis on scientific accuracy and a more grounded premise than their more fantastical counterparts. Many of the best sci-fi movies ever are set within the realm of hard sci-fi, heightening the sense of realism to their stories. We're taking a closer look at this fan-favorite sub-genre and our personal favorite movies within it.

While there are varying opinions about what qualifies as hard sci-fi, each of the movies we're including here certainly have a strong scientific grounding. Even some of the best sci-fi movies of 2026 are clear hard sci-fi projects, breathing new life into the sub-genre. With those qualities in mind, these are the best 15 hard sci-fi movies of all time ranked, each offering their own cinematic verisimilitude to the genre.

After "2001: A Space Odyssey," there was "Marooned," with Gregory Peck's space thriller based on the novel of the same name by Martin Caidin. Peck stars as NASA Director Charles Keith who finds himself working on a desperate rescue mission to save three astronauts stranded in orbit. As the incident becomes more public, Keith is forced to use an experimental spacecraft for the rescue, despite it being untested. Meanwhile, the stranded astronauts grow desperate as they begin to run out of oxygen before help arrives.

"Marooned" was released before the Apollo 13 incident, which similarly saw American astronauts seemingly stranded in space. While things like the movie's experimental spacecraft take it to sci-fi territory, the whole thing feels scientifically plausible. At the same time, the movie also keeps a tight focus on the human stakes, including the response back home and the families affected by the incident. Overlooked by audiences today, nearly 60 years later, "Marooned" sets the template for so many subsequent space disaster movies on this list.

A big factor in a lot of hard sci-fi movies is its production budget, because it's far cheaper to make a grounded sci-fi movie than an outlandishly audacious one. That certainly informs the 2004 indie movie "Primer," written, directed, produced, edited, and starring Shane Carruth, who also composed the score. Carruth plays Aaron, an engineer whose colleague Abe (David Sullivan) develops an amateur time machine in their garage. As the duo explore the possibilities of their invention, they progressively experience the dire consequences of time travel.

While "Primer" may look and feel like a lofi time travel movie at first glance, it refreshingly explores its conflict from a well-thought approach. Things like the process' physical toll on the body from its wider ripple effects are smartly explored throughout the story. The production's DIY nature actually suits the narrative well, given the amateur nature of the movie's central plot device. If you haven't seen "Primer" before, the movie is a must-watch for sci-fi movie fans and a tightly constructed one at that.

1997's "Gattaca" is another sci-fi flick that feels eerily plausible for modern society to follow within the next several years. The story is set in a world where eugenics has become widespread to avoid the birth of babies with debilitating genetic conditions. This leads to society discriminating against those who carry genetic defects, including protagonist Vincent Freeman (Ethan Hawke). Posing as a genetically engineered individual, Vincent's ruse comes under scrutiny in the wake of a corporate executive's murder.

Admittedly, "Gattaca" is the most visually stylish movie on this list, but its concept and the level of technology depicted hold a real world weight to them. The science behind the story's genetic engineering and eugenics feels particularly well-developed as the cornerstone of this dystopian society. The movie goes into meticulous detail how Vincent is able to maintain his deception and how this genetic technology has impacted civilization. A dystopian noir look at the perils of artificial perfection, "Gattaca" is a moody flick that makes the most of its premise.

Filmmaker James Cameron's most underrated movie is the 1989 underwater thriller "The Abyss," with its core themes carried over into "Avatar: The Way of Water." The movie has American and Soviet teams racing to salvage a sunken American submarine from the bottom of the ocean. Leading the American expedition is an oil drilling crew headed by Bud Brigman (Ed Harris), only to find otherworldly entities are involved. As the full scope of this mission becomes apparent, Bud tries to stop hostilities from escalating between humanity and this underwater species.

More than just standing as another Cameron project that heavily involves the water, "The Abyss" also showcases his sharp attention to detail. Cameron takes care to demonstrate the real-world dangers of deep-sea exploration, including the high pressure and chilling temperatures of the watery depths. These elements fuel the tension as much as the strange creatures that Bud encounters, along with Cameron's recurring message that unchecked human aggression is the true enemy. Claustrophobically staged and under-appreciated for years, "The Abyss" is Cameron's unsung classic and as grounded his sci-fi work gets.

The first novel that author Michael Crichton published under his own name was 1969's "The Andromeda Strain," which was adapted for the silver screen in 1971. More intelligently assembled than the standard disaster movie fare of its time, the movie opens with a satellite crashing near a small town in New Mexico. After most of the community dies suddenly under mysterious causes, it's discovered that the satellite brought back a highly lethal extraterrestrial microorganism. The movie follows a team of scientists trying to contain the situation before it can wipe out all life on the planet.

Crichton's work tends to succeed the more firmly that they're rooted in reality before expanding into the fantastical. "The Andromeda Strain" is a prime example of this, still packing a punch over 50 years since its debut. That strong scientific approach to the premise underscores the gravity that this threat is terrifyingly plausible. Still one of the best Michael Crichton movie adaptations, "The Andromeda Strain" offers a grounded sci-fi approach to annihilation by contagion.

While the 1972 adaptation of "Solaris" by Soviet filmmaker Andrei Tarkovsky is one of the best space horror movies ever made, it does veer tonally away from Stanisław Lem's novel. By contrast, Steven Soderbergh's 2002 adaptation is more of a drama and an isolated character study, though some existential thriller elements remain. The movie's protagonist is Chris Kelvin (George Clooney), a clinical psychologist who visits a remote space station only to find most of its crew is dead. As Kelvin investigates the situation, he is shocked to be reunited with his late wife Rheya (Natascha McElhone). who is seemingly alive and well.

While it's a close call, Soderbergh's "Solaris" is a sci-fi remake that's better than the original, mostly because of change in tone and Clooney's vulnerable performance. This elevates the movie's ambiguous existential contemplation, while Soderbergh wisely keeps the sci-fi elements relatively stripped down. At its core, the story is a meditation on grief and guilt while Soderbergh builds his story in a relatively grounded outer space setting. Soderbergh's "Solaris" is both his most understated and boldest project, using the mysteries of the cosmos to explore its emotional themes.

The debut feature directorial project by British filmmaker Duncan Jones is the 2009 indie flick "Moon." The movie is largely a one-man show for Sam Rockwell, who plays Samuel Bell, a technician working alone in a lunar mining facility. As Bell nears the end of his three-year assignment, he begins to hallucinate, while his health steadily worsens. This culminates in Bell coming face-to-face with a doppelganger of himself, as he realizes the disturbing truth about his existence.

With its pragmatically minimalist art design and Rockwell being the only actor on-screen for the majority of the movie, "Moon" keeps its storytelling simple but effective. The idea that the Moon could be mined heavily for helium-3 is rooted in fact, while the technology is never particularly outlandish. Like Soderbergh's "Solaris," Jones keeps its narrative focus tightly on his protagonist which is where its real strength lies. An intimately scaled sci-fi thriller, "Moon" remains Duncan's best work to date, using its grounded backdrop to atmospheric effect.

Among the sci-fi movies that nobody talks about anymore is "Silent Running," which was released in 1972. The movie takes place in a future where Earth is no longer capable of supporting trees, forcing humanity to take its forestry off-world. The story is set in a spaceship serving as a large biome for trees, tended to meticulously by botanist Freeman Lowell (Bruce Dern). When the crew is ordered to destroy the biomes by their corporate overseers, Lowell goes through murderous lengths to defend his carefully curated forests.

Of all the movies on this list, "Silent Running" is the one with the most pointed sociopolitical commentary. From its takedown of corporate greed to its eco-friendly themes, the movie feels like both a product of its time and as prescient as ever. Dern is rarely better than in his performance as Lowell, with his character standing as a portrait of single-minded obsession and carrying much of the movie. Unabashedly direct in its messaging, "Silent Running" deserves wider recognition than it receives from the public these days.

Not every hard sci-fi movie needs to unfold in outer space or revolve around high concept narratives. The 2013 romantic drama "Her" is perfectly set within a more intimate scope, given its premise. Taking place in a near-future Los Angeles, loner Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) struggles at forming a meaningful romantic connection with others. Instead, Theodore grows closer to his digital assistant Samantha (Scarlett Johansson) as she gains sentience, with a loving relationship growing between them.

"Her" is the perfect love story for the Information Age, underscoring that technological advances don't necessarily separate us from connecting with others. The movie's premise feels entirely plausible while also being prescient in the decade prior to the widespread proliferation of artificial intelligence. The tightened focus works well, with filmmaker Spike Jonze keeping the "Her" set intimate for Joaquin Phoenix, as he stays awkwardly vulnerable for much of the story. Understated in its tone and scope but still packing an emotional wallop, "Her" is Jonze's humanist masterpiece in an increasingly digital era.

Among the most celebrated hard sci-fi authors of the 20th century was astronomer and science educator Carl Sagan. The 1997 movie "Contact" adapted Sagan's 1985 novel of the same name, detailing humanity's first contact with extraterrestrial life. After astronomer Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster) detects signs of intelligent otherworldly life, the world is galvanized by the discovery. Though Arroway wants to make contact with these mysterious figures through an experimental device, complications quickly arise.

While there is certainly extraterrestrial interaction to be had, "Contact" is more about the reaction and fallout to confirmation of otherworldly life. Jodie Foster brings that thoroughly human response to the subject matter, while her character guides audiences through the story. "Contact" could've been a much stranger movie, treating Sagan and partner Ann Druyan's tale with tone-deaf disregard for scientific accuracy and characterization, but cooler heads won out. One of the best sci-fi movies of the '90s, hard with its science or not, "Contact" is an understated genre gem.

Upon its debut in 2026, "Project Hail Mary" was quickly crowned as one of the best sci-fi movies ever and deservedly so. Based on the best-selling novel by Andy Weir, the movie has our sun plagued by a strange substance threatening to dim it to catastrophic levels within decades. Molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) is forced to join an interstellar expedition searching for a way to restore the sun's output. This leads Grace to team up with a rock-based extraterrestrial on his own mission to save his planet from the threat of the same substance.

"Project Hail Mary" improves upon Andy Weir's book in key ways, streamlining the story and quietly discarding its more superfluous sci-fi elements. But even with its interstellar partnership, the adaptation retains the source material's penchant for scientifically informed storytelling. That grounds the more cosmic elements as Grace finally enacts his last-ditch effort to save his world from chilly annihilation. Keeping hard sci-fi alive and well into the 2020s, "Project Hail Mary" is a bonafide crowd-pleaser.

Still one of Christopher Nolan's most ambitious movies over a decade after its release, "Interstellar" is the filmmaker's most high-flying tale to date. Like "Project Hail Mary" after it, the movie revolves around humanity at the brink of extinction, forced to undertake a desperate mission for its salvation. In the case of Nolan's story, Earth is rocked by severe dust storms affecting its agriculture, with astronaut Coop (Matthew McConaughey) leading an expedition for a habitable planet. This is juxtaposed by Coop's adult daughter Murph (Jessica Chastain) trying to find a way to create a spacecraft capable of launching into deep space through Earth's gravity.

While there are, of course, creative liberties taken through its premise, "Interstellar" boasts a high level of scientific accuracy. This includes the astrophysics propelling the story like the singularity that serves as the key to its spacefaring scope. Everything from planets undergoing significant time dilation to the gravity equation back on Earth all feel feasible, even with all the cinematic splendor. Christopher Nolan always offers a well-thought approach to even the most fantastical subject matter, and "Interstellar" captures those qualities beautifully.

Another British filmmaker who's excelled at smart sci-fi storytelling in the 21st century is Alex Garland. Arguably the hardest sci-fi story Garland has told thus far, and certainly one of the most effective, is the psychological thriller "Ex Machina." The story follows programmer Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) who stays at the remote home of eccentric tech CEO Nathan Bateman (Oscar Isaac). Caleb is tasked with checking the sentience of Bateman's latest creation, a self-aware android known as Ava (Alicia Vikander) only for things to violently go off the rails.

There is an underlying paranoia with existential overtones that permeate throughout "Ex Machina," carrying its narrative forward. Compared to more overtly cyberpunk stories like "Blade Runner," Garland's 2014 flick takes a much more grounded view on androids and the proliferation of artificial intelligence. This is underscored by its special effects, with the "Ex Machina" VFX avoiding green screen use, preferring practical effects and sets for its execution. A cautionary tale about billionaire vanity projects taking on a hostile life of their own, "Ex Machina" is Garland's most prescient work.

Another adaptation of an Andy Weir novel to mention here is 2015's "The Martian," directed and produced by Ridley Scott. The movie is set in a near-future where humanity has established a research station on Mars as part of an international coalition. After the station's team evacuates from the planet during a severe dust storm, astronaut Mark Watney (Matt Damon) is accidentally left behind. Until a rescue mission can be carried out, Watney has to rely on the tools that he has available and his own wits to survive alone on Mars.

Andy Weir gave the 2015 adaptation of "The Martian" his seal of approval, and we do too. The movie is Scott's most buoyantly light, yet it doesn't compromise the scientific know-how behind Watney's prolonged ordeal. Matt Damon has to perform much the movie alone, expertly conveying his character's intellectual reasoning without coming off as overly dry or talking down to the audience. One of the smartest sci-fi blockbusters of the 2010s, "The Martian" treats its premise well while celebrating intelligence to save the day.

One of the most prolific hard sci-fi authors was Arthur C. Clarke, who teamed up with filmmaker Stanley Kubrick for "2001: A Space Odyssey." The 1968 movie traces humanity's evolution through a strange extraterrestrial monolith that first appeared on Earth during prehistoric times. When a monolith found on the Moon transits a signal to Jupiter, an expedition is mounted to investigate further. This voyage is nearly derailed by the malevolent artificial intelligence HAL 9000 (Douglas Rain) running the team's spaceship.

Given Kubrick's exhaustive attention to detail and Clarke's scientific acumen, "2001: A Space Odyssey" is as hard as the genre gets on film. For as many confusing moments that the movie has, it keeps the audience riveted with its solid grounding. What makes the movie work is its juxtaposition of realistic sci-fi and existential pondering, balancing hard science with cosmic introspection. The best Stanley Kubrick movie, "2001: A Space Odyssey" brings out the best in its filmmaker and co-writer to bring this spacefaring tale to life.

#3439. Mississippi Goddam: Scott Colom Is the Answer to Anyone Who Looked Down on the South

“Mississippi is not who you think we are.”

This is what an older Black woman said to MS NOW’s Nnamdi Egwuonwu as he interviewed Scott Colom supporters on the Tougaloo College campus Thursday night. The crowd was waiting for Colom to speak after his historic victory, becoming the first Black Mississippian elected to statewide office since Reconstruction, and its first Democratic senator in nearly a half century. The woman did not give her name, but her simple statement has tattooed itself inside my brain.

“To understand the world, you must first understand a place like Mississippi” is a more famous cautionary quip that scratches at the same sentiment. If you’ve known anyone from Mississippi, you’ve probably heard it. Everyone cites William Faulkner, even though nobody has definitively sourced it. But as the world looks with fresh eyes on my home state, the wisdom checks out.

Onlookers, including longtime national political strategists, seem surprised by Colom’s win. Mississippians are not. The extremes of the moral universe have always been duking it out down there, which makes Mississippi not strange or anomalous, but illustrative.

There’s no avoiding the facts: Human beings have committed the most brutal violence imaginable against their fellow humans in Mississippi, as a matter of law and legacy. One of the consequences of that horror is that it has become prophecy. It is impossible not to feel a sense—from within the state and from without—of frustration and dread that it is taking way too long to emerge from a racism that has raptured the entire culture.

But to people who do not know Mississippians, who do not understand Mississippi—to those who suggest any right-minded or good people simply up and leave, or think the rest of the country should abandon all hope, or worse, look away entirely—you are missing one of the most important threads in the future of American politics and culture. Colom got at this rub when he said that outlets like Cook Political Report, who prognosticate a “solid R” conclusion, are destructive. “They made it much more difficult to fundraise and are part of the reason the South has been neglected for so long,” he wrote. And if you dismiss possibility in Mississippi, you are compounding the neglect. You are part of the destruction.

You think John McCain was a maverick? Scott Colom is a maverick.

During the race, he drew national attention not only for his prospect of flipping the unflippable, but also because he was doing so through one of the most vivid, creatively engaged, and original campaigns in modern politics. He built a coalition virally, with his twin brother, Andrew Robert Colom, as collaborator, offering “Sheeeeit” to the world (yes, that’s how many white Mississippians really talk), along with a Hollywood-worthy Sinners send-up, and Andrew’s searing spoken-word poem set to the strains of Fannie Lou Hamer. Colom even stood in line at a Trump rally to speak earnestly with voters who would otherwise be against him—I guarantee he won some of them over.

His entire strategy was built on making people recognize Mississippi, in all its underdog idiosyncrasies. He asked Kamala Harris to campaign with him, even as his advisers reportedly told him it would be an error, because he knew she would draw media attention to underfunded hospitals. And he took the phone call informing him that he’d won while wearing a Richard Pryor hoodie. Because we like to laugh in Mississippi, okay?

As Kiese Laymon, novelist, memoirist, and modern-day Mississippi bard, told me, “Once I saw the protein ad, I knew he’d win.”

History doesn’t echo in Mississippi; it rhymes. You can draw a straight line from the murders of Medgar Evers, or those of James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner, to the killings of Jorge Gomez or Renee Good or Alex Pretti. You can draw a straight line from Theodore Bilbo to Tate Reeves to Donald Trump.

As Kiese wrote in this magazine in 2020, Mississippi politics flow from its culture. (Incidentally, Kiese and Colom both attended Millsaps College, about 10 years apart, and had the same thesis adviser.) In “Mississippi: A Poem, in Days,” Kiese describes how he got into “an altercation with two fraternities on Bid Day”—when the students who want to be in the Greek system receive offers from frat and sorority houses. “Some fraternity members wore Confederate capes, Afro wigs, and others blackened their faces.” They called Kiese and his girlfriend the N-word.

I have never written about the heartbreak of seeing the future governor of Mississippi in that group of white boys, proudly representing the Kappa Alpha fraternity and its confederate commitment to Black suffering. I have never admitted that after playing basketball against Tate all through high school, and knowing that he went to a public school called Florence, not a segregation academy, like so many other white boys we knew, it hurt my feelings to see Tate doing what white boys who pledged their identities to the Old South ideologies were supposed to do.

When I saw Tate in that confederate cacophony of drunken white boyhood, doing what they did, I knew he could one day be governor of Mississippi and president of the United States.

That is still the most damning thing I can ever say about a white boy from Mississippi.

Damning things still happen, and will again. Just days ago, as the votes continued to stack up for Colom, the old ugliness reared its head. White women in my hometown, students at the University of Mississippi, were captured on video making racist gestures—gesturing and making sounds like monkeys—at their Black neighbors’ video doorbell. The school, still embarrassingly insistent on calling itself “Ole Miss,” continues to investigate, while the offenders get so much more grace than they deserve from the victims and their families, as you can see in their CBS interview. I feel deep shame in these moments, because I know this is what so many people think Mississippi is. There is no excuse for it, and no explanation beyond the obvious. The shame should be obvious, too, but a white person from Mississippi is compelled to express it.

The women are not from Mississippi, according to a source familiar; one, Alaina Kunes, is from Wisconsin, where a car dealership that bears her family’s name is now being sued for a separate allegation of racist actions. This is not an excuse, but rather a fear: that Mississippi’s reputation for the worst parts of history continues to attract the worst sorts of people.

But this is partly what Faulkner, or whoever it was, meant by understanding the world through the lens of Mississippi: Everywhere we must hope our better angels prevail.

I was born and raised in Mississippi among a large, politically engaged family who have wanted change for generations. When Sargent Shriver turned up unexpectedly at my grandparents’ house for dinner one night, on a swing through the South in a failed presidential bid, my grandmother whispered the urgent directive of “FHB”—“family holdback”—so her five sons would leave enough food for Shriver. This story, and that guest, was a point of pride her whole life. She was an unforgiving George McGovern campaigner; in our family photo album, among the pool parties and Christmas mornings, are pages of Polaroids she snapped of Richard Nixon’s televised resignation.

Local private schools, as I understood them, were inherently racist. Public school was a choice of one, and I got a world-class education in the Oxford school system. (Hyde-Smith attended Lawrence County Academy and she sent her own child to Brookhaven Academy, both segregation academies.) My class of 2000—I came up with the same kids from kindergarten through high school—was roughly half Black and half white, with the skinniest pie slivers of anything else. I left for college and never moved back, but my parents, brother, and extended family are still there. Today, Mississippi’s public-school students are doing better than most of their peers across the nation; my own children in the New York City school system are getting a more segregated, less excellent education than I did.

My father, a green-energy mayor and a Barack Obama appointee to the Tennessee Valley Authority (fired by Trump amid a Republican board takeover), pushed throughout my childhood to take the Confederate flag off the state flag and to remove the Confederate monument that still mars the Oxford Square. I was about eight years old when someone keyed “LIBERALS” into the trunk of our Honda Civic, probably because of the Ray Mabus for Governor bumper sticker. I recall being worried about it, until I saw that my parents were amused.

As white Southern liberals, we were in a tiny minority. And though the mantle was worn proudly, it was more existential than that—you were proud to be a Democrat not because it was one party over another, but because it was a stand-in for compassion, common good, and humanity. And nowhere could this be truer, or more necessary, than in Mississippi. (By way of disclosure, I see no conflicts in telling you all this. As former Time editor Rick Stengel says, “You should be non-partisan, but not neutral. Journalists must be biased in favor of the truth and facts. Biased in favor of democracy itself.” And this is the truth, in favor of democracy.)

Scott Colom and I were born a year apart in the earliest 1980s, during a sort of second-wave new New South rebranding. More jobs were coming into the state thanks to manufacturing; more national attention was being paid to Black Mississippians’ cultural contributions (the Delta Blues Museum was established in 1979). William Winter was governor the years of our respective births, and he gave us free kindergarten. William Allain, whose moment was virtually destroyed by a racist, homophobic GOP slander campaign, followed. And Allain was succeeded by Mabus—who won on the slogan “Mississippi will never be last again.” Now, with the exception of Ronnie Musgrove, the governor has been a Republican since 1992. We’ve never had a Black person, or a woman for that matter. Have you had many good thoughts about Mississippi in all this time? I don’t think you have.

Heavy, Kiese’s devastating and raw memoir of coming of age as a Black boy in Mississippi, written in address to his activist and educator mother, gives his own view into 1980s and ’90s Mississippi: “You worked on Governor Mabus’s campaign and kept talking about how much was possible politically in Mississippi because it was the blackest state in the nation,” he writes. And his mother says to him: “Do you understand what’s possible if we actually get effective radical politicians in place down here?” Kiese responds, “I’m glad Mabus won but hearing about it every day is just kinda mee-guh.” Meager. It was not enough then, and we have plenty far to go.

Heavy was published in October 2018, just before Stacey Abrams turned Georgia purple, signaling to the rest of the country that it was time to take notice of the deeply disenfranchised Southern states.

When I reached out to Mabus, who went on to become Bill Clinton’s ambassador to Saudi Arabia and then Obama’s Secretary of the Navy, he identified the dominoes that knocked toward Colom’s win: the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, rampant corruption, a welfare scandal featuring Brett Favre, and “office holders taking constituents for granted” over decades. Mabus was a young man working for Winter when Colom and I were little, and this election, he said, “brings hope for the future.”

It doesn’t really matter which party you’d like to claim. Repulsive policies will eventually push everyone away. Mississippi Republicans are not moderate, are not descended of gentle governance. (See: Bilbo et al.) This is the state that put “personhood” on the ballot as part of a national antiabortion strategy; fortunately for all y’all, Mississippians rejected the idea of life beginning at conception. Lynn Fitch, the current attorney general, not only effortfully attempted to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election, but she is the signed counsel for the petitioners in the Dobbs brief, which ultimately reversed Roe v. Wade. (Because I keep underscoring to you the infinite refractions of Mississippi, Fitch also went after Colom for one of his ads that used AI; he removed it.) Even the affidavit ballots that have taken so long to count are a result of strident, generational attempts by Republicans to disenfranchise Black voters. Which is why Mississippians knew, as the Colom–Hyde-Smith race came down to those affidavits, exactly in whose favor they would tally up. Were it not for the dedication of young Black canvassers—especially Black women—and homegrown mobilization efforts, things would have gone differently.

“There is a radical history of Black academics, activists, lawyers, and judges who have really been working to see a Mississippi where this was possible,” Kiese emailed me over the weekend. “I am thankful that someone like Leslie McLemore, who was a young member of Hamer’s Mississippi Democratic Party, can see what they worked and died for.”

What does Colom’s win mean for Kiese? “It means that the people, not any party, get what they organize and fight for,” he replied. “Our state taught the world that again last week.”

My privileged position occluded my own understanding of Mississippi’s true potential until I was older. Growing up, I mostly just clocked defeat—every presidential election, every midterm, Mississippi was red as red could be, as Mississippi’s poverty levels ratcheted toward a 21st-century high of 24%. In 2008, John McCain beat Barack Obama in the state by a 13% margin (the two staged a debate in Oxford). In 2016, Trump bested Hillary Clinton by almost 18 points.

After Trump won in 2024, an old childhood friend who’d gone MAGA texted me a GIF of a penis ejaculating stars that reconstituted in the shape of a patriotic eagle. Flash forward a year later, he’s angry about gas prices, and, more striking to me, horrified by the war in Gaza. Colom’s protein ad is for him, and that nerve of enthusiasm it struck is going to keep firing.

Colom didn’t run on pronouns or any numerical strain of woke. He has said he is a fan of Trump’s border security, agrees with him on certain tax policies, and supports the Second Amendment. When asked about improving wages for government employees, he has said he wants to take care of teachers—and cops. As Colom told Jen Psaki in a televised interview, “We gotta be a party that represents our whole country, that understands all parts of the country.”

Now that people outside Mississippi are waking up to Colom, leftists may find his centrism irritating or even offensive. You may find a new reason to look down your noses at Mississippi. It all but promises to provide an opportunity.

So I will just leave you with the brothers Colom.

“They lied about Mississippi. Said that evil lived in one state, but the cotton cow fed the nation. Europe eating off the same plate. They lied about Mississippi. Said the torture was only here, but the banker’s desk in northern mills still dripping blood from hostage tears. They lied to us all. That’s propaganda machine on both sides, running on slander…. Denying the nation condoned it, denying the nation owned it, denying the nation fed off pain…. They lied about Mississippi. Said that evil lived in one state.”

He says, invoking Hamer, “Mississippi Freedom Party began again.”

And the vision of Scott: “There is nothing wrong with Mississippi that can’t be fixed by what’s right.”

Danielle Fishel Went Off About How Soft The Dancing With The Stars Judges And Fans Are On The Men

Riley Green Just Picked The Only Singer He Could To Continue On The Voice After THAT Performance

I love them all, but I really want this couple to win now.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At the very start of Dancing with the Stars' 35th season, I thought Harry Shum Jr. was the ultimate frontrunner. However, I quickly came to love Ezra Frech. His story is remarkable and empowering. Plus, he’s so naturally talented, and he's partnered with one of my favorite pros, Daniella Karagach. So, as the weeks have passed on the 2026 TV schedule, I’ve wanted him to win. However, as each episode has gone by and that appreciation for Frech has stayed consistent, my love for Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov just keeps growing stronger and stronger.

While I always thought Amber was one to watch, she’s proven time and time again that she and her partner are helping set the gold standard for this season. Then, the figure skater went on the Zach Sang Show to talk about her experience on DWTS, and she said something about winning that really made her the frontrunner in my mind. When asked what it’d mean to get Pasha his first mirrorball, the Olympian said:

That would mean the world, because, I’ve said this before, is that I came into this competition, of course, who doesn’t want to win. But it wasn’t like, ‘I need this because I’ve worked my entire life for it.’ Like, I’ve been dancing for two months. Yes, it has been a very intense, very passionate two months of working, but it has been his whole life that he has been dancing. And he’s been on the show for, I believe, nine seasons. And every single year, he has put his everything into every single celeb he’s had.

Pasha has been on the show for eight seasons, and with each year, I love him and his wife, Daniella, even more. Seriously, season after season, I find myself more invested in the pros than the stars. That’s because they’re there year after year, and I get to know them all quite well through the show and social media. So, while I adore them all, and my love for Daniella is very strong, I have wanted Pasha to get his flowers really, really badly.

In his eight seasons, the highest place he’s ever gotten is third, and he deserves a win. Amber is the perfect person to help him do it. As she explained, he wanted to have an athlete as a partner, and she has “the stamina and the physical capabilities” to do tougher dances. She also complimented her partner’s ability to teach, and ended up saying:

There’s no reason that we shouldn’t be able to make this happen besides me limiting myself.

Her drive to do this for her partner is so endearing, and it’s now a big reason why I want her to win. Along with that, the Olympian went on to detail how much work the pros have to do for this show. While it looks hard for the stars, the pros have to do twice as much, and she wants Pasha to get recognized for it, explaining:

He has been putting everything into this, and I really want for everyone to see him succeed. Because it is technically, you know, every year it’s the celeb, but it’s also about the pros. Like, he is putting – imagine how much work I’m putting into it; he’s doing twice the amount. He has to choreograph; he has to do so many visual selections. Like, there’s so much that the pro does for every single show that people don’t see. So, yes, it’s about the celebrity and who wins, but it is also about the pro.

Of course, all the pros have to do this, and I'm sure their stars would praise them the same way Amber praised Pasha. However, her passion is infectious, and that, paired with their fun and high-quality dances, makes them my No. 1 couple.

Plus, of the vets still on the show who have been there for over seven seasons, Mark Ballas, Jenna Johnson, and Daniella have won before; Pasha has not.

So, yes, while I’ll be happy if Ezra and Daniella win, because they are amazing, right now, I’m rooting harder for Amber and Pasha. They are killing it week after week, and Amber’s drive to win for her pro and get him his first mirrorball is making me even more motivated to text “Amber” to 21523 as many times as I possibly can.

Now, to see who takes home the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, make sure to tune in to the last few weeks of Dancing with the Stars on Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET either on ABC or with a Disney+ subscription.

#3437. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.

#3436. James Gunn Addresses Rumors Of Skydance Changes To Superman Sequel Man Of Tomorrow

News that James Gunn and Peter Safran would be "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads shocked the industry. At this stage, there's been no official word on what might become of Gunn's DC Universe, but there has been all sorts of conjecture and rumors making the rounds. One of these rumors suggests that the upcoming "Superman" sequel, "Man of Tomorrow," will be significantly reworked ahead of its 2027 release. Now, Gunn has taken to social media to quash the rumor — though at this point it's hard to know who to believe.

Following the Warner Bros./Paramount merger, DC Studios now belongs to Skydance, and it seems the new ownership has big changes in store. Reports have claimed that Skydance CEO David Ellison will dismantle Gunn's DC Universe following his departure. Meanwhile, Nexus Point News published an article in which it cited sources claiming "Man of Tomorrow" is being trimmed down ahead of its July 2027 release. According to the outlet, planned cameos are being cut and reshoots being planned. If Ellison is, indeed, planning to raze Gunn's cinematic universe, that would make sense. According to Gunn himself, however, it's all nonsense. The director wrote a post on Threads stating:

"There are a lot of untrue rumors going around, but one of them is that Skydance has seen 'Man of Tomorrow' and that all sorts of sweeping changes are being made. No one from Skydance has even seen the movie — the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. So any stories around this narrative are false."

On one hand, it's reassuring to hear that James Gunn will be able to finish his movie without Skydance making changes. On the other, he didn't actually state unequivocally that the new owners wouldn't be altering "Man of Tomorrow," only that nobody from Skydance has seen the movie yet. But given what we're hearing about how David Ellison plans to reboot the DC Universe, and the fact he's appointed a new DC Studios head in Jeremy Latcham, it would make sense for "Man of Tomorrow" to be reworked.

Gunn previously confirmed that Xolo Maridueña's Blue Beetle would return in "Man of Tomorrow." Nexus Point News' report claims that this is one of the cameos on the chopping block following Skydance's Warner takeover. If true, it would frankly make a lot of sense. Ellison clearly has plans for DC moving forward, and he won't want audiences confused by cameos that suggest the return of erstwhile heroes to a universe he plans to dismantle.

Page Six has reported that Gunn is only staying to finish "Man of Tomorrow" because Directors Guild of America rules mean he "could not be removed" from the project. If accurate, this suggests Ellison would have given Gunn the boot from his own movie if he could — adding more credence to the idea that Skydance wants to make changes to "Man of Tomorrow" and the DC Universe as a whole.  According to the director himself, this is all untrue. But everything we've seen and heard suggests otherwise.

A Puck report has claimed that James Gunn and Peter Safran's DC Studios exit was driven in part by cost-cutting. Given all the financial promises David Ellison had to make in order to close the Warner/Paramount merger, and the fact Gunn and Safran were making a tidy little profit for themselves via a deal that gave them significant autonomy as DC Studios co-heads, that makes sense. As such, if Skydance is committed to putting out "Man of Tomorrow," it will want to do all it can make sure it's profitable while also trying not to misguide audiences with cameos and setups for a DC Universe future that simply isn't going to arrive.

It's unclear whether the same rules that supposedly prevented Skydance from removing Gunn from "Man of Tomorrow" will also prevent them from meddling too much in the final product. But it seems almost certain that Ellison will want to have some say in the movie. With Jeremy Latcham now set to oversee DC Studios, clearly the Skydance CEO has a different vision in mind for the brand moving forward. The fact that nobody from Skydance has seen "Man of Tomorrow," therefore, doesn't necessarily mean they don't have major changes planned.

Bearing in mind Gunn and Safran were previously told they would be staying on at Skydance before Ellison suddenly dropped the axe, it's hard to say who knows what over at DC Studios. For now, Gunn clearly believes he'll be able to put out the "Superman" sequel he wants to make, but who's to say what might happen over the coming months. "Man of Tomorrow" is set for a July 9, 2027 release, and a lot can happen between now and then.

#3435. Brandi Glanville Reveals She Had 'Black Mass' Removed During Facial Surgery

Brandi Glanville is sharing the shocking news that she had a “black mass” removed when she recently underwent an exploratory facial surgery.

“They did find some things that they sent away for pathology,” Glanville, 53, announced on the Friday, November 13, episode of her “Brandi Glanville Unfiltered” podcast. “That’s not back yet. However, I have so much fluid in my head it’s crazy.”

During Friday’s podcast, Glanville mentioned that doctors “don’t know yet” what the “black mass” actually is.

“[The doctor] said there were several of them,” she said. “He only took one out. I’m not sure what that is yet. My recovery hasn’t been painful.”

The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills alum confirmed in October that she’d scheduled a facial surgery with Dr. Carlo Henrado in hopes of getting to the bottom of health issues that have plagued her for more than three years.

Glanville initially thought she had a facial parasite in 2023 but was told earlier this year that she may actually be suffering from “highly resistant ESBL Klebsiella and Enterobacter with biofilm, Coccidioidomycosis (Valley Fever), Demodex dermatitis and Mononucleosis.” (The reality star estimated in April 2025 that she’d spent more than $113,000 on treatment options.)

“We are excited because we did get a few answers,” she shared during a post-op podcast this week. “There’s an infection in my glands that is … antibiotic resistant.”

Glanville confirmed she is on “antibiotics almost 24 hours a day” and is starting to “see a difference.”

“I’m excited about that,” she beamed. “I just can’t wait to go back outside and be normal. It’s coming, guys!”

Before going under the knife, Glanville claimed on her podcast that her doctor was going to “take my face off” and “do a power wash under my skin.”

“[The doctor] is, like, literally going in there with a power washer, basically, and knives and all this s***,” she explained. “And then he’s spinning my blood and doing this platelet thing on the inside of my face. We might not want my blood at this point.”

One of Brandi’s friends launched a GoFundMe in September to help her pay for ongoing medical expenses. Kyle Richards, Camille Grammer and Vicki Gunvalson were among the Bravolebrities who donated, helping to push the fundraising appeal to more than $23,600 as of publication.

“I’m honestly overwhelmed by all the love and support,” Brandi wrote via September 12 Instagram Story. “Thank you to every single person who has donated, shared my GoFundMe, checked on me, prayed for me or sent me love.”

In the middle of her latest health crisis, Brandi announced on October 10 that her dad, Guy Glanville, died at age 77.

“I feel guilty sometimes for being happy on certain days,” Glanville admitted on Friday’s podcast. “I often talk to [lost loved ones above] and I know they’re in a better place. This is the hardest time of my life.”
