#3416. Slow Horses Star Jack Lowden Was In Dwayne Johnson's Most Underrated Movie

We just saw Jack Lowden wrap up another successful season of "Slow Horses," in which his character, River Cartwright, reunited with a former love. It was one of the most surprisingly tender installments of the best spy show on TV, with "Slow Horses" Season 6 immediately improving on Season 5 by embracing a darker overall tone (while still maintaining the series' signature sardonic wit). Those who particularly enjoyed this latest season might be intrigued to know that Lowden previously starred in a film that similarly combined a heartfelt emotional core with a dry wit: "Fighting with My Family."

To be clear, this 2019 biographical sports dramedy is nothing like "Slow Horses" in terms of its genre and tone. But it does mix naturalistic drama, action, humor, and heart in a similar fashion to the spy series. That's not too surprising considering the film was written and directed by Stephen Merchant and "Slow Horses" was overseen for its first five seasons by Will Smith, both of whom came up in the British comedy scene of the early 2000s. Merchant is, of course, best known for co-creating "The Office" with Ricky Gervais, while Smith was a writer for, and starred in, the BBC sitcom "The Thick of It."

Another thing tying these two projects together (aside from both being set in England) is Lowden, who delivers one of his most underrated performances in "Fighting with My Family." It also has The Rock in it, if that sort of thing appeals. In fact, the film is also one of Dwayne Johnson's most underrated movies, even if he isn't actually in it all that much.

"Fighting with My Family" is based on the 2012 documentary "The Wrestlers: Fighting with My Family." The film saw director Max Fisher spend a year following the Knight family of Norfolk, who run the World Association of Wrestling from their suburban home. The doc particularly focused on the Knights' daughter, Saraya-Jade Bevis, as she tried out for the WWE. That story, it seems, caught the attention of Dwayne Johnson, who teamed up with Stephen Merchant to give Bevis' story the big screen treatment.

In 2019, Merchant spoke to /Film about "Fighting with My Family," recalling how he'd acted with Johnson in 2010's "Tooth Fairy" and had "got along well" with the wrestler turned actor. The pair evidently stayed in touch, which ultimately led to their collaboration on "Fighting with My Family," which Johnson executive produced and appeared in. "I have no particular interest in wrestling and didn't know anything about it," admitted Merchant. "[Johnson] happened to see a documentary while in Britain filming 'Fast & Furious 6.'" This was the genesis of "Fighting with My Family." After Johnson became acquainted with Bevis via WWE, he reached out to Merchant to write and direct. The comedian accepted.

The film he wrote similarly follows the career of English wrestler Saraya Knight/Paige, played by Florence Pugh, as she works towards a career in WWE. Jack Lowden plays her brother, Zak Knight/Zak Zodiac, who has similar dreams of making it to the big leagues. Only Saraya earns a spot in the WWE's training program, however, and she is forced to leave her family behind to pursue her dreams.

As /Film's Ethan Anderton wrote in his review, "Fighting with My Family" gives WWE fans the movie they deserve. But this is more than a wrestling movie. It's also a heartfelt comedy drama that boasts great performances from both Florence Pugh and Jack Lowden. "Slow Horses" fans should get a kick out of seeing Lowden as Zak Knight. Whereas River Cartwright is the upper-middle class son of a former MI5 head, Zak is a determined youngster who grew up in a council house. It's interesting to see how the Scottish actor renders the latter in comparison to his other best-known role.

Lena Headey and Nick Frost play Zak and Saraya's parents Ricky and Julia Knight, and both of them have a great time in their roles. Then there is, of course, The Rock, who shows up a couple times throughout the movie and is, well, The Rock. Beyond his cameos, though, Dwayne Johnson was invested in the story and did a great job shepherding the project to fruition — as evidenced by the critical response.

"Fighting with My Family" earned a 93% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes and a $41.5 million take at the global box office on an $11 million budget. All in all, then, it was a success, even if it didn't become a major hit with a massive cultural impact. Now, Lowden is said to be one of five finalists to become the new James Bond, so if you want to acquaint yourself with the actor's filmography ahead of what might be the biggest moment of his career, "Fighting with My Family" is a great place to start. The film is available to watch for free on Tubi.

#3415. Forget Ganon, Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s Most Overlooked Boss Finally Gets Its Due

The age of Ganon is over. It's Twinrova's turn to rule

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is iconic for plenty of reasons, but a big part of that is thanks to its villain. Ganondorf is one of gaming’s great bad guys, a reputation that has only been enhanced by appearances in later games like Wind Waker and Tears of the Kingdom. While Ocarina of Time’s Switch 2 remake does the Demon King justice, it’s also a reminder that the Zelda series has another excellent, and far more underappreciated, foe: Twinrova.

First introduced in Ocarina of Time, Twinrova makes for one of the best bosses in Zelda history. In the Spirit Temple, Link encounters two evil sorceresses who serve Ganondorf, Kotake and Koume. They’re classic witches: a pair of bickering old ladies flying around on brooms. The character concept is fun enough on its own, but the fight itself is memorable, too. Link has to use his Mirror Shield to absorb their elemental attacks (fire and ice) and reflect them back at the witches. It all culminates with the duo coming together Transformers-style to become Twinrova, an even more powerful witch.

The sisters’ real star-turn moment happens after Link vanquishes their Twinrova form and they separate once more. Halos appear above both witches’ heads as they begin floating up towards a light. That sets them off into a panic as they realize they are dying, prompting an unexpectedly great sketch comedy routine.

Koume: We’re twins! Don’t try and lie about your age!

Koume: Who are you calling senile?! Is that how you treat your older sister?

Kotake: We are twins! How can you be older?

The remake not only preserves that screwball dynamic, but plays it up tenfold. The witches are fully voice acted, and they sound exactly as you probably always imagined, speaking in cartoon squawks. New animation lets Nintendo go all in on their final argument, as the two taunt and shove each other as they rise into the light. It’s a delightful moment of levity right before Link’s adventure gets serious en route to Ganondorf’s castle.

All of that has left me begging for Nintendo to lean on some Zelda villains other than Ganon in future games. Twinrova got a moment to shine as the big bad of the Oracle games, but they’ve rarely been seen in the 25 years since. There are a lot of villains like that who haven’t been revisited in decades while Nintendo keeps returning to Ganon: Agahnim, Vaati, Demise, Majora, and more. All of them are underexplored in Zelda’s mythos compared to Ganon.

There’s a case to be made, of course, that villains like Twinrova are so special because they’re not dragged out over and over again. They appear in games where they feel relevant to the story and design, so why force them into games just for the sake of fan service? Maybe Nintendo is better off creating new villains, like Echoes of Wisdom’s Null or A Link Between Worlds’ Yuga.

I can get behind that, though there is a good opportunity to revisit Twinrova if Nintendo decides to do so. You can spot the younger version of Koume and Kotake in Tears of the Kingdom, and they play a role in Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment. A new game set in that era, with some incarnation of Link facing off against them, could expand the Zelda mythos in a way that feels natural. After all, the witches are 400 years old (give or take) by the time we meet them in Ocarina of Time. I’m down to see what hijinks the siblings were getting up to at the young age of 104.

Nintendo’s excellent Switch 2 remake recaptures the soul of a masterpiece

#3414. Brad Pitt Helped This Underrated Prime Video Comic Book Adaptation Get Made

If you see Brad Pitt's name in the credits for a movie he doesn't star in, it's probably because the film was produced by Plan B Entertainment, which was founded in 2001 by Pitt, his then-wife Jennifer Aniston, the late Brad Grey, and Kristin Hahn. The production company has many Pitt vehicles on its resume ("Ad Astra," "F1") but that's not all. For instance, Plan B recently co-produced the meta horror magnum opus "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma."

Plan B first ventured into TV with the failed Ryan Murphy pilot "Pretty/Handsome" in 2008, which was not picked up to series at FX. The company has since returned to TV and produced shows across different streaming platforms and networks, with its biggest recent hits including "3 Body Problem" and "Adolescence" for Netflix. But it hasn't had success across the board, as the Plan B co-produced Prime Video time travel series "Paper Girls" was canceled after one season in 2022.

"Paper Girls" adapts a 2015-2019 Image Comic series by writer Brian K. Vaughan and artist Cliff Chiang. The morning after Halloween 1988 in fictional Cleveland, Ohio, suburb Sony Stream, four preteen paper girls — "new girl" Erin Tieng (Riley Lai Nelet), Tiff Quilkin (Camryn Jones) Mackenzie "Mac" Doyle (Sofia Rosinsky), and KJ Brandman (Fina Strazza) — discover a time machine in an abandoned basement. The comic follows them across different time periods. At first, they're just sent to their immediate future in 2016, where they meet a grown up Erin (Ali Wong in the show). But later trips swing back and forth from prehistoric times to the far future.

With its eight episode run, Prime Video's "Paper Girls" merely scratched that surface. Its short life sadly mirrors Vaughan's acclaimed comic "Y: The Last Man" being turned into a single-season show as well.

"Paper Girls" features four kids in 1980s Midwest suburbia, riding on bicycles and communicating with walkie-talkies, who stumble onto a science fiction story. There are undeniable similarities to "Stranger Things," and while they're coincidental (the "Paper Girls" comic was already running when the former premiered in 2016), the story's parallels to the Duffer Brothers' Netflix phenomenon probably helped the TV show adaptation get greenlit.

But compared to the 1980s nostalgia in "Stranger Things," "Paper Girls" takes a harder look at the decade. The very first time we meet Mac in the comic, she insults some local bullies with homophobic slurs — and she's one of the heroes! But that hatred turns out to be internalized. Across the story, Mac and KJ realize their feelings for each other. (That bumpy ride is another thing the "Paper Girls" TV series didn't get a chance to realize.) Compare that to "Stranger Things" Season 3, in which one character (Maya Hawke's Robin) admits she's a lesbian to another (Joe Keery's Steve), and he's totally accepting of it. It's a nice sentiment about what things should have been like, but it's also completely ahistorical.

Another story that hits the same mood as "Paper Girls" is the 2026 time travel Amblin throwback "The End of Oak Street" — for one, both have time-displaced dinosaurs. "Paper Girls" doesn't have as wide a mean streak as "Oak Street," though, making it a happy medium between that and how saccharine "Stranger Things" can get. If you love the "Paper Girls" TV series and crave more, I'd highly recommend the comic as the next best thing. It's a quick read at only 30 issues, and it's got the ending the TV show deserved to adapt.

As a native Southern Californian, I’ve never seen a white Christmas. The closest I can get without getting on a plane is during Disneyland’s holiday season. Every night, without fail, Main Street U.S.A. and the area in front of “It’s A Small World” become a winter wonderland, and it feels like a fantasy. That is, unless it's raining. I didn’t know before exactly why rain would stop the snow from falling upon Disneyland, but someone just made the reason quite evident.

“Disneyland’s Wintertime Enchantment” makes snowfall in Southern California possible every night at 7:30 p.m. and 8:30 p.m. However, don’t count on it if it’s raining. And FYI, there’s a lot of it coming this week after some notable flooding at Disneyland last month. Here’s why:

A post shared by Molly Evans (@happilyevansafterall)

Now, I hate to ruin the magic, but Disneyland snow isn’t actually snow. It’s something that’s been named "snoap" by fans, because it’s practically soap disguised as snow. It's dispersed by hidden rooftop machines.

According to the Los Angeles Times, Disneyland’s snow is made up of 98% water mixed with a non-hazardous, proprietary surfactant (soap) blend. On any other day, the “snow” evaporates shortly after landing somewhere and leaves no trace on guests or around the park. However, when too much water mixes with it, you get a very soapy (and gross) ground!

As you can see in the Instagram post, when the “snoap” and rain happen at the same time, it creates a major slip hazard for the guests. Therefore, it is usually canceled on rainy days. In this recent instance, the guest reports that snow was accidentally turned on at 10:30 p.m., causing an issue everywhere in the park where snow fell.

Even if the snowfall is stalled by rain, most of the other holiday festivities can still happen during such weather conditions. The firework show will have to be canceled during active rain, heavy cloud cover or high winds, but the projections at “It’s A Small World” will typically still run.

The “It’s A Small World” ride also has a special holiday version if you’re not into that song. The World of Color - Season of Light over at California Adventure can also usually hold up unless rain is paired with severe wind or lightning. And you can meet Santa Claus at Mickey’s Toontown Trolley Barn, which is located indoors.

One of my personal favorite holiday traditions is the A Christmas Fantasy Parade. I just love seeing all the characters in their Christmas-themed outfits, too. Over at DCA, there’s also a holiday event called “Guardians of the Galaxy: Awesome Dance Off!” debuting at Avengers Campus. Disneyland’s holiday-themed entertainment runs until January 6 this year, so there’s plenty of time to enjoy this special time of year.

If you’re not able to make it to Disneyland right now, it’s also a good time to check out the 2026 Christmas movie schedule. A ton are available to stream with a Disney+ subscription!

#3412. Andrew Scott On What Makes Elsinore “So Moving”

Although the emotional core of Elsinore is centered around beloved actor Ian Charleston dealing with terminal illness, its star Andrew Scott says the film has as much heart as it does humor.

“The most singular thing about our film I think is the humor in it,” he said during a panel conversation at the inaugural Vanity Fair Screening Room at LACMA on Friday. “The tragedy in some ways is a little bit like Hamlet itself, but you can't make a film about Ian Charleston without having gags in it. He was incredibly funny. Every person [who knew him] said he was just wickedly funny, and flirtatious, and he was always looking towards the light, and he had a certain degree of courage. So that is something I think that we all share as a sense of humor.”

Andrew Scott, Billie Piper, Stephen Beresford and Rebecca Ford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

Elsinore tells the story of Scottish actor Ian Charleson (Scott) who attempts to perform Hamlet at the National Theatre while secretly living with AIDS. Scott has received early acclaim for his powerful portrayal of Charleson. Before the film began Vanity Fair’s West Coast Editor John Ross warned the audience that "first you're going to laugh, then you're going to cry," while watching Scott’s performance.

“I think … why the film is so moving is because [Charleson’s] not wallowing at any point. He was insanely courageous,” continued Scott. “So that to me was the thing that we were the most

insistent on in some ways. And that's really all down to finding actors who in this extraordinary ensemble have a really terrific sense of humor. And we kind of knew that we could, with the screenplay, get the best actors in the country. And I feel we did.”

The panel conversation featured Scott, costar Billie Piper, and writer Stephen Beresford, moderated by VF's Senior Hollywood Correspondent Rebecca Ford, following an exclusive screening of the film.

Billie Piper at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

For Piper, who plays Charleston's close friend Patsy, she relied heavily on Beresford's script for her prep, as well as information she gleaned from those who actually knew Patsy, and Charleston.

“I've spoken to a few members of the family, their friends, and then I sort of cherry-picked things from people I'd known in the beginning of my career, the louder figures in our industry,” she said. “And then I did my own interpretation and just had a good time. It's a very moving story, but I had a lot of fun playing that part. She's a really joyful character to play, I enjoyed the comedy. And I understand that a lot of her jokes are coming from a place of despair.”

Beresford, who has known Scott for 25 years, said he didn't initially think of his longtime friend for the role, but should have.

“The story of Ian, and Ian's Hamlet [performance] is legendary in the British theater,” he said. “So many people said it was the greatest Hamlet they'd ever seen, and that it had this incredible quality. So I knew about the story, and then it was brought to me actually as an idea by a producer who said, ‘What about writing about Ian Charleston, and what about Andrew playing Ian Charleston?’ And then I just thought, ‘Well, why didn't I have that idea myself five years ago?’ So yeah, that's really how it happened, and I started to research it, the details of the story were so incredible, and so moving.”

Stephen Beresford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026.

Scott, who famously played Hamlet onstage 150 times beginning in 2017, prior to filming Elsinore, closed out the panel conversation by reciting his favorite line from the classic tragedy.

“When Hamlet says the line about the war that was going on—and this was written 400 years ago—it just seems so relevant to what he might have been experiencing at the time, which is: ‘I see the imminent death of 20,000 men who for a fantasy, a trick of fame, go to their graves like beds.’ The idea that that was written 400 years ago, and that he was watching 50 percent of his friends die for no reason and be neglected by governments, and derided by the public. And it was just happening, and happening time and time again.”

Scott continued: “The reason that I love it so much is that when I was doing Hamlet myself, of course I wasn't thinking about the AIDS crisis, but the enduring nature of art, something that was written 400 years ago by Shakespeare, could actually be of use to somebody in 1989 and then be reproduced again in 2026 and be of use. And that idea of art being useful down the lines is so moving to me.”

Vanity Fair's Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci, Elsinore stars Andrew Scott and Billie Piper and writer Stephen Beresford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026.

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room pairs this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that includes post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself.

Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

#3411. Aura's Second E-Ink Picture Frame Is Much Improved, and Much Cheaper

Last year, Aura released the Aura Ink, its first digital photo frame using an e-ink display rather than the LCD screens common to the other devices that made them the major player in the market (Aura customers have already uploaded more than one billion photos this year alone). When I reviewed the original 13-inch Aura Ink last year, I recommended it, with a few major reservations. Today, Aura announced its second-generation 10-inch Ink frame, and while I wouldn't exactly say they've solved every one of my issues, the new device is significantly improved—and much cheaper.

Most digital photo frames will remind you of an iPad with a decorative border around it. They're great for displaying hundreds of your photos with vibrant color, but not everyone loves the look, or the fact that these frames always need to be plugged in. An e-ink frame, on the other hand, uses a variant of the sort of low-power screen you'd find in a Kindle Colorsoft—less bright, but more paperlike, and much closer to the look of a traditionally printed photo.The Aura Ink is a great choice if you want a digital frame that looks more like a "real" photo and doesn't need to be plugged in and doesn't light up like a tablet (though it does have a light, it's really to make up for the fact that color e-ink screens don't reflect light very well, and thus can make your pictures look way too dark without an additional boost). You'll still get all the benefits of an LCD frame like the Aura Aspen, including the ability to load photos from anywhere using the versatile Aura app (you can now even text them directly to the frame), but you'll only need to charge it once every few months.

Now for the downsides: Where most digital frames allow you to flick between photos with a swipe, the Aura Ink is much more sluggish—switching from one photo to another takes about 45 seconds. While an LCD can match the colors in your photo exactly, e-ink uses a "dithering algorithm" to blend tiny pixels together to create the illusion of different hues ("millions" of them, according to Aura). In practice, this means up close, your pictures will look rather grainy, and the colors won't be nearly as bright as what you see on your phone screen.

All of that said, the Aura Ink is a great product, provided you know what you're buying, and the new 10-inch model offers some big upgrades over the 13-inch original released in 2025:

Resolution has been bumped up from 150 ppi to 200 ppi, so your images look more detailed and less grainy. (Though the difference is hard to capture in a photo, I can definitely see the improvement when comparing them side-by-side.)

Instead of the six base colors available on the older frame, the 10-inch Aura Ink blends nine different hues to approximate the colors in your images, offering greater color accuracy and improved contrast.

The transition effect when you move between photos has been updated to look more intentional—like waves of color moving across the screen versus a series of increasingly intense flashes.

It's a heck of a lot cheaper: $349, versus $499 for the 13-inch model—though that's still significantly pricier than Aura's most popular offering, the 10.1-inch Aura Carver, which starts around $200 less.

I write a lot about e-ink devices, from e-readers to tablets, and my common refrain, especially with color devices, is that they're great at what they do, but you should understand what they do before you plunk down your money. The Aura Ink will never look as bright and colorful as an LCD frame, and if you want a frame that can switch between images every few minutes or even play video, you'll need to look elsewhere (to maximize battery life, Aura recommends swapping photos on the Aura Ink no more than 12 times per day).

But if you want to display photos that look more like the ones that hung on the walls of your childhood home, in a frame that doesn't need to be plugged in all the time, you'll probably dig it, provided you can stomach the $350 price tag.

#3410. Tomb Raider Remake Gameplay Changes Are Dividing Fans

Lara Croft's original adventure is getting heavily modernized

Amazon Game Studios has released the sixth installment in its behind-the-scenes series about the development of Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis. The remake of Lara Croft's original 1996 adventure is set to be released next year and will update the game for modern players. While that includes graphical improvements, the new video details gameplay changes and not everybody is happy about what was shown off.

The "Combat & Progression Reimagined" video posted on the official Tomb Raider YouTube channel this summer gives an in-depth look at a handful of new systems coming in Legacy of Atlantis. Game director Raul Siquera details one major addition to the remake: Focus.

"When you're taking damage, dealing damage, dodging attacks, you're building your Focus meter," Siquera explained, "Focus allows you to slow down time around you and showcase some of the things that Lara used to do in 1996." In practice this lets players unlock more of Lara's iconic acrobatic moves after building Focus.

Design director Jason Epps detailed two more changes in Legacy of Atlantis: a skill tree and herb collecting. Both of these elements are heavily inspired by mechanics in Crystal Dynamics' Survivor Trilogy, which revolved more around Lara needing to scavenge for materials and upgrade her skills. "When I played the Survivor series and I could suddenly affect and increase Lara's power in the game, I felt much more engaged," said Epps. Crafting takes on a Resident Evil-style system, letting players make items that heal Lara but also give her buffs.

The response to the Focus meter has been fairly muted. In fact, in some of the footage shown off, it looks quite cool when executed properly. The skill tree and crafting, on the other hand, have been met with widespread derision. A ResetEra thread discussing the video is full of comments like, "No sir, I don't like it," and "I hate it." Another user asks, "Isn't she supposed to be a veteran treasure hunter in this game? Why would she be learning new skills at her age?" As the original Tomb Raider was a relatively straightforward game that had none of the RPG bloat that seems to permeate modern games, many hoped Legacy of Atlantis would harken back to this design ethos.

While the additions are divisive, it seems the developers are trying to merge elements of the original Tomb Raider games with the Survivor Trilogy. That's not too unexpected given the series is trying to establish a more unified timeline with new games. Even the skill tree has an interesting twist, as Lara will gain skill points by collecting in-game artifacts rather than leveling up through experience points. In an attempt to reassure fans that Legacy of Atlantis' gameplay won't stray too far from the original, the developers revealed that the entire game can be played with just Lara's dual pistols. Epps said, "If you decide that you want to play with the dual pistols the entire way and be iconic. Absolutely."

Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis is coming to Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X on Feb. 12, 2027.

#3409. This '60s Sketch Show Became One Of The Biggest Flops In TV History

Networks tried all sorts of wild and outlandish ideas in the 1960s as they attempted to wrestle audiences' attention away from their rivals. This was the decade that gave us "My Mother the Car," the show for which Jerry Van Dyke turned down "Gilligan's Island" and which had him talking to his deceased mother via a car radio. The '60s also gave us Sally Field as a flying nun and sitcoms such as "The Hathaways" which featured a trio of trained chimpanzees who were treated like human children by their suburban "parents."

It was during this era that ABC decided to debut its surreal sketch comedy series "Turn-On," and when I say "series," I mean single episode. The show was so poorly received that it was yanked off the air after its debut installment in 1969, and rumors have since emerged that it became the only series in TV history to be canceled while it was airing. That might be a slight exaggeration, but not by much.

1969 was the year the world watched Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin land on the moon, "Star Trek" aired its final episode, and a man who actually did say yes to "Gilligan's Island," Alan Hale Jr. paid a visit to Sally Field's aforementioned airborne nun. But the year got off to a rocky start for ABC when it debuted one of the most notorious flops in TV history.

"Turn-On" was created by Digby Wolfe and George Schlatter, with the latter having created the hugely popular NBC series "Rowan & Martin's Laugh-In," aka "Laugh In," and the former having written for that same series. Their attempt to recreate the magic at ABC was a more lewd, surreal affair that aired once on Wednesday, February 5, 1969, and was never seen again.

Forgotten sketch comedy show "Weird TV" might be the weirdest series of all time, but "Turn-On" isn't far off. For one thing, its concept seemingly had little to do with comedy. As one of two computer engineers explains during its opening moments, "Turn-On" is "the first computerized TV show." What does that mean? Well, in a practical sense, it means every sketch unfolds in a vast all-white vacuum, where the supercomputer supposedly responsible for the show manifests sets and characters. Essentially, the whole thing takes place within the Construct from "The Matrix."

The opening sequence is a bewildering and surreal experience, featuring an array of diverse performers who appear within the Construct in quick succession, including puppets and a woman who plays a sousaphone before bursting into laughter — all scored by an electronic rhythm and synth hits that apparently have little to do with what's happening on-screen. It's the kind of thing that wouldn't be out of place on Adult Swim in the 2000s. In the late-1960s? Let's just say network affiliates were concerned about their ratings.

Things get a bit more blue as the debut episode of "Turn-On" continues. While "Laugh In" pushed boundaries, its ABC counterpart contained more sexual humor. And by "humor," I mean the word "Sex" flashing on-screen above guest host Tim Conway and Bonnie Boland and a "sketch" in which a woman tries desperately to get a box marked "The Pill" out of a vending machine. Meanwhile the show's credits continue to appear throughout the episode as suggestive cartoons pop up from time to time. This mixed media approach sort of calls to mind "Monty Python's Flying Circus," which also debuted in 1969. Unlike that now legendary series, however, "Turn-On" was cancelled almost immediately.

A stub in the February 7, 1969 edition of The Oregonian (via Newspapers.com) noted how local ABC affiliate KATU-TV did not air the "Turn-On" premiere at the behest of its management, who were evidently put off by a preview screening. "The station's management decided certain portions of the program 'are not in good taste and that these portions would be objectionable to a substantial and responsible part of the community,'" reads the report, which also noted that the Associated Press critic Cynthia Lowry had highlighted the "frankly blue jokes" that offended the Oregon affiliate management.

ABC seemed to agree, and it pulled the plug after the first episode went out. According to co-creator George Schlatter, though, the show's swift cancellation came down to a station manager in Cleveland who wanted to keep "Peyton Place," the show that would have run in the "Turn-On" time-slot, on the air. "He started calling the stations as it came across the country telling them they had to cancel this show," Schlatter stated. "[...] He convinced them to cancel the show, so by the time it got to California, the show was off the air, and some of it has never been seen." It's this recollection of events that seems to have birthed the "canceled while it was on the air" urban legend.

The attempts at transgressive humor and surrealism in "Turn-On" feel too try-hard, and the overall experience of sitting through the premiere episode is actually quite unpleasant. That said, it's not impossible to admire Schlatter and Digby Wolfe's attempt to do something different. What's more, we've gotten plenty of awful TV shows with 0% Rotten Tomatoes scores, and I'd much rather watch "Turn-On" than an episode of "Real Rob."

#3408. Hillary Clinton Showed Up For Dinner at Gloria Steinem’s Townhouse

It’s a dark and stormy November night at Gloria Steinem’s townhouse, and Hillary Clinton has something to say about the 2026 election. “One of my most anticipated moments will be watching Donald Trump walk into the State of the Union through the now more than one hundred women members of the House of Representatives. I just want them all to stare at him and say, ‘You fired us from jobs we were qualified for. You insulted us. You demeaned our ambition. You undermined our place in government and society. And we’re here.’”

Huma Abedin, Busy Philips, and Paloma Elsesser.

The former Secretary of State and 2016 presidential candidate is a last-minute but highly anticipated arrival to this dinner honoring Steinem, the late activist. She passed away in September, but the feminist pathfinder was known for throwing these salon-type events (she called them “circles”) at her Upper East Side townhouse, which she bought for just $30,000 in the late ’60s. It’s overflowing with books (I spy Marilyn by Norman Mailer, Jane Fonda’s War by Mary Hershberger, and several Eleanor Roosevelt biographies on the shelves), pictures (there’s one framed of Steinem alongside Mariska Hargitay) and Indian art. (Steinem spent two formative years in the country.) There are magnets in her kitchen of Wonder Woman, Frida Kahlo, and a cloth finger puppet of Hillary Clinton. A political button is pinned to it that says “Another Bitch for Hillary.” The whole place smells like a Cire Trudon candle, and everyone’s drinking negronis. (Which actually isn’t technically very Steinem—her favorite cocktail was a margarita—but the negronis go with the night’s dinner, prepared by Lilia chef Missy Robbins.) Yet this is one of the first events at the townhouse that Steinem herself isn’t here to lead.

Jihae, Lux Pascal, Naomi Watts, and Bethann Hardison.

Amy Richards, a feminist activist whom many consider to be the daughter Steinem never had—a title Richards rejects because her mentor “didn’t want kids”—stood up at one point to tell the crowd that this is what Steinem would have wanted. Growing up with a transient father and a mentally volatile mother, the late activist took near-obsessive care in maintaining a welcoming home she could share with others. “As long as I knew Gloria, she always said, ‘I just want my home to be the way it’s always been.’ She wanted it to be filled with people,” Richards says. “She didn’t grow up with a home. She was traveling the country for the first 10 years of her life and then lived with her mother, who was not very stable.”

At least Steinem’s still here on the wall: Months before her death, she posed for a series of portraits by Paola Kudacki for Weldun, a platform that offers physically adaptive and functional fashion. It was a bit of a small miracle that Steinem said yes. “I will say, Gloria did not always love to be photographed,” Richards says. “Especially in her later years—not because of wrinkles or aging, but she was just like, ‘Aren’t there enough pictures of me?’” Weldun and the Gloria Steinem Foundation are presenting tonight’s dinner, and mementos of Steinem are everywhere. On the fireplace mantle sits a pair of her signature Ray-Ban aviators. But Gloria’s stuff isn’t the same as Gloria herself.

Former secretary of state Hillary Clinton hugging Melissa McCarthy.

Which is probably why, in a crowd of women that include Huma Abedin, Mariska Hargitay, Padma Lakshmi, Melissa McCarthy, and Bethann Hardison—who, at the ripe age of 84, shows up wearing Gucci—Clinton’s unexpected arrival feels seismic, like Gloria sent someone in her place. (Hardison tells me she thinks Steinem used whatever divine power she’s got up there to launch the Blue Wave: “She’s probably saying she helped it happen!”) Whatever your views on Clinton’s politics, she was the first woman to receive a presidential nomination from a major party. Paloma Elsesser and I sit crouched in a corner of the room, glued to the window. “There’s mother,” the supermodel whispers to me as Clinton exits her car into the pouring rain and walks up to the townhouse door.

Guests at dinner honoring the late Gloria Steinem.

“Hi, everybody,” Clinton says as she walks in. The entire dinner comes to a silent halt. “Hi,” the room responds in unison. Madame Secretary doesn’t seem to like the fuss, probably because 30 or so people intensely staring at you when you arrive at a party is objectively unsettling. “Go back to eating!” she says, motioning to the Missy Robbins meal on the table. Clinton sits down next to Naomi Watts and warmly greets Busy Philips, who stumped for Clinton back in 2016. Hargitay blows her a kiss across the table. All anyone wants to do is talk to Clinton about the 2026 election, in which Democrats won at least 55 seats in the Senate and 256 in the House to take both majorities in the US Congress. At the end of the meal—and after a proper catch-up with Shonda Rhimes—Clinton tries to leave, but she can’t. Guests block the door, clamoring to chat her up.

Amid the Clinton traffic jam, I ask Hargitay about the photo. She can’t remember exactly what it is from. “Was it Bravo? Was it with Andy…what’s his name?” But she can guess what she thinks Steinem might say about the blue wave: “There is a God!”

I watch Clinton finally make her exit. It’s late, so I wait several minutes before I descend the stairs to leave too. (I wait for Elsesser, Watts, Hardinn, and Lux Pascal to finish taking a selfie on the steps.) But I spoke too soon: Clinton’s stuck waiting for the coat check, another group of women crowded around her hoping to say something—or, more likely, hoping she says something. With the way this night is going, Clinton might be the last one at the party.

#3407. Here's What We Know About Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday 2026 Sales

Gone are the days when holiday sales had a firm beginning and end. These days, if you're not scouring the internet weeks before the actual date of the event, you will miss out on deals. Black Friday is no exception. Amazon released its official Black Friday and Cyber Monday plans for its sale, but there's plenty that's discounted already, many reaching or matching their lowest price ever.

Amazon is treating Black Friday and Cyber Monday like one long sale. The official sale kicks off at 12:01 a.m. PST on Nov. 19 and runs through Nov. 30.

Yes, you will need to be a Prime Member to shop the exclusive sales during Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Prime membership starts at $14.99 per month. While only you can decide if buying a yearly Prime membership is worth it for you, remember you can always sign up and then cancel your Prime membership once the sale is over: Amazon offers a free 30-day trial, so you can shop during both Black Friday and Cyber Monday before canceling without being charged. Here's how to sign up for a Prime account and all of the benefits that come with it.

#3406. She-Hulk's Tatiana Maslany Starred In A Must-Watch 2026 Apple TV Series

Tatiana Maslany's career exploded in the mid-2010s with her virtuoso multi-character work on BBC America's brainy sci-fi thriller series "Orphan Black." It was a very good show, but the deeper Maslany got into her roles, the more you wondered what she could do in a film or series where her performance prowess could be concentrated on one specific part. Indeed, she proved to be unsettlingly fierce as the vengeful Sister Alice on HBO's dark reinvention of "Perry Mason" and brought all the charm she could muster to Marvel Studios' irreverent "She-Hulk: Attorney at Law." Her talent was undeniable, but the projects weren't proper showcases of her astonishing ability.

This changed in 2026 with the premiere of Apple TV's comedy-thriller series "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed." The show stars Maslany as Paula Saunders, a fact checker (the noblest and most under-appreciated of journalistic professions) who's fighting for custody of her child while looking into the kidnapping and apparent death of a webcam model named Trevor (Brandon Flynn). No less an authority than Stephen King has effused that "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed" is "like Hitchcock came back to do it one more time." Its first season is streaming in its entirety on Apple TV, and it's officially coming back for more. So, now is the time to get caught up before you're 20 episodes deep down a binge hole.

The tone-setting pilot of "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed" was directed by David Gordon Green, who was once a Terrence Malick-ian stylist (see: early triumphs like "George Washington" and "All the Real Girls") before he segued to mainstream movies via broad stoner comedies like "Pineapple Express" and "Your Highness." But while "Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed" possesses a bit of visual sophistication, it's the writing by series creator David J. Rosen and his staff that puts it over the top.

The casting is also key. Jake Johnson is deliciously antagonistic as Paula's ex-husband Karl, who's seeking sole custody of their child while she nurses her anguish with wine and digs into the fate of her newfound internet companion. Rosen and the show's writers pile the complications on with inventive abandon, and Tatiana Maslany surprises every step of the way as a protagonist we simply can't figure out.

"Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed," as mentioned, has been renewed for a second season, so Maslany will get another 10 episodes to explore possibly the best character she's ever been given to play. In the meantime, you should get out to see Noah Segan's "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York," where she is dynamite as John Turturro's daughter. The Maslany-ssiance is upon us.

Danielle Fishel charmed audiences for seven seasons while playing the TGIF fan-favorite character, Topanga Lawrence in Boy Meets World. Not only was the character notable for being involved in a TV relationship that defined goals, but Topanga was also loved for being smart and true to herself. While Fishel has taken great pride in her BMW work, she recently mentioned one regret related to her character that, as a fan, I completely sympathize with.

At the beginning of the ABC sitcom, Topanga was introduced as Cory Matthews’ hippie-like classmate whose otherworldly views always sparked great comedic moments. But by the second season, th flower child had an extreme personality change, where she transitioned to an extremely motivated student and later the object of Cory’s affections by Season 3.

In Fishel, Rider Strong, and Will Friedle’s new book, Book Meets World: The Definitive Inside Story of the Hit Sitcom Boy Meets World (via People), she got real about her character's evolution. She explained how she felt about Topanga's trajectory at the time compared to how she feels now:

Teenage Danielle was more comfortable being the more mainstream Topanga because they wrote her more like me. So I probably didn’t have a problem with it then. Now I think, what a gift to be given a character that has such a sharply defined POV, to be so unique and to have been such a good role model. I knew that she was special. But then, when it changed, and she kind of evolved, I don’t think I necessarily knew to mourn it.

I get what the Dancing with the Stars contestant is talking about. When Fishel previously spoke about Topanga’s personality shift, she admitted that she didn’t even notice the change at the time. Looking back, it’s true that the show was focusing a lot on Topanga’s evolving look, like in Season 2 when Shawn was staring at her chest or Cory fixated so much on her beauty in Season 3. I truly believe Topanga’s complete change was when she cut her trademark long hair and started to look more like many other woman of the ‘90s.

While no one formally told the Dish host that her character would deviate from her weird girl persona, she said she remembered hearing a conversation from the crew about wanting to make Topanga “more normal” for Cory. Yet, even in the Season 6 episode, "Resurrection," Cory talked about missing the old Topanga. I feel like Cory would have grown to like the more off-beat version of his eventual partner.

Something that's interesting is hearing Fishel mention that as a teen, she didn't really mind her character being more streamlined and fitting her own personality. She may not have mourned the transition then, but she certainly does now:

Now I see it, and I so mourn it. I would have loved even little flashbacks to it.

That would have been great. Fans see a flashback scene in “Resurrection” of when Topanga put lipstick all over her face but, in the later seasons, I would have liked to have seen Fishel's character retain traits of who she was early on.

At the same time, we can be thankful that no matter who Topanga grew up to be, she remained throughout the series in general. Some may not be aware that she was originally written to be a recurring character. As a result of her sticking around, fans got to see her transform into a confident young woman, who even became an incredible lawyer, wife, and mother in the spinoff series, Girl Meets World.

While Danielle Fishel now regrets having leaned into Topanga’s personality change, I'd argue that her performance on the show still deserves praise. And, of course, we can love the iconic character for who she was when she was first introduced as well as who she grew into by the show’s series finale. You can watch Topanga’s Boy Meets World and Girl Meets World journeys by streaming the sitcoms with a Disney+ subscription.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3404. Avril Lavigne Welcomes Her First Child At Age 42

Avril Lavigne is now a mom. The 42-year-old Canadian might count songs like "Here's to Never Growing Up" among her hits, but in news posted to Instagram Friday, Avril Lavigne revealed a very grown-up milestone.

Beneath a carousel of three black-and-white photos, Lavigne wrote “Our Mini Fucking Princess has arrived,” followed by emojis depicting a baby bottle, a crown, and a pink heart and bow. One photo shows Lavigne cradling an infant dressed in an animal-print onesie and matching headband, while another shows three pairs of Vans on a skateboard. No other details, including information on the baby's name or if Lavigne has a co-parent, were provided.

Avril Lavigne at the Viper Room in the early 2000s.

A spokesperson for the singer told People that “Avril has been enjoying time with her family while working on her new album and wants to thank the fans for all of their love!”

Lavigne has been married twice: once to Canadian guitarist Deryck Whibley and then to Chad Kroeger, the Canadian frontman of the band Nickelback. That latter partnership ended in 2018, but in 2022 she almost tied the knot a third time, with rapper Mod Sun. That relationship ended in 2023.

Mod Sun and Avril Lavigne attend the 2022 MTV Video Music Awards on August 28, 2022

One constant in Lavigne's life has been strong bond she shares with her parents. When, in May 2025, she brought her mother on stage at Madison Square Garden, she wrote on social media: “Ever since I was a little girl, both my mom and dad saw something in me and encouraged me to practice very hard and pursue my dream of becoming a singer/ musician. They made a lot of sacrifices for me and I could not be where I am today without them.”

Continuing, she wrote, “I am grateful to both my parents. Thank you for everything, I love you both!”

Lavigne was still a teenager when her parents allowed her to leave high school to pursue her dream, and her debut at age 17 was a smash hit. Her success continued with singles including 2002's chart-topper “Complicated" and 2021 song “Bite Me.”

Though Friday's announcement was a surprise to most, Lavigne has never been quiet about her desire to become a mom when the time is right. Speaking with E! News in 2013, she laid out her plan: "I want one or two [kids], but not right now," the then-29-year old said. "Like, in the future. Eventually."

#3403. Grey's Anatomy's Downfall Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

"Grey's Anatomy" has been on the air since 2005, which is to say that it's experienced a handful of high highs and very low lows. Shonda Rhimes' medical drama, which premiered as a humble mid-season replacement and became one of the longest-running shows in the history of its medium, stars Ellen Pompeo as surgical intern turned award-winning general surgery attending and hospital owner Dr. Meredith Grey, who lives, loves, and learns alongside her colleagues and who has a knack for picking up cases that connect to her personal life in some way (as all of the doctors do, honestly).

(I say it "stars" Pompeo, but there's a technicality here; Pompeo technically left "Grey's Anatomy" as a series regular in Season 19 in 2022, but still provides voiceover and appears on the show often enough that she's still the main character for all intents and purposes.)

There are, if I'm being honest, many parts of "Grey's Anatomy" that one could identify as a major series downfall, like the time Dr. Isobel "Izzie" Stevens (Katherine Heigl) has ghostly physical intimacy with her dead fiancé before figuring out it's a brain tumor, the time a plane crash kills most of the show's surgeons, or every time a wedding is interrupted by a dramatic, ridiculous problem. The issue? Many of those lows are followed by highs (as Heigl's Izzie leaves the series, there's a hospital merger followed by a two-part finale in Season 6 that's a legitimate series highlight). That's why I'm pointing to a true point of no return for "Grey's Anatomy," and I am truly sorry to say that, despite my respect for the show's commitment to "realism" during a terrifying time for the entire world, the 17th season of the medical drama, also known as the "COVID season," is its downfall.

At face value, it makes total sense for a show like "Grey's Anatomy" to address the very real COVID-19 pandemic head-on; because the characters also dressed in protective medical gear, there was an air of practicality to the whole thing to boot. Here's the problem: the way they addressed it was straight-up bonkers. Partway through Season 17, Meredith develops a pretty serious case of COVID-19, which sidelines her (and, to an extent, Ellen Pompeo) for the remainder of the season's run, giving her a truly bizarre storyline where she sees dead loved ones in dreams in a random seaside location that fans like me simply refer to as the "coma beach."

Instead, fans of the series couldn't escape the pandemic surrounding them, and to make things worse, the show's best quality — its genuinely funny and smart dialogue — fell by the wayside in the process. Meredith may have eventually recovered from her severe case of COVID-19 and left the coma beach behind after Season 17, but the show wasn't able to pull off the same feat ... and as it continues, you can feel the slip in quality with each passing season.

I know better than most people that "Grey's Anatomy" has its fair share of detractors; I've been watching this damn show since it premiered, and it's one of the longest relationships of my life without comparison. I'll be among the first to admit that a lot of it is heightened and silly — and I got the chance to interview a friend who's a real doctor for this very site, who confirmed that it's the least realistic televised medical drama by a country mile.

Still, I'll go to the mat for a lot of seasons and episodes of "Grey's Anatomy." Shonda Rhimes, while she was still hands-on with the series, was a masterful dialogue writer and gave actors like Sandra Oh (who left the series after the Season 10 finale) unbelievably sharp monologues with regularity. The chemistry between most of the original actors was undeniably great, its jokes often hit their mark beautifully, and remember that two-part Season 6 finale I mentioned? "Sanctuary" and "Death and All His Friends," which chronicles a devastating mass shooting within the walls of the central hospital, is one of my favorite TV episodes ever ... and I'd stack it against plenty of prestige dramas any day.

That's what makes the fall of "Grey's Anatomy" particularly painful for me. I'm committed to the proverbial bit by still watching it, but it's painful. Instead of quippy dialogue that feels like a tennis match, characters over-explain everything in the preachiest way possible (like a female doctor explaining to a male counterpart that women get Brazilian butt lifts because society influences them into it). "Grey's Anatomy" is a pale shadow of what it once was, and it all started in Season 17.

#3402. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3401. 8 Near-Perfect Sci-Fi Miniseries that Hook You in the First Episode

Designed to be binge-watched over the weekend

The best science fiction stories have a habit of going on forever. Franchises like Star Wars, Star Trek, and even Alien enter the world with such incredible momentum that we're still making sequels and spin-offs all these decades later. After all, part of what makes sci-fi so great is the opportunity to imagine alternate entire worlds, galaxies, and universes, and then explore them indefinitely. But sometimes, you just want to watch something that can be finished in a single weekend. That's where miniseries come in.

Sci-fi stories are a dime a dozen, but very few genre stories manage to make an unforgettable impact with the miniseries format. This makes sense. Shows like The Expanse or Westworld need more space to flesh out their multi-season storylines. That said, some sci-fi miniseries accomplish a lot with less. Whether you’re looking for an action-packed show or one that is more philosophical in tone, these eight entries make for a near-perfect viewing experience that can be wrapped up in just a few days.

Stories set in a post-apocalyptic dystopia usually require some time to establish the rules of their worlds, but Station Eleven rewards us with 10 enthralling episodes that hit hard from the very start. Set 20 years after a flu pandemic that led to the collapse of human civilization, Station Eleven follows a group of survivors who make a living by performing as a theatre troupe. Instead of embracing nihilism, Station Eleven focuses on grief as a shared language between survivors, who try to heal through artistic endeavors. There’s also plenty of violent conflict, but the resolutions are satisfying and earned.

After serving as showrunner for Lost and The Leftovers, Damon Lindelof helmed Watchmen, penned as a sequel to Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons’ popular 1986 comic book. The miniseries draws from the source material, continuing the story of iconic heroes and villains like Doctor Manhattan and Ozymandias, while also introducing new characters to reflect how their world has evolved. In the show, a white supremacist group inspired by the Watchmen character Rorschach clashes with the Tulsa Police Department, who are forced to conceal their identities to avoid being targeted. Angela Abar (Regina King), also known as Sister Knight, is a detective investigating the murder of her friend, but she stumbles upon long-hidden conspiracies related to vigilantism, which has been outlawed in this reality. Watchmen excels in puzzle-box plotting, which is grounded in real-world historical trauma and a nuanced understanding of superhero mythos and how it evolves.

Time travel shows like Dark have elevated the genre like never before, but Bodies reinvigorates it with just eight episodes. Based on Si Spencer and Dean Ormston’s graphic novel, Bodies opens with the appearance of a corpse in the Whitechapel area of London. The same body, however, shows up at various points in time: 1890, 1941, 2023, and 2053. The four detectives involved with the case approach it differently, as their investigation is guided by the prevailing mood of the times. This is intriguing to watch, as a detective working during World War II sports a different sensibility than someone living in the Victorian era. Bodies makes good use of its talented ensemble cast, and it's a perfect binge-watch over your next rainy weekend.

You might know Russell T Davies as the driving force behind the Doctor Who revival, but he also wrote Years and Years, a dystopian sci-fi drama that’s quite emotionally devastating. Set between 2019 and 2034, the series follows the Lyon family, who witness the rise of a controversial politician named Vivienne Rook (Emma Thompson). This is a time of great political instability in Britain. Technological progress goes hand in hand with economic upheaval, affecting the everyday lives of the Lyons. Years and Years is perfect for anyone who likes realistic sci-fi that holds up a mirror to a possible future that is more bleak than hopeful. The plausibility of the premise makes it super effective, with Rook emerging as a chilling antagonist that evokes troubling parallels to real-world politicians of the current times.

The original six-episode anime FLCL is nothing short of a masterpiece. FLCL follows Naota Nandaba, a 12-year-old whose mundane suburban life is shattered by the arrival of Haruko Haruhara, an alien woman who runs him over with a Vespa and then hits him with a bass guitar. Soon, robots and weapons begin emerging from inside Naota’s head after the injury, which Haruko uses as a portal while carrying out an intergalactic mission. This coming-of-age adventure, produced by Gainax and Production I.G, sports a standout visual identity, thanks to a seamless blend of traditional cel animation and 3D CGI. FLCL works with flawed characters, creating a raw emotional resonance that feels special in this unique standalone tale.

Although Scavengers Reign had the misfortune of being canceled by HBO Max after one season, this animated sci-fi show retroactively works well as a brilliant miniseries with a tantalizing cliffhanger ending. The story is about the survivors of a damaged cargo ship stranded on an alien planet, whose vivid vegetation hides unpredictable dangers. Although the survivors are separated into three groups, all of them witness an odd symbiosis between the flora and fauna of the region, along with a complexity that has never been seen before. The planet feels like a character in its own right, forcing every survivor to closely study its bizarre characteristics and life cycles. Scavengers Reign leans into a 1990s aesthetic, inducing hypnotic beauty and environmental dread at the same time.

Alex Garland, best known for sci-fi movies like Ex Machina and Annihilation, created Devs, a sci-fi thriller that defies straightforward analysis. A cutting-edge tech company named Amaya offers a coveted position on its mysterious quantum computing team to Sergei (Karl Glusman). When tragedy strikes, Sergei's girlfriend Lily (Sonoya Mizuno), who also works as a software engineer for the same company, becomes involved in a mystery that starts feeling more surreal and abstract by the second. Devs is Garland at his surreal, unnerving best, and the show’s eight episodes take their sweet time to arrive at a complicated conclusion about determinism and free will. Despite its slow-burn, the show keeps you hooked with its intricate structure and compelling arguments about human nature.

Any sci-fi list is incomplete without an alien invasion story, and V fits perfectly into these expectations. Well, almost. Kenneth Johnson’s (Bionic Woman, The Incredible Hulk) two-part miniseries opens with extraterrestrial beings known as the Visitors extending an olive branch as they land on Earth. They seek aid for their dying world, offering knowledge about their advanced technology in return. After the government accepts this offer, a covert infiltration begins, with Visitors rapidly gaining power in political positions. V subverts expectations by turning its invasion premise into a grounded political allegory about fascism and resistance. Instead of leaning into the tropes of the time, this 1983 show uses documentary-style realism and nuanced drama to tell a story worth remembering.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

In another universe, ABC didn't try to re-invent V, and just remade it.

When we received word that James Gunn was being replaced at DC Studios, my first reaction was shock, which then transitioned into disappointment.

I’ll be the first to admit that even though a lot of people seemed to like his version of Superman, I was not one of those people. Ditto for Supergirl, which, even though he didn’t direct it, was still under his watchful eye. So, one might ask, well, why do you even care then that he got the boot? The answer is simple.

I just like James Gunn! I think he’s a wonderful creative, and even though Superman and Supergirl didn’t hit for me, that doesn’t mean that I didn’t want him to keep cooking. It just meant that I wanted to see what else he had in the oven. I’ll explain.

First off, even though I didn’t particularly love Superman, I’ll tell you what I disliked even more - Man of Steel, which, even despite a rewatch, I still think is pretty bad. I’ve since reappraised Zack Snyder’s Justice League, and I now dig it, but here’s the thing about Zack Snyder and his now defunct Snyderverse - it was kind of boring. So much so that when it was time to say goodbye to it, I was pretty happy. It had definitely run its course.

Even though Zack Snyder did much darker versions (both literally and figuratively) of DC staples like Superman, Batman, Aquaman, The Flash, and Wonder Woman, that’s just it…he stuck with the familiar faces. Not so with James Gunn, who entered the DC universe with a new version of Suicide Squad, only to parlay that experience into eventually becoming the Co-CEO of DC Studios with Peter Safran.

From there, he greenlit WEIRD projects. Yes, we’re still getting The Batman: Part II (I hope), but from what came out of his tenure, we also got stuff like Peacemaker, Creature Commandos, Lanterns (which I’ll get into soon), and Clayface (which I’ll also get into soon). From stuff we heard rumors about, there were also supposed to be film versions of The Authority and Swamp Thing, plus TV series based on Booster Gold, Waller, and Paradise Lost. So, just a really diverse and different DC from what we’ve gotten in the past. And now, that will likely never come to be, which sucks.

I’m definitely part of the problem, because even though I started watching Lanterns, I missed a week or two and just decided that I would watch the whole show once the season was over. Now, with the news of James Gunn leaving, we might as well just say that the series is probably over, because we very well may not ever get a Season 2. That said, I didn’t hate what I saw of Lanterns, and it was taking risks that I’d never seen from a live-action take of these characters before.

In other words, even though I haven't finished it yet (And I might not now at all), I still think it was a step in the right direction. The same goes for Clayface. It wasn’t quite the horror movie I thought it’d be, but I do love that a relatively obscure Batman villain could get a movie of his own, and that it could still get number one at the box office. This wasn’t a movie about The Joker, which is a character who everybody knows. This was a movie about Clayface! And I can’t see something like that getting the greenlight from anybody besides Gunn.

Now, we’re getting another Marvel guy as Jeremy Latcham is replacing Gunn and Safran. The verdict is still out on him, and like Gunn, I’ll gladly let him cook. It just stinks that Gunn is already going away. Well, I don’t particularly care, but at least the fans are still getting a Superman follow-up in Man of Tomorrow, so I guess that’s worth something, right?

Rich is a Jersey boy, through and through. He graduated from Rutgers University (Go, R.U.!), and thinks the Garden State is the best state in the country. That said, he’ll take Chicago Deep Dish pizza over a New York slice any day of the week. Don’t hate. When he’s not watching his two kids, he’s usually working on a novel, watching vintage movies, or reading some obscure book.

#3399. Los Javis Are “Living a Dream” As La Bola Negra with Penélope Cruz, Guitarricadelafuente, and Miguel Bernardeau Collects Honors

While La Bola Negra continues to amass various accolades and early awards, like the Best Director award at this year's Cannes Film Festival and the Audience Award at the Toronto International Film Festival, directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo are extra grateful and overwhelmed by the film's reception and success in their home country of Spain.

Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

“You can't plan the miracle,” Calvo said during a panel conversation moderated by Ricky Martin at the inaugural Vanity Fair Screening Room at LACMA on Friday. “We’ve done many projects and each one of them has, they've all been good, but you never know when it's going to happen. And with La Bola Negra, we thought it was a very specific story and we thought that our audience was going to like it, but we never knew it was going to hit everyone. I think it's about to become the second highest grossing movie in the history of Spain. For me, the most beautiful part of it is the videos of the people hugging after the screenings, giving tissues to each other, comforting each other.”

Miguel Bernardeau, Guitarricadelafuente, Penélope Cruz, Javier Calvo, Javier Ambrossi and Ricky Martin at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

La Bola Negra follows several gay men whose lives are bound together by their identities, love and loss, and the looming presence of the Spanish Civil War. The acclaimed Spanish language drama spans nearly a century and stars Miguel Bernardeau, Álvaro Lafuente Calvo (the singer known as Guitarricadelafuente) in his first major acting role, Carlos Gonzalez, Milo Quifes and Penélope Cruz.

Guitarricadelafuente at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

Following an exclusive screening of the film on Friday, Martin moderated a panel conversation featuring directors Ambrossi and Calvo, and stars Cruz, Guitarricadelafuente and Bernardeau. Calvo said they are all riding high on the positive audience reactions and reception. “Creating this sense of community and hearing people saying, ‘This movie changed me. It really made me understand things about me.’ The power that art has, we forget it, but then this happens and … the rest is a dream. The rest we're living is a dream.”

The directors also consider having Cruz play a small but pivotal role in the film to be part of their living a dream. When Martin asked Cruz how her longstanding allyship to the LGBTQ+ community shaped her intention or performance, she said, “I don't even ask myself that question because it's such a part of me, of the way that I was raised. My very young parents, my parents had me when they were 21. It was a house where the values were about respect and it was just like breathing. They didn't even have to sit us down and give us a lecture about it, it was the way my family was living by example. And on top of that, then I had my other master Pedro Almodóvar who I've worked with for seven movies. And I always remember growing up thinking, why is he not the president of our country? Because he was huge in a time where his presence was really necessary, not only through his films, but also by the things that he was saying. So I feel like all of that has shaped me.”

She continued: “So when I have in my hands the possibility of playing somebody like Nené Romero, that is a reminder that unfortunately not everyone in the world feels the way we feel about everyone having a right for respect, everyone having a right to be themselves.”

Ricky Martin at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

For Martin, a Bola Negra superfan who admitted he was nervous to be asking questions instead of answering them, the actor and musician said he found out about his hosting opportunity only the day before and despite the nerves couldn't pass up the opportunity to help celebrate the film.

“I usually answer the questions, I never ask the questions, but I needed to be here,” he told the audience. “I saw this film and for a while I was in the movie. I was really touched. The acting, the way it was written, people are crying because that's just the way it is, [really moving].”

Miguel Bernardeau at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room pairs this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that includes post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself.

Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

#3398. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.
