#3397. Michael Bay And David Fincher Worked Together On An Unexpected Project That Still Holds Up Today

It's a rare thing when two equally well-known artists collaborate behind the camera. An auteur director team-up doesn't happen often, but it's certainly not unheard of. This year alone, we've seen the news that Steven Soderbergh is helping out Matt Reeves with "The Batman Part II," while Quentin Tarantino has handed the "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" character of Cliff Booth over to David Fincher for the upcoming Netflix spin-off. That latter director, as it happens, isn't a stranger to blending his creative DNA with another filmmaker. Famously, Fincher took over the troubled "Alien 3" after it had been developed for years, and inherited a script structure from director Vincent Ward that he isn't thrilled with to this day.

Around the same time, the budding film auteur (who was then still primarily known as a music video director) was approached to make a video for the rock star Meat Loaf's 1993 single "I'd Do Anything for Love (But I Won't Do That)." According to Craig Marks and Rob Tannenbaum's 2011 book "I Want My MTV: The Uncensored Story of the Music Video Revolution," Fincher and Meat Loaf's vision was pretty much what the finished video became, a Gothic riff on "Beauty and the Beast." However, Fincher's price tag caused Meat Loaf to look elsewhere for the video's director, turning to none other than an up-and-coming Michael Bay. (That's one version of the story, at least; more on that later.) Though the two didn't directly work together on it, the final video is, in its own weird way, a collaboration between the pair.

Although Michael Bay and David Fincher technically worked together at the production company Propaganda Films, their relationship was definitely more complex than just coworkers or collaborators. As various colleagues and other luminaries who worked at or with Propaganda detail in "I Want My MTV," Fincher was already a star internally given his extensive work on numerous successful music videos, and this was something that the young Bay was all too aware of. Employees told Craig Marks and Rob Tannenbaum that Bay would follow Fincher around the Propaganda offices constantly, with some people already considering him a younger version of Fincher.

This comparison came to a head when Meat Loaf approached Fincher with the gig for "I'd Do Anything for Love." According to Meat Loaf, the musician pitched Fincher with a "Beauty and the Beast" premise for the video, which Fincher allegedly loved. However, Fincher supposedly gave Meat Loaf a quote of $2.3 million, which Loaf balked at. He continued:

"So he came back a few days later and gave me a budget of $1.7 million. I said, 'David, we don't have that kind of money.' And Fincher said, 'Well then, get Michael Bay.' That's the last time Michael Bay was the cheaper option."

So, in Meat Loaf's version of the tale, the vision for the music video was the singer's idea, Fincher couldn't make the budget work, and the then-cheaper Bay got a hand-me-down project which he spun into a hit video.

In Meat Loaf's version of what happened with the "I'd Do Anything for Love (But I Won't Do That)" music video, the video was an idea had by the singer which changed hands from David Fincher to Michael Bay. However, according to Propaganda Films producer Joni Sighvatsson, it was his idea to pass the torch from Fincher to Bay, and as such, the video ended up being the one and only collaboration between the two filmmakers. As he recalled:

"Fincher was very expensive. He and the label were at an impasse over the Meat Loaf video, so I said, 'Why don't we just give this to Michael Bay?' Fincher gave it to Bay, we ended up spending $750,000, and it was a seminal video. Michael directed, and it was David's concept. That was the first and last time Fincher and Bay collaborated."

It's very possible that Sighvatsson is merely aggrandizing the story of the "I'd Do Anything for Love" video, making it sound like it's the result of two now-famous auteurs rather than just one. Or it's possible that he and Meat Loaf have hazy memories of what went down and how. All we really have to go on is the video itself, which remains one of the most visually rapturous short films of the 1990s. It's the most perfect visual encapsulation of Meat Loaf's sound, all theatricality and opera. It's got Bay's fingerprints all over it, of course, from a fetishization of hardware and sunsets to the way every woman is shot like a supermodel. Yet the video's Gothic flavor and trappings feel more Fincheresque. However it happened, the video is a gift, and we should probably thank all three men for it.

#3396. Zara Tindall Shows Cheltenham Why She's The Queen of Race Day Dressing

Zara Tindall didn’t let the cold snap stop her from enjoying a day at the races on Friday. Accompanied by her close friend Dolly Maude and country-set favorite fashion designer Jade Holland Cooper, the daughter of Princess Anne and granddaughter of Queen Elizabeth II brought a dash of regal glamour to the proceedings following a glitzy night out in support of Prince William.

And while the sun may have been out, the Olympic equestrian still needed to wrap up against the chill. Tindall opted for a long plaid coat from L'Agence, a Purdey roll-neck jumper in brown, and a fascinator from Sally-Ann Provan. She accessorized with a new pair of Hector Lion earrings, a new Fairfax & Favor handbag, and completed the look with leather boots, also from Fairfax & Favor.

Zara Tindall joined in the action at Cheltenham Racecourse on Friday

Dolly, on the other hand, wore an avant-garde feather coat with knee-high boots and what looked to be a pair of emerald tights.

The pair were last spotted together in October, when they attended the William Hill Showcase Meeting at Cheltenham, but their friendship goes way back. Long considered Zara’s best friend, Dolly became Princess Anne’s lady-in-waiting in 2024. A former NHS midwife, she helped to deliver Zara’s third child, Lucas Tindall, on the floor of Zara’s bathroom at Gatcombe Park after the plan for the birth went awry in 2021.

Jade Holland Cooper and Zara Tindall on day one of The November Meeting at Cheltenham racecourse

But Dolly’s bond with the niece of King Charles III goes back long before that. (Not for nothing did Zara’s husband, Mike Tindall, joke that the 53-year-old is “more important than I am.”) Dolly was Zara’s maid of honor when the pair tied the knot, and when Zara split from her then-fiancé, jockey Richard Johnson, in 2003, the pair moved in together—they still live close by in the Cotswolds.

Having worked as a maternity practitioner in the NHS in Gloucestershire for 13 years, Dolly also did some philanthropic work using her maternity expertise, working in the unit of a hospital in Kambia, Sierra Leone for a month in 2013. At Kambia, she taught staff basic nursing skills. Before qualifying as a nurse, Dolly studied fashion and Cordon Bleu cookery at Eastbourne College of Food and Fashion, graduating in 1989.

Zara Tindall also braved the stormy weather for a day at Cheltenham with Dolly in October

Dolly Maude is known for her love of horses—a passion she shares with Zara and Princess Anne—and is often seen in Ascot’s royal box alongside the Princess Royal. In March 2024, she made her first official appearance as the Princess Royal’s lady-in-waiting, a momentous occasion that marked a new phase of her enduring bond with the royal family.

The royal confidant has four children with her husband Chris: Billy, who studied at Swansea University; Nell, who trained at the Central School of Ballet; a keen skier, Ted; and Mary.

Princess Anne's daughter wrapped up in a warm plaid coat and roll-neck jumper

Concerning Dolly’s appointment, another friend of Mrs. Maude's told The Telegraph, “She’s such a great girl. For the Princess Royal, it’s a perfect fit because of their shared love of dogs and horses. She’s not only extremely close to Zara, she also gets on brilliantly with the Princess. She’s fiercely loyal and discreet. It’s a great match.”

While much of Zara Tindall’s time this season has been spent touring the country’s most prestigious racing meets, she still found time to support her cousin, Prince William, at one of his treasured annual traditions. The Prince of Wales helped to put together the Tusk Conservation Awards at Raffles on Wednesday night and invited Zara to the celebration of conservation, alongside Lady Amelia and Lady Eliza Spencer and the Marchioness of Bath.

Dolly Maud made her debut as lady-in-waiting for the Princess Royal at the 2024 Commonwealth Day Service in March

Zara showcased her characteristically elegant style, donning a sapphire-blue Rebecca Vallance short-sleeved midi number, aptly named the “Crown Jewel” dress, which she paired with Kiki McDonough earrings. It is not the first time that the royal has lent her support to Prince William’s second-longest patronage: she also joined the crowd at the Tusk Awards in 2025, donning Rebecca Vallance again, and tearing up at the Prince of Wales’ speech in honor of those who gave their lives as rangers.

Zara Tindall and the Marchioness of Bath at the Tusk Awards

#3395. What to Expect From Best Buy's 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales

For all intents and purposes, Black Friday sales are already here. There are plenty of deals out already, even though we're weeks away from the actual event. One of the reasons for that is the competition retailers have with each other to be the first to get your money. One of the retailers that is making the biggest early splash is Best Buy, confirming their entire plan for the rest of the year. Here's what you need to know.

Best Buy has announced the following events:

DoorBoosters: A Halloween sale from Oct. 30 to Nov. 1.

Early Black Friday Deals and Doorbusters: The official start of early Black Friday deals on Nov. 6. New deals will drop every Friday.

Black Friday Doorbusters and Deals: Best Buy says this will be its main sale, starting on Thursday, Nov. 19 and running until Nov. 28 with deals on "computing, gaming, home theater, wearables, and more."

Cyber Sunday and Monday: Best Buy is extending Cyber Monday to five days and says you can find deals going up to 50% off select tech.

Last-minute savings: The Christmas sale will run from Dec. 18 until Dec. 24.

You don't need to be any kind of member to shop Best Buy's Black Friday in July sale; however, it is free to sign up for a My Best Buy membership, which will get you free shipping. If you join one of their paid subscriptions (My Best Buy Plus for $49.99 per year or My Best Buy Total for $179.99 per year), you'll get faster free shipping, exclusive prices and deals, an extended 60-day return window on most products, and access to select sales, like the Member Deals Days sale that is going on right now. Paid members will also earn extra rewards from both the current sale and the upcoming Black Friday in July sale.

You can find deals on TVs, laptops, headphones, video games, electric bikes, and more. There will be new deals every week in stores, on its website, and in the Best Buy mobile app. They'll offer price matching, meaning if the price drops further during the sale (Dec. 24), they will match it and offer a refund.

Here are the best deals I've found so far. I'll be updating these deals throughout the sale, so make sure to come back and see what's new. Remember that new deals drop every day.

Best Buy price matches its own products, so if a product drops in price later, you'd get those savings too, but it does not cover any deals coming from a competitor's Black Friday sale. There are some other important exceptions you can read in more detail here.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

The other major retailers doing Black Friday sales are Amazon, Target, and Walmart. Currently, Amazon has many early deals, seeing their lowest prices yet. Target has some week-long deals and a Deal of the Day. Walmart will have three Black Friday and Cyber Monday shopping events. Nowadays, large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

Alan Ritchson’s hit show, Reacher, has fortunately been renewed for Season 5, but the action star has also been delving into new kinds of projects in the meantime. While he’s soon to play an action hero in the Navy SEAL biopic about Mike Thornton, he’ll also be co-starring with Arnold Schwarzenegger in a buddy Christmas flick, The Man With the Bag. While Ritchson may already have an entry on the upcoming Christmas movies schedule, he's talking about another wild yuletide role he believes he'd nail.

After Reacher blew up, Alan Ritchson had an incredible number of Hollywood offers that he said were “mostly action stuff.” No surprise there, given how well the actor has embodied that role. Still, he is also starting to expand his comedy resume, and The Man With the Bag is the latest entry in that list.

With the comedy thing in mind, it's worth pointing out a fan recently took to Threads to ask what kind of role Ritchson should take on next. The star himself responded with an amusing idea I really want to become a reality:

Yes, please! We’ve seen plenty of movies where Santa has an eccentric relative, like in Fred Claus, Arthur Christmas and Noelle. However, we've never seen movies about any relatives of the naughty Mr. Grinch. If Ritchson ever played The Grinch’s “grosser, fatter cousin,” that could create levels of comedy similar to Chris Hemsworth playing an overweight Thor in Avengers: Endgame. Seriously, can someone speak to Dr. Seuss' estate about this?

Another reason I'd love to see this is because it would mark another chance to subvert tropes with a Christmas movie. For example, it was entertaining to see David Harbor playing a savage Santa giving season’s beatings in Violent Night. So, if we can see a tough guy like the Titans actor make The Grinch look like he belongs on The Nice List by comparison, I’m all for it!

When his bag of Christmas presents gets stolen, Claus recruits a local thief (played by Ritchson) to show him how to perfectly perform the heist to retrieve the bad.

Honestly, this is the perfect action hero duo for such a holiday flick. And, while Ritchson is known for playing tough guys, we’ve seen his comedic side come out in roles like The Wedding Ringer, Playdate and Lazer Team.

So, while Alan Ritchson's upcoming holiday film should be fun, I'm keeping my fingers crossed that he does play the “grosser, fatter cousin” of The Grinch, as he desires. For now, though, look forward to seeing him and Schwarzenegger in the The Man With the Bag, which will be available to stream with a Prime Video subscription starting on December 2nd.

#3393. I Can't Wait to Ignore the Main Story of GTA 6

Have fun robbing stores, I'm going snorkeling

It's hard to believe, but after years of waiting, we're less than a week away from the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6. Tons of people are planning to take time off from work or school in order to sink their teeth into Rockstar's newest adventure. Many of them will be diving headfirst into Jason and Lucia's story, taking on high-stakes robberies to see how the couple's ascent through Vice City's underworld plays out. But for me, the "grand theft auto" of GTA 6 is actually the least intriguing element of 2026's most anticipated game. I couldn't care less about shooting people and stealing cars. I'm far more excited to explore the vast, glorious sandbox Rockstar has created.

One of the major draws of Sega's Yakuza series is that it provides a fantastic virtual tourism experience. When I visited Tokyo for the first time, I walked out of Shinjuku Station and knew exactly where I was, having spent so much time as Kiryu running around the streets of Kamurocho. I'm hoping for a similar kind of experience with GTA 6. I've never been to Miami, but I'd like to go someday. Now I can check out all those cool Art Deco buildings and take a fan boat through a swamp without spending IRL money on bottle service. Pound for pound, video games are the cheapest form of vacation out there, and this one's shaping up to be a doozy.

I'm also looking forward to meeting all the wonderful weirdos Rockstar has crafted to inhabit this dazzling sandbox. One of my favorite elements of Red Dead Redemption 2 was simply talking to people and watching their reactions. If you kick off a fistfight in Valentine's saloon and get thrown in jail for the night, passerby will scold you and warn you not to "cause trouble" the next few times you visit. My favorite memories of that game have little to do with hunting O'Driscolls — it's all the dumb shenanigans I bumbled into while ignoring the main campaign, like doing an oopsie and shooting a man when I just wanted to steal his sick raccoon-skin cap, then getting run out of town by multiple lawmen and racking up a hefty bounty as a result of my thieving ways.

GTA 6 promises to up this kind of immersion by several orders of magnitude. Back in August, thanks to a New York Times feature about the game, we learned that Rockstar created an entire studio just for NPCs. "Once we managed to accomplish that level of interactive fidelity in a more sparsely populated version of America 100 years ago, we were already imagining what it would be like if we could do that at the scale and density of a modern environment," Rockstar North co-head Rob Nelson told the Times. If GTA 6 feels more like Red Dead 2 than GTA 5, I'd be delighted.

Based on what we've seen in the Netflix Extended Look and various previews of the game, GTA 6 will have literally dozens of minigames and optional activities to distract me from the central plot. These include fishing, jet skiing, mini-golf, scuba diving, lifting weights, hunting, racing, fan boating, billiards, basketball, and parachuting. There's even an in-universe animated TV show, Macca and Friends, that I'm sure is going to be ridiculously in-depth, just like Red Dead 2's movie theater in San Denis. I mean, I guess I'll shoot some people in GTA 6 if I really have to, but honestly? I'm just here for the vibes.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

#3392. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

#3391. 25 Years Later, Dumbledore's Best Sorcerer's Stone Line Is Still The Greatest Harry Potter Quote

In the wizarding world of Harry Potter, Albus Dumbledore is often referred to as one of the wisest and most powerful wizards in history ... so, it's lucky for the titular boy wizard that Dumbledore just happens to be the headmaster of his magical academy. In the original Harry Potter film franchise (which is getting a new life, in a way, with the forthcoming HBO Harry Potter TV show), Harry Potter, as played by Daniel Radcliffe (who may not watch the HBO reboot series), leaves his humdrum life with his mean non-magical relatives behind and starts attending Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, run by Dumbledore (Richard Harris in the first two movies before the legendary actor passed away in 2002, at which point Michael Gambon took over). There, he meets his best friends Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger (Rupert Grint and Emma Watson), learns how to cast magic spells, and has his first encounter, so to speak, with the Dark Lord Voldemort who tried to kill him as a baby.

Let's all be honest: Dumbledore sort of gets all the best quotes in the Harry Potter franchise. After all, his entire purpose is to dispense wisdom, so he drops a lot of stone-cold bangers. But what's his most memorable quote from the first movie, "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" (which hit theaters on November 16, 2001)? We think we've pinpointed the perfect Dumbledore line from this film 25 years after its release.

During his first Christmas at Hogwarts, Harry receives the Cloak of Invisibility from an anonymous friend who leaves him a note telling Harry it belonged to his late father James. Emboldened by this gift, Harry starts exploring the halls of Hogwarts by night, and one evening, he stumbles upon a room containing a mirror that shows him not only James but his late mother, Lily, and even the extended family he never got a chance to meet. Understandably, the orphaned Harry becomes obsessed with visiting the mirror every night, and despite his confusion when Ron sees something completely different in said mirror, he returns until he finds Dumbledore waiting in the mirror's little room.

Dumbledore explains that it's called the Mirror of Erised, and it shows you your deepest desire. That's why Harry sees the family he never knew, and it's also why Dumbledore tells Harry, "It does not do to dwell on dreams, Harry, and forget to live." Dumbledore is right: Harry's devotion to seeing his family every night in the mirror is a short-term comfort that's terrible for the child's overall mental health, and even though Dumbledore tells him the mirror is moving to a different location anyway, Harry does promise not to look for it again.

Not only that, but in the third act of "Sorcerer's Stone" (as Harry looks for the titular object), we learn that the mirror is part of the defense system that keeps the Stone safe when Harry stares into it and receives the stone not to use but to have. In this way, Harry isn't dwelling on dreams, he's utilizing the mirror to achieve a vital goal.

#3390. 25 Funniest 'Peanuts' Comics from the 1960s That Prove Charles M. Schulz Is Unbeatable

And maybe Charles Schulz’s funniest-ever story

The year 1964 was an election year in America. After assuming office in late November 1963 following the assassination of President John F. Kennedy, Democratic President Lyndon Johnson was running for reelection on a platform of civil rights and combating poverty. His opponent was Republican Senator Barry Goldwater, who ran on a conservative platform of smaller government. Johnson ended up winning in a landslide with 61 percent of the popular vote and 44 out of 50 states voting for him.

As is the case with every presidential election year, the race was the number one news story, and it invaded many other aspects of American life, up to and including the immensely popular comic strip Peanuts, albeit in a very Peanuts-appropriate way.

Beginning on Oct. 5, 1964, Charles Schulz launched a month-long story about Linus running for school president. His sister Lucy convinces him to run and acts as his campaign manager, while Charlie Brown becomes his running mate. Linus runs a pretty savvy campaign, conducting rousing speeches about the same nonsense real politicians do, talking about “moral decline” and other amorphous platitudes. Linus even reaches 92 percent support in the polls at one point, but on Oct. 21, the campaign takes a shocking turn that changes everything.

The story is probably Schulz’s funniest-ever long-running story. The whole build-up to the big shift is a brilliant slow burn, while still being quite funny along the way. There are a lot of amusing political points that Schulz makes about our system, some of which still feel pretty prescient. While most Peanuts comics work just fine out of context, this 25-day arc is best enjoyed in its entirety, to get the full effect (or at least some of the same effect) newspaper readers experienced back in 1964.

Perhaps Linus’ face in panel number three should have prepared people for where this story would go.

It’s pretty sad that teachers' salaries are still such an issue more than 60 years later.

Linus is officially nominated here by Schroeder, who can’t seem to skip an opportunity to bore people about Beethoven.

Linus’ acceptance speech puts up a serious red flag when he says he may do away with elections. This is one of those things that feels especially relevant in today’s political climate. I would not have taken Linus for a fascist.

After his nomination and acceptance speech, Linus brings in his vice presidential candidate, Charlie Brown. I think I agree with Lucy here when she says “Good Grief!” to the choice. I mean, just look at the Christmas special (which aired a year after this). Linus is an excellent, inspiring public speaker, while Charlie Brown can’t even direct that goofy little play or pick out a decent tree. He’s not meant for leadership.

I, for one, think Linus should have nominated Snoopy for vice president. Sure, it’s a gimmick, but there have been several times in US history where America would have been better off with a dog as VP (just look up a guy named Aaron Burr).

“The press is against me!” also feels like it could have run today with equal relevance.

You may have noticed that this series skipped Oct. 11. That’s because the Sunday strips had to be standalone, as many people only got Sunday papers. Also, because they were in color and had wider distribution, Sunday strips had to be completed much farther ahead than the daily strips.

This is just bad journalism on Violet’s part.

Linus’ propensity for religious fervor is so incredibly funny. What’s even funnier is how effective it is.

All of these ideas are super-solid and should happen in real life.

#3389. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3388. How To Rob A Bank Pays Tribute To A Bruce Willis Movie With A Clever Easter Egg

There's something of a paradox when it comes to making legitimately good crime action movies. On the one hand, most filmmakers want the action to be as accurate and based in reality as possible, whether it be robbing a bank, taking down a security truck, or whatnot. On the other hand, they don't necessarily wish to inspire criminals who would copycat a crime they happened to see in a movie, especially as that's an instance where all publicity doesn't necessarily equal good publicity. (Remember the brouhaha over a crime allegedly inspired by 1995's "Money Train," a case which only just reached a resolution a few years ago?)

The irony of the new crime action film "How to Rob a Bank" is that it intentionally wishes to exist on the edge separating these two sides. The film, written by Mark Bianculli and directed by David Leitch, concerns a group of friends who, upon becoming radicalized by the various injustices of the current U.S. wealth gap, decide to become bank robbers. Their gimmick is hiding their crimes in plain sight, filming themselves in the act and detailing exactly how they did it for their YouTube channel (all while hiding their identities, naturally).

Thus, Leitch and Bianculli have to include a bunch of real-world tactics and hardware without going too far. To help accomplish this, they have their bandits (who've dubbed themselves the Wolf Pack) borrow a technique from the sequel to the bonafide action classic that is "Die Hard," i.e. 1990's "Die Hard 2." And while the characters never mention the movie on-screen, the inclusion of a trick used by that film's villains works as both an Easter egg homage to that movie as well as a bit of real-world verisimilitude, as this particular tactic does sound like it could actually work.

In "Die Hard 2," the terrorists holding Washington Dulles International Airport hostage around Christmas are former U.S. Army soldiers who've been corrupted by a military drug lord. After Bruce Willis' John McClane their plans while getting a quip or two in, the airport brass call in a military counter-terrorism unit. Then, during the subsequent firefights between the counter-terrorism unit and the terrorists, each group makes a point of switching to clips for their machine guns labeled with blue instead of red stripes. Eventually, McClane discovers this code means blue for blank rounds and red for live rounds, revealing that both units are working together.

While the terrorists in "Die Hard 2" have devised a fairly elaborate scheme, the blank-vs-live rounds element seems fairly simple and self-explanatory. In other words, it has an authenticity about it, which is why its use in "How to Rob a Bank" feels smooth rather than belabored. The Wolf Pack want to make their robberies feel threatening to the authorities they encounter and only elect to use live rounds to save their own skins. As such, adopting the blue and red labeled gun clips makes for an easy to understand visual code, so much so that the characters in the film barely have to explain it to the audience.

For those who know "Die Hard 2," this is a cute Easter egg calling back to that film's intuitive code system. Yet, for those who don't know, the element still completely works, and its realism adds to the movie's credibility. Who knows if anyone has used it (or will) in real life, but it helps "How to Rob a Bank" exist on that edge.

One Piece Season 2 ended with the reveal that Mr. 0 was actually Crocodile, a member of the World Government's Seven Warlords of the Sea. This title grants him immunity from the Marines. In exchange for being the World Government's ally, warlords can continue with their pirate activities.

With One Piece season 3 finally tackling the Alabasta arc, Crocodile will officially step out of the shadows to enact his plans to hijack the Alabasta Kingdom's throne from Vivi's father, King Cobra. While he becomes the new season's main villain, another popular antagonist will begin to cast an even bigger shadow over the entire narrative: Blackbeard. Luffy's brother Ace, portrayed by Cobra Kai star Xolo Maridueña, will finally be introduced during the Alabasta arc. Because of Blackbeard's overpowering Devil Fruit gift and manipulative strategy, Ace's unsanctioned solo revenge mission eventually leads to one of One Piece's most heartbreaking story arcs to date. The writers could easily start laying the groundwork for Blackbeard's live-action arrival in the upcoming season.

Luffy and Blackbeard are ideological mirrors of one another, sharing many similarities from their unwavering belief in dreams to having the mysterious "Will of D," to their ambitious goal of claiming the One Piece. #3386. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3385. Miles Teller Opens Up About ‘Paper Tiger,’ Adam Driver, and Losing His Home Before Filming James Gray’s Movie

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Neon will release “Paper Tiger” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

An actor who started at 22, Miles Teller earned rave reviews out of the gate for his debut performance in “Rabbit Hole,” when he was signed swiftly by CAA, followed by “Whiplash” and “The Spectacular Now.” He has worked steadily ever since, with everything from auteur fare like “Whiplash” and studio franchises such as “Divergent” and “The Fantastic Four” to his name. Holding his own opposite Tom Cruise in the blockbuster “Top Gun: Maverick” pushed him into the limelight, but he was still playing Rooster, the son of radar intercept officer Nick “Goose” Bradshaw (Anthony Edwards). Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

His latest role in James Gray’s “Paper Tiger,” which earned raves at Cannes, sees Teller play a real grown-up, Irwin Pearl, a Queens engineer and family man opposite Scarlett Johansson as his wife Hester, and Adam Driver as Gary, his older brother, a former cop. No longer the onscreen son of a leading man, Teller is now firmly in father roles. Irwin is slowly building a solid business when his brother offers a quicker route to success. Alas, the naive Irwin goes for the idea and, during an unscheduled night reconnaissance, blunders with the Russian mafia, seeing things he should not see.

I sat down with Teller at the Carlton Hotel in Cannes after the movie wowed in its world premiere. He was seeing it for the first time. We do not count fake standing ovations at IndieWire, but I was there and can vouch that it played well. The dynamic between Driver and Teller is powerful, with Johansson holding her own in the middle. Even though the movie did not land a Cannes prize, it will play the fall festivals and enter awards contention.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Anne Thompson: You’ve played the Cannes game before.

Miles Teller: I’m one of those actors [where] it’s pretty hard to watch yourself. I always have a hard time. I was here with Nic [Winding] Refn for this limited series that we did [“Too Old to Die Young”]; that was my first time at Cannes. I’ve done Cannes with “Maverick.” It’s truly an overload of the senses.

You’ve never given this kind of performance before.

Hopefully, your taste evolves as you get older. It struck me that on my first film, “Rabbit Hole,” I was playing the wide-eyed teenager, and we filmed the majority of that movie in a house in Queens. And now I’m playing the part of the parent.

That was your breakout. You revealed some strong emotions related to your own car accident. I’m so sorry you lost your home in the Palisades Fire.

When I met James for this movie, our house had just burned down. And I had just lost my grandfather. We were renting a place in Santa Barbara, and then I got the call saying James wanted to meet me for this. That infused this story and performance with a lot of love as well, because of that feeling of home that Keleigh [Sperry] and I had lost. I’d lost it with my grandfather, but then also just the physical place where you can have people come gather, where you have memories attached. We did not have that, so that probably came through.

Do you believe that you have to grow up a bit before you can find your way in Hollywood?

If you want to have a long career, the audience, hopefully, that you attract in your early 20s, as they get older, and they start having kids or not having kids, but just getting more life experience under the belt, you want to reflect that in your choices as well. And James makes movies for adults, he deals with characters. I’ve loved every one of his films, and I’ve always felt like he gets incredible performances, so I was excited to play a man at this point.

Every actor is going to get to a place where you know it’s tough because you do something that has some success to it, and then people want you to keep doing that same thing, whether that’s from the studio side or you keep getting scripts that are that same kind of thing.

When I started out with “Rabbit Hole,” and then I wanted to audition for comedy, they’re like, “he’s not funny.” And then you do comedies, and you want to be going back to drama, and they’re like, “Willard from ‘Footloose,’ what are you talking about?”

I remember “Bleed for This.” [He gets up to close the shutters to block the noise for my audio, and pours me some water.] That was a point where I was 27, and I said, “OK, I want to step up and play, not the funny friend. Playing Vinny Patz, as a five-time world champion boxer, very much a man’s man, absolutely, that was something. But it always comes down to a director, oftentimes taking what I feel is a chance on me, casting me in a role that I haven’t necessarily shown those abilities before, but believing that I could do that.

You had to carry the TV series “The Offer,” in which you play Al Ruddy, who produced “The Godfather,” running interference between Francis Ford Coppola, Robert Evans at Paramount, and the mafia. That must have been tough.

I was intimidated by portraying Al, to be honest with you, not just his bravado and accomplishments, but it felt like I was playing somebody who had more life experience than I had at that point, and there was a certain maturity to that. I enjoyed that Al, being a man of action, if he takes a step back, he’s taking two steps forward. Typically, there’s five or six different producers doing all these things: that was all Al.

In “Paper Tiger,” there’s one scene between you and Adam Driver where you get into a fight. Your face was shaking with anger.

I know. I saw that. Yeah, there was a twitch going on there. At least in my own life, your family can get to you in a way that nobody else can. Those feelings are so deeply rooted and established from childhood, so I guess in that moment, and neither one is fully aware of the ramifications of the Russians, this deal going bad, and how it’s affecting that person in their life. In that particular scene you’re letting out. It’s not just about what they’re talking about right there. It’s an entire lifetime of misgivings — he’s going to let him have it. When that’s happened to me in my personal life, you feel so bad afterwards. It’s a horrible feeling when you’re not talking to a sibling or your parents, and often it’s hard to make amends.

How did James Gray base this film on his own father’s experience?

With his father, that was the biggest regret. He took it to his deathbed, the fact that he brought this [danger] into his home, and his family became collateral damage for his business ambition. [In the movie] the venture that he went into, to go into business with his brother, he makes a mistake that was very naive. I think it’s easy to forgive this mistake. When I read this script, I had a ton of empathy for this family in this situation, and then also what Hester is going through.

Did you have any models for your character in this movie? Your own father was an engineer.

No, he was a project controls manager, but worked nuclear. The men that I grew up around, my father and my grandfather, were strong men, but very sensitive, and were dependable, reliable. My grandfather was married to my grandmother for 60-something years. I never saw her open a door for herself. I never saw her carry her own bag. He was a Marine, but he also was well-versed in world history, and he was a sweet man who was never afraid to show that side of him, but he also would stand up for himself, or his wife, or his kids, whatever it is. He took a lot of pride in that.

I found it refreshing, even comforting, to watch a movie about a kind, loving family man who’s good at his job, who’s competent. He’s a good dad. You haven’t shown that side to such a degree.

I felt immensely for this father and husband. It was clear he loves his kids, and he’s trying to lead by example, and to show them that success in life is not based on the car you drive. He wants to show them that you can build something on your own merit, and if you work hard and treat people right, that you can earn it.

Those values are no longer as respected as they once were. So, if you were to look back at your career, you did some studio work, like the “Divergent” series. Have you made a course correction? That comes with maturity, too, when an actor recognizes what they want to do rather than doing what people tell them to.

Early on, I didn’t want to feel like I was repeating what I had just done. I didn’t want people to be able to expect what I was going to do next. I always want to defend young actors in their careers, because people say, “Oh, why did you make that choice? Why did they make that choice?” You’re just hoping to get a role, and it’s less than 10 percent of people in SAG who pay their bills off acting alone. We all want to work on the best material with the best directors and the best actors. There’s an ebb and flow. I used to be more critical of work other people were doing, because you get thrown into this rat race when you’re first starting out.

Who were you competing with? Who was in your class?

It was me, and Michael B. [Jordan] and [Robert] Pattinson and Shia [LaBeouf] and [Zac] Efron was big, “The Hunger Games” stuff was blowing up. As I’ve gotten older, I appreciate and have respect for longevity, if you can hang around. I always wanted to contribute. When I was going to the Lee Strasberg Institute at NYU, and looked on the wall, there’s all these incredible actors that went through there. I hold acting and actors in such high regard, whether it’s theater or film or TV.

You seem to be delivering performances at such a level that you keep getting more work. The work itself is selling you. You had to counteract some bad press. Did that hurt you in terms of getting roles?

That was so mishandled. The reason why I have not done profiles is because I said, “Wow, if I’m not doing this interview on camera, this person can misquote things or put things out of order or say things that didn’t happen.” It felt like such a violation of what actually transpired. I told my team, “Guys, I don’t think I’m doing this again, because I’m reading this and this doesn’t sound like me to me. This is not life, so why would I ever want to be a part of something where they can just put that in?” So it’s unfortunate that being a good person, that doesn’t sell. People want to click on the negativity. If you go to bed and put your head on your pillow and how you treat people truly, that’s what matters. That [2015] interview was like 12 years ago.

Some people still remember. Well, casting directors know who you are and what you can do.

The actors, the directors, the crew, the producers, you can’t hide who you are when you’re on set.

Legal questions surround the Michael Jackson estate and his lawyer, John Branca, who you play in “Michael,” which has grossed $707 million worldwide. What’s going on with the sequel?

They had to rework the third act of the last movie. As far as the sequel goes, I know they’re working on it. I haven’t had any direct discussions, other than the team is excited to complete that story.

#3384. 7 Decades Later, the Most Satisfying Movie of All Time Is Free on YouTube

It’s widely considered to be one of the greatest films ever made.

Sometimes, all I’m looking for in a movie is a really great performance. I don’t need grand adventure or killer special effects or stakes so impossibly big that I can’t relate to them. I just want to be moved by an actor (and a script) with as few frills and distractions as possible. Currently, for free (with ads) on YouTube, there is a movie that contains no less than 12 of those kinds of great performances, and it's one of the most satisfying films ever made.

12 Angry Men begins at the very end of a trial, just as the jury is about to go deliberate. This is a murder case where a son is being accused of stabbing his father to death. The judge reminds the jury of their duty, and that the sentence for this person, if convicted, will be death. Silently, the young man who barely looks to be out of high school looks at the jury and a couple of members look back. Then the jury goes off into the jury room.

The men pile in and take a few minutes to get settled, but once they do, the foreman suggests they take a vote to see where everyone stands. Of the 12-man jury, 11 of the men believe the man is guilty, while the 12th man is unsure. From there, the discussion unfolds about whether to convict or not.

That’s literally it, and that’s all you need.

To bring home my point about no frills, 95 percent of this black-and-white movie from 1957 takes place in the jury room (just the very beginning and the very end don’t). The movie is just 12 guys in a room talking and making their points, arguing, and revealing their prejudices. The characters don’t even have names, they’re just called “Juror 1,” “Juror 2,” etc. And while Henry Fonda, who plays the dissenting Juror 8, is the star of the movie with the most compelling performance, every single one of those characters is given something interesting to do and is a fully fleshed-out character in their own right.

Juror 1 is played by Martin Balsam, the foreman and the steady hand who leads the discussion, but even he finds himself shaken by the arguments that break out in the room.

Juror 2 is John Fiedler, a character actor who may be best remembered as the voice of Piglet. He’s an easygoing, seemingly weak man, but he learns to stand up for himself in the room, especially after he’s insulted or it’s revealed that bigotry is part of the reason why some of the men who agree with him want to convict.

Lee J. Cobb is Juror 3, a loudmouth jerk determined to convict. He’s easy to root against because of how obnoxious he is, but he becomes more and more sympathetic once you figure out the source of his anger had more to do with his own estranged son than it does with the accused.

Juror 4 is played by E. G. Marshall. He’s a cold, analytical man who presents the best, most logical case for conviction.

The Odd Couple’s Jack Klugman has one of the most sympathetic character arcs as Juror 5. Like the young man whose life is in their hands, Klugman is a “slum kid” and he objects to the innuendos about the accused based on his social standing.

Juror 6, played by Edward Binns, is an understated blue-collar guy who is easy for the viewer to identify with.

Jack Warden is the kind of character actor who makes you go, “Oh, I know that guy,” even if you’re not sure from what. He was in The Great Muppet Caper as Kermit and Fozzie’s boss at the newspaper and in Dirty Work as Artie Lange’s dad. As Juror 7, he often steals the show by cracking jokes and making it very clear that he’s got tickets to a Yankee game after this and he really doesn’t want to miss it.

Then there’s the star of the film, Henry Fonda as Juror 8. He’s a principled, thoughtful man who originally dissents not because he’s sure of the innocence of the accused, but because he’s just not sure. He thinks, because this is a death penalty case, that they should take the time to discuss everything — a man’s life is at least worth that. His performance is moving and the arguments he makes are compelling, but the movie isn’t just him convincing everybody. He states his points and, one by one, more people come to his side by bringing up their own points and even convincing themselves. It’s the unique kind of performance that is both commanding and, in many ways, quite subtle.

Juror 9 is Joseph Sweeney, an old man who is easy to overlook, but he makes some of the most profound observations about the trial.

Juror 10, played by Ed Begley, is a bigoted business owner who is determined to convict simply because of the defendant's unspecified ethnicity. (A key point to the case is that it took place in a New York City slum and the accused murderer is darker-skinned than everyone on the jury, which is incredibly relevant to how things proceed in the jury room.)

Juror 11 is George Voskovec, a European watchmaker who also finds himself a target of some bigotry in the room.

Finally, Juror 12 is Robert Webber, an ad man who doesn't really care about the proceedings, but eventually rises to the occasion.

Written by Reginald Rose, 12 Angry Men was directed by master filmmaker Sidney Lumet, famous for films like Dog Day Afternoon, Serpico, Network, and many others. 12 Angry Men was his directorial debut and he shows tremendous wisdom in just letting the actors do their thing. Relatively early in the movie, it becomes clear that the trajectory of the film is that each man changes their minds, one at a time. But the interesting part is the why of each man.

Most compelling of all is to figure out when you, the viewer, switch sides. Going into the jury room, the majority is convinced of the man’s guilt because the case they just witnessed was convincing. The evidence appears to point in favor of conviction, and it's laid out, at first, to make sure the viewer is also on the side of conviction. But one by one, the men change their minds and the experience of watching the film is that you, at some point, change your mind, too.

#3383. The Apple Watch's New 'Siri Recap' Feature Is Even Creepier Than I Expected

The “Siri Recap” feature that Apple announced in September is finally available in a developer beta, and I’ve spent the last 24 hours with the feature turned on. It’s even more unsettling than the “Live Rewind” feature that launched at the same time. It listens to all my conversations, and produces summaries that are both helpful and deeply creepy.

I have a button in the watch’s Control Center that can turn the recapping abilities off, but if I forget to do so, Siri listens to everything. I’ll get a recap of my entire evening, presented in roughly hour-long chunks, including things I would have completely forgotten I had even heard about.

The recaps somberly mention silly memes my kids were laughing about, and make major bullet points out of offhand remarks from brief conversations. If a conversation sticks to a single topic, I’ll often get a reasonably good summary of it, with specific facts and numbers highlighted; but just as often, Siri will get confused and mix up several topics or completely mishear a name or phrase.

Apple has four features that it considers part of “audio intelligence":

Music recognition, better known as Shazam. We’ve had a version of this on the Apple Watch for a long time now, although it has some improvements and now identifies music automatically.

Sound recognition, which can notify you about doorbells and babies crying. A version of this launched in 2020 as an accessibility feature.

Live Rewind, which gives you an on-wrist transcript of the last 15 seconds of detected speech.

Siri Recaps, which summarizes entire conversations for you to read on your phone.

Live Rewind had the flashiest demo from the Apple event: A server rattled off the day’s specials at a restaurant, and then the Apple Watch-wearing diner checked his watch to see a readout of exactly which dishes had just been mentioned. The utility is both obvious and kind of unnecessary: Why wouldn’t you just ask the server to repeat the list while they’re standing right there?

I haven’t found myself using Live Rewind, except out of curiosity about how the feature works. I discovered that it doesn’t pick up song lyrics very well, and also that by the time I think to check what was just said in a conversation, more than 15 seconds has passed since the part I was unsure about. I haven’t yet found a reason to use it for real.

But Siri Recaps? Those are both useful and unsettling. I enabled the feature, and decided to test it out later. But since it was on, it dutifully listened in as I picked up my son from school and gave him an update on an ailing family member’s health. We stopped by the library, and along the way we chatted about a variety of things: holiday travel plans, library policies, and the possibility of humans living in space in the future. Siri was listening to it all.

At least for now, the feature is only available in a developer beta, so sign up for that now if you want to try it. You'll need an Apple Watch Series 12 (or Ultra 4) and an iPhone 16 or better, excluding the 16e. (I have a 16 Pro, so I'm good.)

After you're updated to 27.3, go into the Watch app, tap Siri, and turn on Siri Recap. You can set a schedule for when it should listen (for example, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., if you want it on for the work day but off for the evening). You'll need to set a passcode on your watch, and you'll be guided through a step to upgrade your audio connection. The control center on the watch will have a button you can use to turn Siri recaps on and off at will. To read your recaps, go to the Siri app on your phone.

But still: I feel weird publishing the contents of these recaps, because they do contain things that people said to me in what they assumed was a private setting. I had the feature on when I attended a choir practice, and Siri recapped the brief chats I had with other choir members before and after practice. (Interestingly, it did not recap any of the quiet conversations I had with fellow sopranos while the tenors were rehearsing their part. I’m not sure if the watch was unable to hear us over the music, or if Siri is programmed not to listen when music is being played.)

Because speakers aren’t identified, it seems Siri doesn’t know what to do when there is a disagreement. A human note-taker would jot down that Person A made a point in favor of something, and person B made a point against. But when my son and I disagreed about how likely space colonization might be in the future, the recap didn’t reflect the separate positions that were put forth. It summarized the conversation as including “debating the feasibility and timeline of human space colonization and asteroid mining,” which isn’t exactly accurate, but close enough.

When it comes to the content of the discussion, the recap notes a bullet point of “skepticism regarding permanent space colonies within the next 100 years.” It didn’t include my reasons for being skeptical, and didn’t mention my son’s opposing viewpoint at all. If I were using this recap to jog my memory of the conversation, it wouldn’t be all that helpful.

Details are sometimes egregiously incorrect. After a discussion about a family member’s health, the recap had notes on the prognosis of “father.” The family member we discussed is not anybody’s father. Names in general seem to be a problem; I recommended a book to my son, and the recap includes notes about the content of the book, but not its title. The book’s author appears in the introduction to the recap (sort of a summary of a summary), but not in the content of the recap itself where the book is mentioned.

I should probably turn Siri recaps off. It seems wrong to let people chat with me without letting them know that their conversation is being ... well, not technically recorded, but basically recorded.

But it’s so tempting to leave it on so that I can review my day. Some of the details in the recaps are useful, like the dates that were discussed as options for a holiday party. The recaps will be deleted in about a week (unless I save them to the notes app), so if I want to remind myself of a conversation a few days ago, I should be able to scroll back through my recaps and find it.

I would be a fool to rely on the recaps, though. The most important points of a conversation are often left out; Siri doesn’t know what’s actually important, and there’s no way to guide it as to what to pay attention to. Specific details can be wrong, as I mentioned. There’s also no way to control when a “conversation” starts or stops, unless you are turning the recap feature on and off from the watch.

And there’s more: Not only are names usually omitted (wait, who did she say I should ask about that project?), the few identifiers that make it into the recap, like names of events, are often wrong. Subjects of discussion are often conflated in really unhelpful ways: My husband mentioned paying for certain course registrations for one of our children, and later I talked to that child about an unrelated exam. The recap got all of these things mixed up with each other and was wrong about pretty much every detail. About all the recap could usefully do is to remind me that something about AP U.S. History was discussed. Reading the recaps can be like reliving your day entirely in the passive voice.

#3382. Patrick Stewart Had A Small But Important Role In One Of The Best Animated Movies Of The '90s

It feels impossible to do justice to the late Sir Patrick Stewart with mere words, but we can attempt it. One part of his incredible legacy is voice acting; how could he not try his hand there when he had such a magnificent voice? Stewart's defining voice role is probably the eccentric CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock on "American Dad." Casting him against type there is the whole joke. Patrick Stewart, famous for playing dignified, fatherly authority figures like Captain Jean-Luc Picard and Professor Charles Xavier, is the one saying all of Bullock's ridiculous, profane, and unhinged lines, which become even funnier read in his baritone voice.

The folks behind the biblical epic "The Prince of Egypt" also knew the weight Stewart's voice carried. At Steven Spielberg's suggestion, DreamWorks Animation adapted the first stretch of the Book of Exodus, or how the prophet Moses (Val Kilmer) — raised as an Egyptian prince — discovered his true heritage and led his people out of bondage. Patrick Stewart plays Pharaoh Seti, adoptive father of Moses and the man who ordered the massacre of Hebrew babies that made Moses' mother send him away. Stewart/Seti has only a few scant scenes in the movie's first act, but he casts a shadow as wide as any pyramid over the rest of the film.

As with later DreamWorks pictures, "The Prince of Egypt" employs celebrity voice casting: Kilmer as Moses, Ralph Fiennes as Moses' brother/Seti's son Pharaoh Rameses, etc. But here, it mostly works — mostly. Jeff Goldblum as Moses' brother Aaron is a distracting bit of casting where you hear the actor first, not the character. "Prince of Egypt" doesn't disguise Stewart's voice either (you probably couldn't with a voice of such power), but it complements his character to a chilling effect.

In "The Prince of Egypt," Seti first appears admonishing his two sons for being reckless in a chariot race. He's especially harsh on his heir, Rameses, explaining that "one weak link can break the chain of a mighty dynasty." When Moses asks his father to go easier on Rameses, Seti offers understanding (and pure dramatic irony): "Moses, you will never have to carry a burden like the crown I will pass to Rameses."

Pretty typical Patrick Stewart, right? Seti is stern but reasonable, some of the same qualities that made Captain Picard such a respected leader. His respect-commanding voice is even more effective as a disappointed father, too; would you want to hear "I'm disappointed in you" from that voice?

But then Moses learns the truth about where he came from, and how. Seeing his son in despair, Seti is gentle but also doesn't deny he had a generation of Hebrew babies murdered as population control. The animation and Stewart's performance work in perfect sync. In Seti's whispered tone, he sounds genuinely pained. Even if his claim "sometimes, for the greater good, sacrifices must be made," rings hollow here, Seti's thousand yard stare tells us that maybe he does feel the weight of what he did and realizes he's damned for it.

But then the kicker comes: He tries to "comfort" Moses that the babies cast into the Nile "were only slaves." The dissonance of Seti loving his own family and also being a genocidal enslaver is potent, but sadly believable. Fittingly, this is also the last time we see him in the film, because the bond he shared with Moses has been severed.

"The Prince of Egypt" is one of the most gorgeously animated films ever made, and it's not only the animation that's beautifully crafted. The storytelling is sharp and mature. It sits at the very fine line of being simple enough for kids and complex enough for adults; Moses and Rameses being turned from beloved brothers to enemies by forces much bigger than themselves is painful to watch.

Right off, "The Prince of Egypt" is an unconventional title for the Exodus story; after all, the whole story is about Moses rejecting that life for his people by birth. (Compare it to the 1956 biblical epic titled "The Ten Commandments.") But the movie paints Moses' deliverance of his people as bittersweet, since it cost him the brother he loved.

Though not nearly as controversial as Nikos Kazantzakis's book (and later Martin Scorsese's film) "The Last Temptation of Christ," "The Prince of Egypt" similarly invents human drama from scripture. "Last Temptation" works from the tenet that Jesus was both fully divine but also fully human. So, then, wouldn't he be afflicted by man's foibles and doubts? The Book of Exodus holds that Moses was raised as an Egyptian in the Pharaoh's own family. Wouldn't Moses, then, feel pained about having to turn his back on the home where he was raised, even if he recognized the necessity of God's plan for him?

Part of the tragedy is that this only flows one way. After Moses learns the truth, he can't look at the enslaved Hebrew workers without thinking their birthright is also his. Conversely, neither Seti nor Rameses clock that the son/brother they love would've been just another of those slaves. It's an excellent use of Patrick Stewart, twisting our relationship to his fatherly presence and providing an undercurrent of darkness to it.
