#3381. All 9 Major New & Upcoming KPop Demon Hunters Releases, From New 6-Episode Series To A Sequel

With very little advanced hype, KPop Demon Hunters changed everything for Netflix in a way that made their lack of preparedness look like a mistake. The animated musical is now Netflix’s biggest movie of all time, of course, and yet neither the streaming giant nor Sony were confident enough to have plans to expand the franchise in place.

There have been other KPop Demon Hunters releases since, of course, including books, trading cards, a long-awaited LEGO set, and video games, but the bigger releases won’t start landing until 2027, by which time it’ll be two years since the original movie released. And it’ll take even longer for the sequel and a reunion with Huntrix (and possibly The Saja Boys).

With KPop Demon Hunters fans still hungrily running to pick up new releases and find out news about other upcoming drops, now’s the perfect time to fill you in on what’s just arrived and what’s coming right up to 2029.

By far the most exciting upcoming release for KPop Demon Hunters fans is the sequel, but unfortunately, it's going to take an awful long time to get here. When KPop Demon Hunters 2 was quickly announced after the success of the first movie, early reports claimed that the studio's goal was a 2029 release. While it's good news that it's happening, having to wait another 3 years for it feels like torture.

Beyond that, fans can probably look forward to more adventures and possibly spin-offs, especially if the studio heeds the excitement for Sajja Boys' project. Again, we're talking about a long time in the future here. It seems likely that Netflix will fill the gap with more shorts and more releases, release events like merch drops, and perhaps more books, until eventually we get to 2029.

Details on the sequel are somewhat understandably absent, but it would seem inevitable that Huntrex will return, that they will face another battle to save Earth, and that Rumi's backstory will be further explored. Hopefully, we'll also see the return of Geno, at the very least, to rekindle his romance with Rumi. Of course, if the first movie is anything to go by, we'll also get a new crop of addictive songs.

A little over a year after the arrival of the first movie, Netflix introduced a brand-new hub page for KPop Demon Hunters with new content. As well as hosting the movie and the sing-along version, the hub also came with a new six-episode playlist series, Stories. The stop-motion episodes tell more stories for Huntrix and The Saja Boys from behind the scenes, and it's now available to stream on Netflix.

On top of that, Netflix also released a three-episode mini-series titled KPop Toy Creations, which comprises mini episodes inspired by the film, and also a four-episode Play Games with Us series, which is also stop-motion and includes competitions and challenges inspired by the original film. It's essentially companion content to keep the fans engaged, just as the new weekly release of choreography videos was unveiled ahead of the hub's release.

For fans looking for the best edition of the movie and a way to ensure it remains in your collection forever, the Criterion Collection has just dropped its own KPop Demon Hunters physical release on November 3. The special edition includes new companion content, including a making-of documentary and all of the following:

It’s widely expected that Netflix and Sony will release shorter-form spinoffs of KPop Demon Hunters before the sequel arrives, with major clamor from the fans to see some Derpy and Sussie stories at the very least. That expectation was somewhat set by the apparent reveal of short film, Debut: A KPop Demon Hunters Story, back in September 2025, for which an MPA Classification and Rating Administration filing appeared.

Speculation suggests Debut will be an origin story revealing how the band came together, thanks to the title, but little is actually known. So far, a release date hasn’t been revealed, with Netflix typically keeping that information locked down.

Just launched on October 27, 2026, and running through February 1, 2027, the Toca Boca World x KPop Demon Hunters collaboration saw stylized depictions of the movie’s characters added to the popular open-world game. If you haven't already, you can pick up iconic looks inspired by Huntrix and The Saja Boys, both in terms of their everyday style stage outfits that can be mixed for personalization. There's also a new in-game music player that includes four of the movie's original songs - “Golden,” “How It’s Done,” “Soda Pop” and “Your Idol" - which can be used as players' own soundtracks up until November 23.

So far, we've only had one LEGO set for KPop Demon Hunters with the Derpy and Sussie set that landed on shelves back in August, but the original announcement came with a promise of 2027 sets. So far, there's not been any information on what those sets might be, but we can reasonably assume we'll get a Huntrix set, a Saja Boys set, and possibly a larger set featuring Gwi-Ma and the underworld. Leaks posted by BrickFanatics suggest fans can expect five KPop Demon Hunters LEGO sets and a polybag release on May 1, 2027, ranging from $24.99 up to $129.99. Nothing is confirmed there, but they have a good track record.

November has also seen another new KPop Demon Hunters release, as the KPop Demon Hunters: The Official Screen Comic Boxed Set is finally available to buy. Bundling two volumes together, the special edition revisits the story as a graphic novel across 700 pages and has some special features worthy of its title as the ultimate collector's item, including the lyrics to both of the original songs added for the deluxe version of the soundtrack:

There are other 2027 books coming for KPop Demon Hunter fans, including KPop Demon Hunters: Official How to Draw Netflix KPop Demon Hunters, which is set for March, and KPop Demon Hunters: Official Paper Dolly Dress-up Book, coming in April. Neither really expands the franchise in any way, but nice to have for fans.

KPop Demon Hunters fans now have a chance to enjoy the world in a completely new way, as Immersive Gamebox is teaming up with Netflix to launch an interactive gaming experience across select U.S. locations - starting with Dallas, which launched on November 12.

The game will be playable by two to six players over a 60-minute session and uses lightweight motion-tracking headsets, projection mapping, and touch-sensitive walls. Players will be able to create their own animated avatar, joining Huntrix to protect the Honmoon through a series of mini games. Tickets start at $39, while the VIP Package, priced at $99, includes all-day access to the VIP Lounge, including complimentary snacks and refreshments and a choice of a VIP-exclusive tote or plush bag clip, as long as supplies last.

In what will surely be a major revenue driver, Netflix and AEG Presents have announced that a KPop Demon Hunters world tour is on the way. Tour locations have not yet been announced, but it’s expected to kick off in 2027, with 150 stops across the world. You can sign up for more information here.

It’s unclear who will actually be performing - whether it would be the vocal stars of the movie or officially endorsed Huntrix and Saja Boys stand-ins as tends to be the case in smaller-scale unofficial events. Either way, it’s going to pull in a lot of families. And it will be a remarkable shock - and a major business mistake - if Netflix don’t release a KPop Demon Hunters Concert Film both theatrically and then on the platform.

#3380. Jensen Huang’s Biopic Feels Inevitable — The Right One Might Be Impossible

Hollywood loves a visionary, especially one whose biggest gamble eventually made him a billionaire. But the trouble with making a biopic about a tech mogul actively shaping the future? That kind of story often refuses to sit still long enough to be told before ending in calamity.

When it comes to Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, any filmmaker hoping to get ahead of the microchip company’s uncertain next chapter may already be too late. Or is it still… too early?

On Thursday, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as CEO and board member, effective immediately. And no reason was given for the departure: a rather extraordinary development for someone who helped build the company into one of the most powerful and lucrative forces in artificial intelligence. For Hollywood, it’s the kind of twist that practically demands a screenplay. Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

Huang’s rise from teenage Denny’s employee to the face of the AI boom always had the makings of a prestige drama. Now there’s a corporate disaster — involving an alleged Chinese espionage operation and reports of multiple extramarital affairs — at the end of it. Hot dog! Still, it’s anyone’s guess whether that fiery conclusion can seem genuinely relevant by the time film and TV creatives get around to adapting it.

The entertainment industry has spent much of 2026 demonstrating how difficult it is to dramatize Silicon Valley while the real people involved keep making headlines. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” for example, opened to just $5.5 million in North America. That’s a disappointing debut for the follow-up to David Fincher’s “The Social Network,” which won three Oscars including best adapted screenplay.

Revisiting Facebook through the perspectives of whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), Sorkin attempted to turn Mark Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) and his social media platform’s disastrous effects on politics and public discourse into a satisfying sequel.

Of course, audiences had already spent years living with the very real consequences of Zuckerberg’s company’s actions. And in his “D+” review for IndieWire, Ryan Lattanzio described Sorkin’s approach as “less old-fashioned than completely out of date,” criticizing a falsely triumphant finale that failed to reconcile how little had actually changed in the world after the investigation’s revelations came to light.

While Sorkin was late to the party, Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” has had the good fortune of arriving right as things have been starting to get worse. Dramatizing OpenAI’s chaotic 2023 firing and rehiring of Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield), the dark comedy finds absurdity in the gap between Big Tech’s grandiose promises and the frequently clownish folks making them.

In his “B-” review for IndieWire, David Ehrlich praised the coming film for recognizing how “deeply fucking stupid the road to superintelligence has turned out to be.” He also questioned its tendency to simplify an ongoing story into something more resolved than it is. (Suffice to say, any film that tries to predict the cultural conversation also risks declaring history finished too soon.)

“Artificial” has benefited from some remarkable timing, too. Amazon MGM dropped the project after entering into a partnership with OpenAI — with sources telling the Los Angeles Times that the script’s critical perspective on artificial intelligence specifically contributed to the decision. Neon eventually acquired it, and a well-received New York Film Festival premiere helped build some serious awards-season momentum for routine Oscar contender Guadagnino.

Then came the U.S. midterms, during which voters across the country backed restrictions on data-center development. That makes the questions about who controls AI and who actually pays for its consequences feel spectacularly urgent, effectively turning a simple boardroom fight into a existential consideration of society with significantly heavier stakes.

Of course, tech biopics don’t necessarily have to predict the future to be powerful.

Consider Hulu’s “The Dropout,” which won Amanda Seyfried an Emmy for playing Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Four years later, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s boundary-breaking documentary “You Can See Everything” once again made Holmes a viral sensation — even bringing Seyfried into contact with the woman she portrayed.

As IndieWire TV critic Ben Travers recently argued, “The Dropout” remains effective precisely because it didn’t pretend to know everything about Holmes in 2022. Fielder and Oppenheim’s contribution often gets so close to its subject that Holmes’ motives become difficult to pin down, while the series maintains enough separation to keep her actions and victims in focus.

“Sometimes a healthy distance provides greater clarity,” Travers wrote.

That’s a useful lesson for anyone hoping to next adapt the life of a Silicon Valley billionaire before history has finished passing judgment on them. And in Huang’s case, there’s already plenty of material to work with — before pretending to know how his former employer’s whole saga ends.

Having cofounded Nvidia in 1993, Huang nearly lost the company after betting on a method of rendering video-game graphics that Microsoft effectively rendered obsolete. With Nvidia running out of money, he then scrapped its original technology and made a last-ditch gamble on a new chip that ultimately helped save the business.

Huang eventually helped develop the graphics-processing infrastructure that would make his company’s hardware essential to the AI boom. Fast-forward to a public apology to his wife and throw in a leather jacket? Hollywood could probably have a trailer ready by Christmas.

But that would also be the easiest, and potentially least interesting, version of Huang’s story, right? Nvidia’s success was built on the backs of countless engineers, researchers, and developers aside from Huang. The fallout within the AI giant will impact everyone.

A truly great movie about Huang and Nvidia would need to understand the company’s founding and survival, follow the enormous risks Huang took with that future, and then seriously interrogate what happens when a single corporation becomes indispensable to the technology rapidly reshaping nearly all of modern life. Those are three(!) very different artistic ambitions. Considering the entertainment industry’s own increasingly lucrative partnerships with AI companies, and Amazon’s offloading of “Artificial,” there’s reason to wonder just how much scrutiny Hollywood would be willing to apply to the innovators they are in business with.

Which brings us back to the question of when to make a Jensen Huang biopic.

The tech industry is moving faster than filmmakers can reasonably hope to keep up with, but the bigger problem may be that news around the Silicon Valley story most worth telling is changing just as quickly. A film about the man who helped build the future we’re facing might have been an easy sell a few years ago. These days, the more pressing issue is what kind of world Huang actually put in motion — and whether Hollywood can afford to doubt it in public.

#3379. I Ain't Got No Body: The Various Non-Corporeal Aliens In Star Trek Explained

Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

One of the primary features of "Star Trek" is theoretical biology. Given the wide panoply of alien species on display throughout the franchise, audiences have been invited to ponder alternate evolutionary paths besides the one that happened to bring us into being on Earth. What kind of planetary conditions would be required to form, say, a hyper-intelligent crystalline being? How did a horta evolve? What will we evolve into in the future? Will our brains adapt to become psychic over time? According to the "Star Trek: Voyager" episode "Threshold" (one of the show's most outraging to fans), it was revealed that humans will eventually evolve into giant salamanders.

This leads to a few logical evolutionary extremes, like the fact that some species on "Star Trek" have evolved into beings of pure energy. "Star Trek" has many examples of non-corporeal aliens who can only be perceived as light, as a psychic presence, as a sound, or as a vision beamed directly into our inferior, corporeal brains. To cite a notable example: In the original series episode "Is There In Truth No Beauty?," audiences were introduced to the Medusans, a highly intelligent, telepathic, and empathic species whose light-constructed bodies are so wildly complex that any human looking at them would instantly go mad. Only a mentally disciplined species like the Vulcans could look at a Medusan, and even then required a special filtered visor (pictured above).

These kinds of aliens expand the audience's mind as to what can be considered life.

In looking at fictional non-corporeal species, "Star Trek" expands our horizons. We're invited to ponder new perspectives about basic concepts like evolution, time, the nature of consciousness, and, perhaps, our own relationship to the cosmos. Non-corporeal entities are one of the coolest ideas "Star Trek" has to offer, and their recurring nature is a constant reminder that life is more complex, and the cosmos more ineffable, than we could ever hope to imagine.

On "Star Trek," non-corporeal aliens tend to appear as lights or clouds or glowing mists of energy. One might recall the smoke-like alien that made Kirk nervous in the episode "Obsession," one of the more underrated episodes of the show. Others might immediately think of Zefram Cochrane's glowing, cloud-like "companion" in the episode "Metamorphosis." That entity had the ability to sort of intuitively communicate with Cochrane (Glenn Corbett), and could also heal diseases and sustain human life beyond its usual biological barriers. A common theme of non-corporeal entities on "Star Trek" is that they are godlike and powerful, able to tap into the powers of the universe in ways we don't understand.

The Medusans may be one of the most popular non-corporeal entities on "Star Trek," but fans of "Deep Space Nine" would surely want me to acknowledge the wormhole aliens, a.k.a. The Prophets. In that show's pilot episode, "Emissary," Benjamin Sisko (Avery Brooks) travels into a stable wormhole and encounters bodiless creatures who can only communicate with him by appearing as people from his memories.

The wormhole aliens from "Deep Space Nine" are so, well, alien, they don't understand concepts like linguistic communication or linear time. They don't see cause leading to effect, but rather a widespread series of events that happen all at once. Sisko has to do the impossible, and explain the human habit of seeing time as a straight line.

And, of course, there are many species of godlike beings on "Star Trek" who often take the form of humans, despite not having physical bodies. Q (John de Lancie) from "Star Trek: The Next Generation" is one of these beings, as is Trelane (William Campbell) from the original series. Those two beings tend to see corporeal humans as lesser species and amuse themselves by taunting and playing with them. Less whimsical is Kevin Uxbridge (John Anderson), a member of a powerful energy species called the Douwd. Kevin took the form of a human, married, and witnessed his wife killed, leading him to, in a moment of ill-temper, commit instant galaxy-wide genocide of a single species. He's the deadliest character in all of "Star Trek."

The list goes on. Q tormented the Calamarain, which exist as ionized gas. There are the Organians, the Lights of Zetar, and the godlike Metrons, the latter of whom oversaw the fight between Kirk (William Shatner) and the Gorn in the episode "Arena," and plenty of other examples. In most cases, non-corporeal entities are so far beyond human experience, it's difficult to communicate with them, much less come to some kind of diplomatic understanding.

But sometimes non-corporeal entities do become our friends. On "Star Trek: Prodigy," the character of Zero (Angus Imrie) is a Medusan who managed to construct a robot-like vehicle for themselves, allowing them to interact with us flesh-beings without exposing themselves. Sometimes the ineffability of the cosmos works in our favor.

#3378. Jujutsu Kaisen Drops New Designs For Yuji, Megumi, And Yuta Ahead Of Big Season 4 Return

Jujutsu Kaisen is giving fans another reason to look toward Jump Festa 2027, unveiling fresh character illustrations that put recognizable sorcerers in a coordinated cheer squad theme. The colorful artwork features Yuji Itadori, Megumi Fushiguro, and Yuta Okkotsu, alongside two important Culling Game characters.

Rather than teasing an episode or revealing a major plot development, the illustrations from @animeupdates on X offer a playful promotional look at the cast ahead of the franchise’s next event. Their arrival is timely, as the anime’s fourth season is in production and Jump Festa is scheduled to deliver information about its continuation.

The new artwork was announced by the official Jujutsu Kaisen anime account and Anime Updates for Jump Festa 2027. Its cheer squad theme features five full-length portraits in separate colored frames. Kinji Hakari appears against yellow, Kirara Hoshi gets pink, Yuji is framed in orange, Megumi in teal, and Yuta in blue.

All five characters wear dark school-style outfits, but their individual poses and accessories give the portraits distinct personalities. Hakari stands with his arms folded and a confident grin, while Kirara winks beneath her dark bangs and pink accents. Yuji looks especially upbeat, smiling broadly with both arms raised behind his head.

Megumi has a restrained expression and holds a long weapon diagonally, while Yuta wears a blue headband with one gloved hand visible. The color panels make the group feel coordinated without making the characters interchangeable. It is a lighter visual concept for a series whose Culling Game storyline is anything but cheerful.

The choice of characters is also notable. Yuji and Megumi have been main characters in the anime since its early episodes, while Yuta’s role has grown increasingly important following Jujutsu Kaisen 0 and the later story. Hakari and Kirara, meanwhile, are closely tied to the Culling Game material that the next season will continue adapting.

The illustrations are tied to Jump Festa 2027 booth, where the company plans to sell Jujutsu Kaisen merchandise using the new artwork. The booth is among the event’s manufacturer exhibits in Hall 9, and the announcement confirms related products are coming. Specific formats, prices, and sales details have not yet been disclosed.

Despite its 2027 name, Jump Festa will take place December 19 and 20, 2026, at Makuhari Messe in Chiba, Japan. The convention spans exhibition halls 1 through 9 and 11, with general hours from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. both days. Admission is free, but visitors need advance approval or an invitation.

Jujutsu Kaisen also has a Jump Super Stage on Saturday, December 19, from 3:25 p.m. to 3:55 p.m. Japan time. Guests include Junya Enoki, Mikako Komatsu, Kazuya Nakai, and Daisuke Namikawa, Japanese voice actors for Yuji, Maki, Hakari, and Choso. The program will revisit Season 3 before sharing the latest Jujutsu Kaisen Season 4 news.

The event matters because the anime’s fourth season, officially titled The Culling Game Part 2, is in production at MAPPA. Season 3 adapted the first portion of the Culling Game, leaving the larger conflict unresolved. The next installment will move the story into its next phase, with surviving players and shifting alliances facing greater danger.

Jujutsu Kaisen Season 4 was announced after Season 3’s finale in March 2026, and MAPPA released a teaser trailer in June confirming production. A super teaser visual followed on August 29, placing Ryomen Sukuna at the center of an ominous image. However, the studio and production committee have not announced a premiere date.

Jujutsu Kaisen Season 3 just ended, but the anime is far from over. Here's everything that fans should know about Jujutsu Kaisen Season 4's release.

Jump Festa’s official Jujutsu Kaisen stage announcement promises a Season 3 look back and the latest information about Season 4. The December presentation is a more concrete source of anime news than the cheer squad art. Fans may learn about the next season’s progress, though no release date or new trailer is guaranteed.

#3377. 15 Years Later, Jamie Lannister’s Best Game of Thrones Quote Is an All-Time Fantasy Hit

Jamie remains a fan-favorite for a reason

Many factors have helped make George R.R. Martin’s A Song of Ice and Fire one of the most beloved fantasy series of all time, and one big reason is HBO’s adaptation of the dark fantasy epic by showrunners David Benioff and D. B. Weiss. The eight-season adaptation brought Martin’s vast, stunning world and complex central characters to life. Jaime Lannister, played by Nikolaj Coster-Waldau, was one such character. And like many others in Game of Thrones, he had poetic one-liners that captured his nature and helped define his place in the story over the years.

Unlike Ned Stark, whose blunt and severe demeanor left little room for elaborate remarks, Jaime Lannister seemed to have an arsenal of memorable quotes and cutting one-liners. His words reflected both his standing as Tywin Lannister’s beloved son and as Lord Commander of the Kingsguard, as well as the complicated reputation he carried throughout Westeros. To many, Jaime was a man without honor, and his sharp remarks often seemed to echo the way others judged him.

With so many banger quotes from Jaime, it’s tough to pick the best one. Still, we think we’ve narrowed it down to a line that captures a key part of Jaime’s character and a central fantasy theme.

Of all the meaningful lines Jaime delivers over Game of Thrones’ eight seasons, one perfectly highlights a key theme that often serves as a source of strength in stories, regardless of genre: love. Martin, however, twists that theme in a way that helps ensure Jaime goes down as one of fantasy’s most memorable characters.

In the show's first episode, “Winter is Coming,” Jaime delivers his best line to his sister, Cersei, shortly after Bran Stark, the youngest son of Ned Stark of House Stark, catches them locked in an incestuous romantic embrace in one of Winterfell's towers.

Turning to Cersei, Jaime gives a self-assured smirk and says:

Moments later, Jaime pushes Bran out the open window — triggering a chain of events that leads to eight seasons of warfare, seedy politicking, and epic fantasy unlike anything ever seen before.

Love is a powerful emotion that drives stories across every genre and format. It is love that causes Jack to sacrifice himself for Rose in Titanic, and it is love that protects Harry from dying from Voldemort’s killing curse in Harry Potter.

Game of Thrones may be a dark fantasy tale in which nobody is truly safe, but that does not mean its characters are one-dimensional. Both D&D and Martin have made it clear that even the most loathsome among them can feel love and form deep attachments.

Those feelings do not necessarily make them kinder or less dangerous. On the contrary, in some cases they will commit monstrous acts for the people they love. That is clearest with Jaime, who is capable of killing a boy if it means his secret relationship with Cersei isn’t exposed to the rest of Westeros.

Jaime committing heinous acts for the love of his sister proves just how obsessive and toxic that love can be. It’s only when Jaime realizes his sister cares more about power than about being with him that he eventually wises up.

Unfortunately, Jaime’s toxic bond with Cersei has been a foundational part of him since childhood. Even when Jaime eventually leaves Cersei’s influence and forms a romantic relationship with Brienne of Tarth, sleeping with her after the Battle of Winterfell, it’s not enough. When Jaime hears of Cersei’s precarious situation in King’s Landing in the final season, he abandons Brienne and the Starks to rush back to the capital to try to save Cersei from her own folly.

Ultimately, this final act of love for his sister leads to Jaime’s downfall. Even as the Red Keep begins to crumble, Jaime refuses to leave Cersei’s side. They came into the world together, and so it only makes sense that they leave it together too.

As Aemond Targaryen explained to Jon Snow in A Game of Thrones: “We are only human, and the gods have fashioned us for love. That is our great glory, and our great tragedy.”

#3376. ’12 12 12′ Review: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s Ticking-Clock Heist Thriller Runs on Broken Time

Every episode of “12 12 12” opens with the same explanation of its title: Citing the fictitious law enforcement manual, “Principles of Crime, FBI Research Center, 4th Edition,” Anthony Mackie explains, “A high asset robbery, professionally conceived, is 12 months in planning, 12 hours in execution. A bank robber who’s not caught within 12 days is not caught at all.” Then the screen splits horizontally to reveal images from the 12 months of preparation, the 12 hours of execution, and the 12 days when thief extraordinaire Paul Galvin (Jamie Dornan) does his best to elude Mackie’s obsessed FBI agent Jack Strickland. And then, we’re off to the races. Related Stories ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne Sizzles in Peacock’s Brutal Trauma-Drama About Crime-Solving Sisters ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations

The heist genre, in theory, seems ripe for this kind of temporal manipulation. A game of wits between cops and criminals typically involves plenty of twists, many of which pull the rug out by flashing back to show where, when, and how it was placed so stealthily underfoot. Also working in “12 12 12’s” favor is the genre’s familiarity: There will be “getting the team together” montages, there will be unexpected hiccups in the days and hours during the robbery, there will be chest-thumping meetings between our confident cop and the equally confident con artist. Throw in the complex heist itself and the tense escape soon after, and there appear to be enough recognizable pieces that jumbling them up shouldn’t prove too confusing.

And “12 12 12” isn’t confusing. It is, however, convoluted. Taking a serpentine route through well-trodden territory does more to undermine our enjoyment of an otherwise well-mounted chase than it does to liven things up. Heists are inherently exciting. They’re exciting in conception (when master thieves can wow us with their slick plans), they’re exciting to see carried out (when the shit hits the fan and even the most astute architects have to think on their feet), and they’re exciting to get away with (when safety is within reach, but it could be snatched away at any moment). Anticipation, suspense, and anxiety work to form a natural arc, and disrupting that arc over and over, every hour for eight hours, in service of a few extra twists — and to extend what’s obviously a movie-length story across eight hours — simply isn’t worth it.

On that note, let me get this minor but essential point out of the way now, quickly and clearly: Jamie Dornan needs more weird roles, not more conventional ones. We saw what he can do in “Barb and Star Go to Vista Del Mar” (a modern comedy classic). Let the man cook — or sing or dance or all three at once! He can do it! Honestly, I believe he can do anything. (Remember the bee movie?! No, not that bee movie — the other one.)

Anyway, here his character’s only unique attribute is his brilliant… planning. He’s got a mind for details, and he uses it to map out every possible contingency before embarking on his elaborate heists. Caught in a bind with his dumbass brother (Jack Kesy, doing his best Travis Kelce impression), Bobby lays it out in aptly blunt terms: “Paul, you’re the fucking plan guy, so plan me a plan.”

But the only plans Paul wants to make these days are for his family: He’s happy working on fishing boats off the coast of France and coming home to his wife, Severine (Agathe Rousselle), in their little apartment above a bar. He’s bonded with his father-in-law, Serge (José Garcia), who’s the Marxist papa Paul never had, and he’s got a kid on the way.

Unfortunately, Bobby can’t stop being Bobby and winds up indebted to the wrong people; people who don’t just want their money back, but who want more money to make up for the inconvenience. And since Bobby already owes more money than either brother could ever pay back, Paul has to take on one last job to free his brother — and himself — from their lives of crime.

Too bad that puts him back on Jack’s radar or, I should say, squarely on Jack’s radar, since Jack is nursing a (secret) grudge against Paul from years earlier. Ever since, he’s been obsessed with catching the one criminal who’s eluded his grasp. He wants revenge, he wants “respect,” he wants to win — “12 12 12” throws out a number of motivations for Jack early on that clearly don’t paint the full picture. They’re placeholder reasons until the show deems it time to dig into what’s really driving him to move to Zurich, hole up in a shitty police station, and wait for Paul to try to steal something.

Mackie, who’s reunited with his “Falcon and the Winter Soldier” director Kari Skogland, gives great determined face, and Dornan is the softest, sweetest guy on the FBI’s most-wanted list. Thankfully, co-creators Dudi Appleton and Jim Keeble don’t ask their lead characters to betray their core identities amid all the twists and turns, shading Jack as more of an antagonist (all-consumed and, thus, single-minded to a fault) and Paul as more of the protagonist. (He doesn’t want to steal, but now that he must, he’s going to do it the right way.) That helps keep our rooting interests in line, which goes a long way toward a satisfying emotional payoff, even when the momentum ebbs and flows with every flash-forward, -back, and -sideways.

With slick locations and clever-enough problem-solving, “12 12 12” should satisfy die-hard heist fans (but not “Die Hard’s” heist fans). It just takes a circuitous route to scratching that itch, and that’s almost as aggravating as not scratching it at all.

“12 12 12” premieres Friday, November 13 on Apple TV with two episodes. New episodes will be released weekly through the finale (Episode 8) on December 25.

#3375. 10 Hacks Every Reddit User Should Know

If you're looking for discussions, recommendations, or advice online, it's hard to avoid Reddit. From mainstream sports to niche crafts, it does seem that there's some kind of Reddit community for everyone. (And if there's not one, you can make one yourself.) If you're using Reddit, here are 10 hacks you should know about to improve your experience on the site.

Reddit used to let everyone view your post and comment history, but in recent years, you can make your profile private. You can hide your posts, comments, and the subreddits you're a part of. If you want to do this, click your profile icon once you've logged in to Reddit, and go to Settings > Profile. Alternatively, you can follow the direct link to Reddit's profile settings page. Click the drop-down menu next to Content & Activity, and select Hide all. You should also turn off Online Status on the same page to stop people from seeing when you're using Reddit.

Old Reddit lets you use the site's classic design, and I prefer it to the more modern UI. Old Reddit looks dated, but it doesn't have infinite scrolling, distracting animations, and a bunch of features designed to increase the time you spend on the platform. It's no wonder that Reddit is making it harder to access this version of the site. As long as it's around, you should switch to Old Reddit for a cleaner reading experience. You can do that by going to Reddit Settings > Preferences and enabling Default to Old Reddit. You can also visit old.reddit.com, though you'll need to sign in for access

Many subreddits use custom themes that range from beautiful to borderline unusable. If you want a more consistent UI across the site, you should disable these custom subreddit styles. Go to Reddit Settings > Preferences and turn off Use community themes. If you're using Old Reddit, click the preferences button in the top-right corner, and under "display options," disable allow subreddits to show me custom themes.

A multireddit is a feed that shows posts from a customized group of subreddits. You can think of it as a way to break out of Reddit's algorithms, and create your own Reddit feed. I use multireddits to follow all sports-related subs I'm interested in. I even have one for gaming, and one for fountain pens. It's a great way to create interest-specific feeds, and if you make them private, no one else can see them. To create one, click the Create custom feed button in the left pane in new Reddit. In the Old Reddit design, click the Create button in the left pane. Be sure to select the Private button to keep it from showing up for others. You can add as many subreddits as you like to the list, and bookmark the feed to access it whenever you wish to.

Reddit has recently adopted an Instagram-like experience for its feeds. It removed the ability to sort posts by new, controversial, best, etc., and instead offers "For You" and "Following." If you dislike this change, you can bypass it. I use Reddit on mobile Safari, and I recommend an extension called Sink It for Reddit. It can automatically redirect you to Old Reddit, and there's a feature that optimizes it for mobile, which brings back the old sorting options. You can also use third-party apps such as RedReader for Android, or RDX for Reddit on an iPhone or iPad to restore the old sorting options for Reddit posts.

After all these years, Reddit's built-in search still leaves something to be desired—at least, on the surface. To find posts on Reddit faster, use search filters on the site. For instance, adding "title:" to your search will limit the results to post titles, and boolean operators such as AND, OR, and NOT also work for advanced searches on the site.

#3374. NBC Breaks SNL's 52-Season Rule For An Undeniable Industry Shift

For more than five decades, Saturday Night Live has relied on some of entertainment's biggest names to attract audiences. From Hollywood actors and chart-topping musicians to professional athletes, NBC's long-running sketch comedy series has traditionally featured hosts whose careers were established through mainstream entertainment.

However, as the industry continues to evolve, SNL is beginning to recognize that celebrity status is considerably different from what it once was. Social media has fundamentally changed how audiences discover and engage with entertainers, creating an entirely new generation of celebrities whose influence rivals that of established Hollywood stars.

Platforms like YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram have become launching pads for successful entertainment careers. Despite the growing popularity of digital content creators, Saturday Night Live has largely maintained its traditional approach to selecting hosts throughout its impressive 52-season run. That changed on November 7, 2026, when comedian and content creator Druski became the first digital-native influencer to host the series.

While his appearance was already a significant milestone for Saturday Night Live, the episode's remarkable ratings proved just how valuable internet personalities could become to traditional television. More importantly, Druski's success could fundamentally change how NBC approaches the show's future, potentially opening the door for an entirely new generation of hosts.

Throughout Saturday Night Live's 52-season history, the show has typically reserved its hosting opportunities for established figures in entertainment. Actors frequently appear to promote upcoming films or television projects, musicians use the platform to reach new audiences, and professional athletes occasionally step outside their comfort zones to demonstrate their comedic abilities. Even the show's stand-up comedian hosts generally arrive with careers built through traditional comedy clubs, television appearances, or major comedy specials.

Importantly, SNL has previously embraced performers who developed followings online, including several of its own cast members. However, those opportunities typically involved bringing digital talent into the show's established ensemble rather than handing an internet personality the responsibility of hosting an entire episode. Druski's appearance marked the first time a digital-native creator received that distinction, demonstrating NBC's willingness to reconsider what qualifies someone for the coveted hosting opportunity.

Found an error? Send it info@screenrant.com so it can be corrected.

The decision also reflects how dramatically the entertainment industry's definition of celebrity has changed. Druski did not need a breakout movie role or a successful network sitcom to become recognizable to millions of viewers. Instead, he built his audience independently, proving that digital creators can establish the kind of cultural relevance traditionally associated with Hollywood stars. By welcoming him to Studio 8H, Saturday Night Live acknowledged that its next generation of influential hosts might emerge from platforms that didn't exist when the series first premiered.

Druski's Saturday Night Live debut was more than a historic first for the NBC comedy series. It was also an undeniable ratings success, suggesting that embracing digital content creators could be an effective strategy for attracting new audiences. According to Nielsen's Live+Same Day figures, the November 7 episode attracted approximately 5.6 million television viewers, making it the show's most-watched broadcast in two years. This represented an 8% increase over the previous week's episode, hosted by Inde Navarrette, which had already established a season 52 high.

Perhaps more importantly, Druski's appearance delivered impressive results among younger viewers. The episode attracted an estimated 1.5 million adults aged 18–49, an 18% increase over the previous week. It also earned SNL its strongest performance among viewers aged 18–34 in more than four years (via USA Today). These demographics are particularly significant because they demonstrate the show's ability to attract audiences who increasingly consume entertainment through digital platforms rather than traditional television.

The success extended beyond NBC's linear broadcast. Druski's episode became the most-watched Saturday Night Live installment in Peacock's history (via The Wrap), although the streaming service has not released its exact audience figures. Meanwhile, clips from the episode generated an astonishing 424 million views across YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, and X within three days. While these social media figures count video plays rather than individual viewers, they demonstrate the extraordinary reach that an internet personality can bring to an established television institution.

Of course, Druski cannot receive all the credit for these numbers. The episode benefited from a strong college football lead-in, musical guest The Strokes, and several high-profile appearances. Nevertheless, the combination of traditional television success, record-breaking streaming performance, and widespread social media engagement gives NBC a compelling reason to reconsider its hosting strategy. Rather than treating Druski's appearance as an isolated experiment, SNL could begin regularly welcoming digital creators whose established audiences offer opportunities for continued growth.

Although Druski's established following undoubtedly contributed to his Saturday Night Live debut's success, the episode also demonstrated why his particular brand of comedy translates so well to television. Rather than forcing the internet personality to abandon the exaggerated characters and absurd situations that made him famous, SNL embraced those strengths. The result was an episode that balanced the show's familiar sketch comedy format with the unpredictable humor audiences already associate with Druski.

His opening monologue established that approach immediately. Druski enthusiastically celebrated the opportunity while joking about the restrictions placed on his performance, including his inability to promise that he wouldn't violate the show's rules. The monologue also featured a surprise appearance from Emma Stone, his co-star in the upcoming film The Catch. Although the segment was relatively brief, it allowed Druski to introduce himself to unfamiliar viewers without sacrificing the humor that made him popular online.

Saturday Night Live's best guest hosts bring their own unique energy to the show while fitting neatly into the sketch show's goofy sense of humor.

Several sketches played directly into his comedic strengths. In "Dru Can See Everything," Druski parodied disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, leaning into the elaborate physical transformations that have become a defining feature of his online videos. Meanwhile, "Birthday Girl" featured him portraying an excessively demanding birthday celebrant, while "Bubu Mobile" paired him with Marcello Hernández as employees at a Dominican phone store. These performances showcased his ability to create distinctive characters while working alongside the established SNL ensemble.

However, Druski wasn't the episode's only attraction. Its political cold open featured an unexpected appearance from Texas Senator-elect James Talarico, while Weekend Update addressed the aftermath of the midterm elections. Musical guest The Strokes also delivered two performances, adding another recognizable name to the broadcast. Combined with Druski's enthusiastic hosting performance, these elements helped make the episode appealing to viewers beyond his existing fanbase.

Ultimately, the episode's popularity suggests SNL does not need to reinvent itself to accommodate digital creators. Druski succeeded by bringing his established comedic identity into the show's existing format, demonstrating how both sides could benefit from the collaboration. If NBC wants to replicate that success, embracing more internet personalities could be vital for keeping Saturday Night Live culturally relevant for another generation.

Saturday Night Live airs Saturdays at 11:30 EDT on NBC.

Saturday Night Live is a live television sketch comedy and variety show created by Lorne Michaels, premiering in 1975. It features comedy sketches parodying contemporary culture and politics, performed by a rotating cast. Each episode is hosted by a celebrity guest and includes musical performances.

#3373. 7 Prime Video Action Shows With No Bad Seasons, Ranked

Prime Video has a fantastic slate of originals. In fact, some of its newest shows have counted among the most talked about this year. And many of them fall into the action genre. From secret spies to law enforcement, military men and women, superheroes and super not-so-heroes, ghouls, and villains, the list is extensive, the shows filled with memorable characters.

Some shows waver and dip, losing their luster eventually and overstaying their welcome. But the best action shows on Prime Video don't have a single bad season among the bunch. Sure, two of them have only streamed one season so far. But these singular seasons were so incredibly entertaining, you won't be disappointed by watching them.

Not since Thelma & Louise have we had such a fun, female-centric buddy action adventure comedy like Ride or Die. Hannah Waddingham is a downright badass as elite assassin Judith Burton. She has hidden her identity from her best friend Deborah "Debbie" Claybourne (Octavia Spencer) since they became friends years prior. But current circumstances mean Debbie is in for a wild ride she never saw coming, and is going to be introduced to a side of her friend she didn't know existed.

The series, one of the best Prime Video shows in 2026 so far, is so fun throughout its eight episodes. It's as much a story of female friendship and dealing with childhood trauma as it is an action-packed show. But there are also fantastic fight sequences with engaging choreography, and intense physical and emotional moments. The fact that two female actors lead the story is refreshing. Sadly, Ride or Die was cancelled after its first season. But it's a fantastic weekend binge-watch with the gal pals or partner that provides a satisfying ending.

One of those enduring Prime Video shows that no one talks about, The Legend of Vox Machina has streamed four seasons already and will be coming back for a fifth and final season. The adult animated fantasy series based on the first Dungeons & Dragons campaign called Critical Role, follows a seven-member team embarking on a mission to avenge the murder of their town's rulers. The story develops from there in subsequent seasons as the characters grow and the battles evolve.

Initially, the series was funded through a Kickstarter campaign, yet it has since become one of Prime Video's most enduring originals. In her Season 4 review, Collider's Victoria Luxford says the show remains just as strong, a "funny, thrilling, and surprisingly deep fantasy series that balances fan service with a story that won't leave newcomers alienated." Once you have powered through The Legend of Vox Machina, check out its spin-off/sequel series The Mighty Nein.

One of the most polarizing shows of this decade, The Boys was set up to satirize the current political and societal landscape, and ended up becoming like a mirror of the times. The story in the satirical superhero series, a Prime Video show with no bad seasons, centers around an alternate world whereby humans live among those with superhuman abilities. Some of these powers are typical, like superhuman strength, speed, laser eyes, and invisibility. But others are more gruesome, vulgar, even offensive. And what these "Supes" do is nothing close to heroic: they're focused on feeding their egos and the pocketbook of the company that manages them, not actually helping others.

The Boys is subversive, politically commentative, and extremely violent. It isn't a show that everyone will like. But some will appreciate the deep meaning masked behind blood, gore, and a record number of male appendages and expletives. If you dig in to the root of the show, it's actually one of the smartest shows on television. Watch the entire five-season run and follow it up with the companion series Gen V.

I might be in the minority, but I actually like Neagley better than Reacher. Both shows are fantastic, but Neagley came out of the gate strong with its first season. And with a Season 2 renewal, it will likely get even better. The character of Frances Neagley (Maria Sten), who is first introduced in Reacher, is much more layered than Reacher fans realized. She shows up on that show as a trusted confidante, someone Jack Reacher (Alan Ritchson) knows he can count on to get the job done, no matter how challenging. He knows she will have his back and will always be two steps ahead, able to anticipate what he might need. This is emphasized in Neagley where Frances is clearly valued at the private investigation firm where she works. But she's also just as rebellious and against the rules as her friend Reacher is. The ensemble nature of the show introduces conflicting personalities that come together to form sort of a ragtag team.

The story in Season 1 follows Frances' investigation into the death of an old friend, which leads her to a dangerous cult and strange experiments. It has all the elements you'd expect from a good action crime show, including intense hunts, lots of engaging fight scenes, and emotional backstories that draw you into the characters themselves, not just the plot.

Having only just recently binged all of Reacher, the show's flow is still fresh in my mind. The later seasons are arguably better than the first two, but there still isn't a bad season among the bunch. Season 1 sets up Ritchson as the first actor to truly embody the character as he is in the Lee Child books. The stakes rise higher in Season 2, and the personal connection to the cases grows and becomes more intimate with each passing season.

The action and intensity is amped up in later seasons, too, with some of the most intriguing villains. The fact that the action crime drama has so much source material to work from with Child having written 31 novels about the character to date, there's no shortage of exciting stories from which to draw. If you love action shows, Reacher is among the best, with a protagonist who towers over his prey, doesn't flinch when he has to kill a bad guy, yet has the softest heart and strongest moral code. With at least two more seasons already confirmed, it's a good time to binge-watch the show and catch up on all the literal action.

Mark Grayson (Steven Yeun) just wants to be a regular teenager, but he doesn't have that chance. He's the son of the most powerful superhero on Earth, Omni-Man (J. K. Simmons), so he has a duty to serve. That means honing his skills now that he's coming of age and his latent powers are starting to show up. That's the set-up for the story in Invincible, an adult animated superhero series from Robert Kirkman that has become a huge pop culture phenomenon.

Even though it's animated, Invincible is very violent, gruesome, and graphic, so this isn't necessarily a show to watch with young kids. The stories are also quite mature. But the show is completely bingeable and addictive, adding depth to an otherwise thin story of good guys versus bad. Earning widespread acclaim, Invincible has already been renewed for two more seasons, continuing the story as Mark grapples with a shocking truth about his dad and fighting an evil group looking to conquer Earth.

The action doesn't start immediately in Fallout, but when it does, it happens in a big way. And the Prime Video show hooks you in the first five minutes. It begins with a betrayal in an underground bunker and expands to include the Earth above where there's nothing but conflict. Based on the video game franchise of the same name, Fallout follows Lucy (Ella Purnell) and her journey to find her kidnapped father, leaving the safety of her underground home for the first time. She comes across interesting and dangerous people, including The Ghoul (Walton Goggins), who has an interesting backstory and who is on a mission that eventually overlaps with Lucy's.

You'll see everything from Radroaches (giant, mutated cockroaches) attacking humans to robots, men in robotic armor, mutated creatures, undead ghouls, and a lot of eccentric personalities as people do whatever they can to survive in this post-apocalyptic world. The show wonderfully introduces new groups and characters each season while the journeys of Lucy and The Ghoul make progress and eventually come together. With only two seasons so far and a third on the way, considering there are five main video game stories and six spin-offs or mobile titles, there's lots more story to tell. If you like seeing unique fight scenes that you won't see in any other show, Fallout won't disappoint.

#3372. Stardew Valley Meets Night in the Woods in One of 2026's Scariest New Games

I thought I knew what to expect from Village in the Shade after attending NIS America's pre-launch preview event in September. The villagers would be quirky but likeable, and things would probably get at least a little twisted, though nothing too terrible. Nippon Ichi Software's non-Disgaea games get pretty dark, as do the Labyrinth games and Yomawari. But they're dark on a small-scale, personal level, and rarely do they have something poignant to say. Village in the Shade tossed all my expectations out the window within the first few hours and, since then, has quickly rocketed up my list of the year's best games.

Village in the Shade starts with a child frolicking in the fields, running through dappled woods, skipping over rivers, and doing normal kid stuff. Then they fall down a hole and die, or so you'd think from the amount of blood on-screen, except they climb out and start walking again like nothing happened. Something did happen, though. The local carpenter and a hunter find the child, who happens to bear a striking resemblance to a kid who vanished years ago. Not that the idea brought anyone joy. They seem worried, actually, but Rin, the de facto mayor of Kagatsu Village, decides the child may be of use.

Rin initially seems like a Tom Nook caricature. She's fixated on profit and productivity, stuffs you in a ratty little hovel, charges you for it, and decides your value based on how much you do for the community. There's a bit of subtle commentary from her about min-maxing supposedly relaxing games to get the most out of them, and I thought this poke at established cozy staples would be the extent of Rin's personality. But NIS had something much more interesting in mind, which became evident the next in-game day when Rin threw a baby goat down the village well as an offering. One life out of the village in exchange for another life in. Balance must be maintained.

It likely comes as no surprise to hear this following a sentence that includes the words "threw a baby goat down the well," but Kagatsu Village is a weird place. A good quarter of the people who live there agree with that assessment. Even so, they don’t seem to have much of a choice but to stay and deal with it. Their families lived at the foot of this mountain for generations. Leaving would be tantamount to betrayal of everyone past and present, and who knows what might happen then?

Rin and Kagatsu Village under her rule are the epitome of toxic communalism. She's sincere in her dogged determination to put the village first — frighteningly so at times — but either overlooks or just plain doesn't understand the harm of ignoring the individual. Part of Kagatsu's code is that every favor must be met with appropriate compensation, which is great for people with mercenary dispositions. It’s less great if you just want to help a friend out with no strings attached. You're also not supposed to pry into anyone's affairs or share their secrets, no matter how upset they are or whether they're gathering poison as part of a murder plot. As long as the collective is intact and moving forward, every sacrifice is permissible. And mandatory.

The most common sacrifice is a monthly fee, like a tax, though to Rin's intense frustration, people tend to get around it. Some perform a service. Others give food or necessary items. Those with nothing to give, or who flat-out refuse to give anything, are taken to the local clinic where the doctor draws a rather alarming amount of blood. Blood figures quite prominently in Village in the Shade. There's the monthly offering, of course, along with a spate of serial killings 10 years in the past — around the time you disappeared from the village, in what's surely a totally normal coincidence. On some nights, one of the bridges leading to the center of town is covered in blood.

I'm a coward and haven't ventured beyond the bridge on those nights, so I don't know why the blood is there yet. Nighttime is dangerous in Kagatsu Village. Untold horrors slither down the mountain and haunt the streets and alleys, and dealing with them is much more nerve-wracking than I originally thought. The preview session showed the very first haunted incident, a linear segment where the ghost of an old man chases you through the village. It was pretty tame. The rest of the hauntings are not. Village in the Shade uses a drumming sound like a heartbeat and a tremor effect on the screen when danger approaches, and they increase in intensity the closer you get to the source of it. That, plus a general lack of defensive capabilities and places to hide, is enough to get the adrenaline going during evening wanderings. Stealth and bloody death were not on my bingo card when I started this game, and the intensity of these moments — plus just how at odds they are with the sedate daytime routine — make them standouts.

The "weird rural place with a terrible past" and its critiques on collectivism aren't entirely uncommon in Japanese media. Ryukishi07's Higurashi: When They Cry springs to mind as one of the stronger examples of it, and, more recently, there's The Summer Hikaru Died and even Nintendo's Emio — The Smiling Man. The concept is typically reserved for anime or visual novels, though, and I've yet to come across a good example of the storytelling style in more interactive media. Who'd have thought a farm-sim could make the perfect fit for it? Certainly not me.

But it does, and even the calm routine surprised me. Most farming games in the last decade have done very little to shake up the daily chores, and even Stardew Valley followed a pattern familiar from old Harvest Moon games. Village in the Shade holds little back at the start and throws a lot of crop variety, processing machines, and progress at you. I'd upgraded my tools once by the first summer, reached level 50 of the mine, and harvested enough spring crops to get them all to silver rank in quality.

It's not too easy, though, and NIS didn't skimp on the farming just to facilitate storytelling. In that first summer, I divided my fields (plural, as I bought a second one with my springtime earnings) into planned segments. There were flower fields for producing honey, flowers for selling, and a smaller plot for gift flowers. Crop-producing trees had a section all to themselves. The furrowed vegetables — Village in the Shade lets you alternate between tillage and furrows to encourage faster growth for some species — had a section all to themselves, just because uniformity looked nice.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

While I hadn't created rice paddies yet, that didn't stop me from spending thousands of yen on seedlings while the store had them in stock, and I created a special bed of edamame beans that I'd let ripen into autumn for a soybean harvest. Meanwhile, at the other end of the homestead plot sat my beehives, smelters, smithing station, mayonnaise maker, and pickling barrels. I had full access to cows, ducks, chicken, horses, and sheep despite being early in the game, too.

And all of this is for the good of the village. With more crops, more money, and more goods, you can fulfill more requests and improve Kagatsu, giving it a better chance at surviving into the future. Well, assuming there's enough people left to live there when the future arrives. Regardless of how things play out, I'm frankly astonished at just how well Village in the Shade tells its story and wraps it around familiar farm-sim routines. As we head into the twilight of 2026, this one definitely deserves a spot on the lists of the year's best games.

#3371. 10 Hacks Every Hulu User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you don't like the content Hulu is suggesting for you, you have several options to curate your recommendations. "Disliking" a show or movie removes it from your Home view and You May Also Like entirely, so the only way you'll see that content is if you search for it. You can dislike on the Details page if you're watching on your TV or use the thumbs down on mobile or web. (The "Like" button will obviously influence your algorithm in the opposite way). If your "Continue Watching" queue is cluttered with shows you started but didn't like enough to finish, you can remove them from your watch history as well as the My Stuff list. This, too, will allow content to remain searchable but not suggested in other areas of the app.

If PIN protection is enabled, users must enter a four-digit PIN when switching between profiles on a single account. This is intended as a parental control feature, since it's available on non-Kids profiles and can keep children from accessing more mature content on an adult's profile. However, you can also enable this feature to keep other users from seeing your viewing history and preferences or influencing your algorithm by watching their content under your profile (accidentally or on purpose). To set up a PIN, log into your account on Hulu's website, select your profile, and go to Manage Profiles > Parental Controls. You'll have to choose a PIN and enter your password to confirm the changes.

Another approach to protecting your profile and algorithm is to set up separate profiles for specific use cases, such as when you have guests or if you host watch parties for certain shows. This keeps content from influencing your recommendations and prevents other viewers from seeing what's in your watch history or saved content (especially if there are things you want to keep private).

If you find that subtitles and captions are too bold—or not visible enough—you can change the font, color, size, and style from the default so they enhance your viewing experience rather than detracting from it. Hulu allows you to adjust the color and opacity of the font, background, and window so you get the right contrast, and you can also select the specific font and font scaling. On your streaming device, go to Settings > Subtitles & Captions, then hit the back button on your remote to save your preferences. You can update these settings on mobile and desktop as well.

If you have a long list of shows and films to watch but can't decide what to start next, look for the "Expiring Soon" badge to see which titles are leaving the service in the next two weeks. Badges display the number of days remaining, so you can determine what to prioritize and whether it's worth diving in based on how much time you have to finish before the expiration date. Go to "My Stuff" to monitor saved titles that are expiring soon.

If you've been watching Hulu under an account shared with family or friends and need to switch to your own subscription, you can transfer your profile to keep your watch history and settings intact instead of starting from scratch. You can initiate a profile transfer on a TV-connected device. Note that account holders have to approve transfer requests within seven days, and once expired, transfer requests cannot be resubmitted—so be sure to let the primary user know that you've made the request.

If you've shared your Hulu login information with friends or activated your account on devices you don't own, you may want to regularly audit where your account is being used and remove any that don't need access. This includes TVs in Airbnbs and hotels. If you stay logged in, unauthorized users may have access to your Hulu account and personal data. You can see activated devices (and their activation date) under Your Account > Watch Hulu on Your Devices > Manage Devices. Click Remove next to old or unrecognized devices.

Hulu has an offline mode that allows you to download shows and movies to watch when you don't have a network connection. This is useful for traveling or when you know your wifi or cell service will be limited. Downloads are only available on supported iOS and Android devices, which means you may have to consider how much space your content takes up. You can select High for video quality if you want maximum resolution, but you may want to choose Standard if you are short on storage. This option is available under Downloads > Settings > Video Quality on iOS and Account > Settings > Downloads > Video Quality on Android. Note that once you click play on downloaded content, you have 48 hours to watch it before it expires—so don't start it unless you are ready.

If you have a Hulu + Live TV subscription, you must designate a "Home" network, which determines the local channels included in your plan. You can update your location up to four times within a 12-month period, but this limitation is meant to prevent viewers outside a household from sharing a subscription. Hulu does allow you to stream live TV on mobile when you're away from your home network (within the U.S.) as long as you access your account on that network every 30 days. If you travel often, check in with your mobile device frequently to avoid being locked out when you're away. Note that you can still watch streaming content with no restrictions.
