#3370. In Shana Feste’s Films, Gender-Flipping Cinema’s ‘Tradition of Celebrating Damaged Men’ Is Its Own Reward

Shana Feste knows her filmography might be a bit tough to pin down. Some directors like to stick to a certain genre. Not Feste. Some only like to work with certain stars. Not Feste. Others enter a franchise and never look back. Not Feste.

But over the course of nearly two decades behind the camera, Feste has carved out a particular sweet spot, regardless of the genre or the cast or the wider world her stories fit inside: She likes complicated women. Not unlikable women, but messy women, contradictory women, women who get things done their own way. It’s a signature unto itself.

“My filmmaking, my history, people have not really known what to do with me. I’m making a comedy, I’m making a horror film, I’m making a genre thriller,” Feste told IndieWire during a recent interview. “But I do find that they’re all starting to build into each other, especially the trajectory from ‘Country Strong’ to ‘Run Sweetheart Run’ to ‘Heartland.’ I’ve always been drawn to women who don’t behave correctly. I’ve always been interested in women who don’t grieve correctly, who mother incorrectly, who love incorrectly. I just want women to have the freedom to behave in this contradictory, destructive, funny, selfish way and be given the same freedom that male characters are given.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

Another shared characteristic between Feste’s complicated women: They may be messy or unexpected, but they tend to get shit done. In her new film “Heartland,” getting shit done is at the center of the story, as the Nashville-set drama follows Jessica Chastain as Misty Jones, a former country-singing superstar who left the business after her designation as the, ahem, “cunt of country” became too much to bear. She’s thrust back into that world after her niece, rising star Charlie Heart (Carter Faith), goes missing. Misty, being Misty, takes it upon herself to get to the bottom of an increasingly dark and twisted mystery, no matter what it takes.

“I am a mom of three, 51, and I’m like, ‘Let’s write about some women who get shit done,’” she said. “I find a lot of those women exist. I’m living in the South now that I see those women every day and am inspired by them. We have this long-established cinematic tradition of celebrating damaged men. But when women behave similarly, they could be labeled as hysterical or dramatic or that word, unlikable. I want to prove that wrong.”

For the (complicated, messy, extremely capable) character of Misty, Feste said, she initially tapped into her longtime love of film noir. She always gravitated toward the Humphrey Bogart types, she said, but wondered what might happen if they gave those sorts of roles to women. That also fed into the dark underbelly of the Nashville scene that the film interrogates, a perfectly noir-ish idea.

“It could have been any city, but specifically this dark underbelly had to do with the music world,” Feste said. “Sadly, it was a common experience for a lot of artists that I spoke with. It was an experience that I’ve experienced in our industry, and it was all too relevant. When we were making the movie, a lot of conversation around Diddy was happening. He had just been arrested, and things were coming into light. We thought, oh wow, this is such a topical moment. And I’m like, it’s always topical, sadly. Whether we’re Epstein, Diddy, Weinstein, this is always going to be in the world, sadly.”

But Feste is also someone who loves this world and wants to celebrate what’s good and true about it. “Country Strong” was about making it — and maybe even making it again — even at great personal cost. “Heartland” just ratchets that sensibility up.

“I wanted to lean into the secrets and the dark corners and the underbelly, but I also will always celebrate the artistry and the storytelling of country music,” she said. “Misty says one line that really speaks so much to me about what the film is: ‘You don’t deserve country music.’ It takes a lot to deserve country music in my eyes. Country music is like the apex of storytelling. So to point out someone who doesn’t deserve country music, I mean, that’s a big insult for me.”

Feste started writing “Heartland” around four years ago, mostly because she was really missing the world of country music that framed her 2010 music drama “Country Strong.” “My father died about eight years ago, and I found myself listening to a lot of country music when he died,” she said. “In the years after he died, going back to the music that he loved, that he used to play for me in the car when we were driving on road trips, I realized that when you’re a writer, you don’t know quite why you write something until years later. And I realized, oh, I’m really missing my father.”

She was also eager to reteam with her “Country Strong” collaborators Jenno Topping and Randall Poster, two people who Feste said have believed in her the most over the course of her career. (Topping and Poster both produced “Heartland,” with Poster also serving as music supervisor, as he did on “Country Strong.”) “When I’m having my darkest days about, I don’t know, me and what I create and my career, knowing that they believe in me has always been such a huge lift,” Feste said. “So having them help me tell this story was just monumental. It was being with someone that you knew had your back the entire time.”

If “Heartland” sees Misty feeling ill at ease in the very spaces that used to celebrate her talent, Feste had the opposite experience. Six films into her directing career, she said “Heartland” let her approach her work in an entirely new way. And it felt good.

“What was really valuable with this experience is that I felt completely comfortable saying, ‘I don’t know,’ and I don’t know if I’ve ever felt that way,” she said. “Certainly not with my first few films, feeling like as a woman, I had to know every answer from every head of department immediately. It was only working with this group of filmmakers, Jenno and Randy and [production designer] Naomi [Shohan], some of my heads of production, that I knew that they saw my vulnerability not as a weakness, but as a strength. I was able to say, ‘I don’t know, what do you think?’ That’s where a very new form of collaboration happened that I haven’t experienced in my career, and with Jessica as well.”

Casting Chastain was an easy call for Feste. She wanted someone who could sing and who was admired in this space, but Chastain’s way of working and approach to on-set life gave Feste more to work with than she could have dreamed.

“I always want my films, especially when we’re shooting a movie that takes place in Nashville, to feel authentic, and I knew Jessica already had a huge buy-in from this audience. The South, they love her from ‘George & Tammy,’” Feste said. “And Jessica can sing, and that is another qualifier. Whenever I’m making any kind of movie with music, I want the actors to be able to sing their own material. But I think most of all, Jessica is one of the biggest champions of other women that I’ve ever met.”

It was freeing for Feste to say “I don’t know,” but Chastain also made it clear that she was there to support Feste’s vision and leadership.

“There were certain times on set where it would get a little loud or kind of disorderly, and people would be talking and having opinions, and no matter what, she’d be like, ‘Shana, sorry, I couldn’t hear you,’ and it was like this just gentle reminder, ‘This is who is leading the ship right now for me,’” the filmmaker recalled. “It was done in the classiest, most polite way.”

That approach turned the collaboration into more of a partnership. When Chastain had an idea, Feste was eager to listen. Even a decade ago, she said, that might not have been so easy for her.

“If I had been the director that I was 10 years ago, it would’ve scared me to death, because Jessica is not afraid to come into a scene and say, ‘OK, wait, that might not be serving us. Let’s throw that idea out of the window. What if we did this?,’” Feste said. “As a director, I’m planning, and every shot is in my head, and I’ve done the work, and I’ve done the homework, and I’m the A student. And to be able to relinquish control and admit when my idea wasn’t the best idea and she’s coming in with a stronger idea because she is Jessica Chastain? She has done the work. She has made this character so rich. This wasn’t a scary experience. It was actually going to elevate the scene and make it work even better.”

It was always the plan for Feste’s stars to also sing their songs to add to the film’s deeper authenticity. “When I’m watching movies that feature performing artists, and there’s so much hype, and they’re playing this celebrated musical performer, and then they come on, and we hear them sing and we’re like, have they been re-voiced? It’s just kind of mediocre? You just kind of lose your authenticity. You lose the ownership of the movie,” she said.

Casting Jennifer Nettles was something of a no-brainer for Feste, and so was actually directing the country superstar. “I didn’t know how to direct someone how to move on stage. That is something that’s not in my repertoire of directing. I can direct someone talking about their divorce in a bedroom, but how to command a stage and move your body? That is something that she learned over 20 years of experience being a superstar,” she said. “Most of the time I said, ‘Just speak to the audience like you are at the Opry, like you’ve done a thousand times. Make it your own.’ She did so much heavy lifting for me.”

So too did Carter Faith. In early discussions about the five characters in the film who are musical artists, Feste said she and Poster were constantly trying to figure out who they would sound like in the real world. Was Misty an Emmylou Harris? A Miranda Lambert? And who was young rising star Charlie Heart? Was she a Taylor Swift type? Poster had an easy answer: She sounds like this actual rising star, Carter Faith. And when it became clear that Faith was able to and interested in auditioning for the role? Serendipity.

“She was like a breath of fresh air,” Feste said. “I remember asking her, ‘Carter, what do you think you have in common with Charlie?’ And she said, ‘Well, we both have boy names.’ My heart exploded. It was the most non-Hollywood endearing response. Then I heard her story of how she was eating red beans and rice, crashing on couches, calling all of these places on Lower Broadway just to get an audition to be the performer at 10:00 AM on a Monday morning. She is someone who really moved to Nashville the day she graduated from high school to make it. She was Charlie. So much of her experience was exactly what the character was going through. So it was only the question of, are you brave enough to access all that trauma of how you got here? And she was absolutely, she said yes, and she trusted me, and it makes me emotional thinking about it because that’s an incredible trust to have.”

Faith also wrote the lyrics to the song that plays at the end of the film, which Feste sees as “dialogue that I could never write.” All the songs in the film and on its soundtrack, including the ones Feste simply imagined as titles first, like “Texas Land,” or that her stars like John Hawkes wrote or that Poster commissioned, add to the film’s incredible authentic feeling and sound. “Working with musical performances in film, it is so additive because it just takes the storytelling to another level. It’s beyond the dialogue. It’s beyond physical blocking. It tells story in this just purely emotional, raw, beautiful way,” she said.

Next up: In true Feste fashion, she’s working on or thinking about a variety of other projects next, including the next chapter of the “Dirty Diana” story, which she first cooked up during lockdown, a TV series about a Southern family, and her “dream project,” which is about Texas bank robbers. Mostly, she said, “I really want to continue working in this space. I want to continue telling stories about messy, complicated, vulnerable Southern women. I think that’s my bread and butter.”

#3369. 7 Best Things About the Original Xbox That Aren't Halo, Ranked

When Microsoft entered the console market with its Xbox brand, people outside the company didn’t necessarily have high hopes. Throughout the 1990s, the industry was dominated by Japanese hardware companies like Nintendo, Sega, and Sony. But Microsoft meant business, and its first console effort provided some excellent reasons to give the brand a chance.

One of the best reasons to own an Xbox was undoubtedly Halo: Combat Evolved, with a compelling first-person campaign and a multiplayer mode that kept people busy for dozens or even hundreds of hours. Bungie’s sci-fi epic shifted a lot of hardware units, but it wasn’t the only reason for players to be excited. Here are seven of the best things about the original Xbox that aren’t Halo.

The Xbox came out during a difficult time for Sega. The company had just ended an unfortunate string of hardware failures that concluded with the death of the Dreamcast, its final console. That platform had offered all sorts of great games, but they didn’t connect with wide audiences because everyone was too focused on the PlayStation 2, which offered a built-in DVD player that made it a particularly attractive prospect.

Microsoft offered Sega a way to present its own vision for a console future without devoting all of its resources to challenging hardware. A string of terrific Sega titles hit the Xbox during its early years, and Microsoft promoted them aggressively, from Jet Set Radio Future to Sega GT 2002 and even more niche affairs like Gun Valkyrie. That support persisted throughout the console’s life, and also produced Panzer Dragoon Orta, one of the very finest games on the system.

Commercial tie-ins weren’t huge news by the time Burger King released a series of three video games near the end of the Xbox life-cycle. They had been around for some time, particularly during the Atari 2600 era. In 1983, Chase the Chuck Wagon even built a game around a dog chasing a wagon, which consumers obtained by sending in UPC labels clipped from bags of Purina dog food.

Burger King brought that convention back with Sneak King, PocketBike Racer, and Big Bumpin’. At the time, Burger King advertised heavily in print and on TV with its creepy “king” character, who featured in each of the games. To get a copy, players paid a small fee while placing an order for a value meal. The games worked on both the original Xbox and the newer 360, a cross-generation wonder that people have largely forgotten.

Players naturally associate Microsoft with Halo, which it published on behalf of Bungie. Fable, from Lionhead Studios, kicked off another successful franchise that’s scheduled to return early in 2027 with a reboot from Playground Games. But the giant publisher also took chances on less conventional fare during the era.

One such game was Kung Fu Chaos, which offered a parody of ‘70s B-movie chaos. In a slapstick fighting brawler along the lines of Power Stone, players survived perilous environments and talked trash to their opponents until one fighter emerged the victor. The edgy humor doesn’t hold up well today, but plenty of players had fun with it at the time.

Other unusual releases from the time included Phantom Dust, a deck builder with 3D arena battles, and Voodoo Vince. The latter was a platformer featuring a voodoo doll roaming New Orleans. To harm enemies, he had to inflict damage on himself through dangerous maneuvers, like setting himself on fire. Players never knew quite what to expect from Microsoft Game Studios at the time, and it was wonderful.

First released on Nov. 15, 2001, the original Xbox missed the ‘90s by only a little bit. As it helped define the 2000s gaming scene, it did so with help from one powerful component: the hard drive.

Players suddenly had a lot of space to store their game saves. They could install them directly to the device, no longer relying on separate memory cards. If they preferred, they could also rip audio CDs to the drive and then play their favorite titles accompanied by their favorite music. You haven’t lived until you’ve played Dead or Alive Xtreme Beach Volleyball while Creed, Nickelback, and Avril Lavigne croon in the background.

Unlike today, when a required install for a game like Grand Theft Auto 6 can eat up roughly a third of your available space on a PlayStation 5, the original Xbox supported large libraries without flinching. That made it an especially good time to be an Xbox fan.

Formerly known as Tehkan, the game publisher that became Tecmo (and later Koei Tecmo) published its first original console game on the Famicom in 1986. Traditionally a Japanese publisher, the company nevertheless made a name for itself in North America, thanks in large part to the classic Ninja Gaiden series.

Unexpectedly, Tecmo threw considerable support behind the Xbox hardware, and with excellent results. Ninja Gaiden (later released in an expanded form as Ninja Gaiden Black) became one of the hardware’s biggest successes. Tecmo also brought over the excellent Dead or Alive fighting game series, which felt like the perfect match for Microsoft’s powerful system. The beautiful environments and the detailed fighters within them provided ample eye candy to remind players that console gaming had come a long way since the 8-bit figures they remembered stomping on turtles only a decade prior.

Graphics were still a huge differentiator, and Tecmo was arguably the era’s developer that did the most to prove the Xbox was a graphical powerhouse.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Console gaming had a certain feel to it by the time the Xbox arrived, and Microsoft quickly pushed some boundaries. Today, many games release on PC alongside their console counterparts, but that wasn’t the case back in 2001, when Xbox began building bridges across some of the biggest gaps.

On Xbox, we got to see some games that surprised us, like The Elder Scrolls 3: Morrowind, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, and even Sid Meier’s Pirates. Microsoft also published versions of the original Fable across the two platforms, and the role-playing epic felt just right on both. And MechAssault made a big splash when Xbox Live launched, proving the power of the hardware to provide compelling online play experiences.

The Dreamcast deserves credit for making some early efforts in the same arena, but the Xbox stuck the landing. In the process, it set Microsoft up to enjoy the even more successful generation that followed with the Xbox 360.

By the time the Xbox came around, the strong relationship between Rare and Nintendo had soured enough that the time was ripe for someone else to swoop in and acquire the most storied software developer in Twycross, England. Microsoft saw the opportunity and went for it.

Although it has failed to capitalize on the Rare acquisition the way people once thought it might, Microsoft did acquire some early gems in the years before Sea of Thieves. Grabbed by the Ghoulies and Conker: Live & Reloaded both launched on the original Xbox. The latter served as one of the final Microsoft releases on its first console. A remake of the surprisingly vulgar Nintendo 64 classic, it provided not only a visual overhaul of the single-player campaign, but multiplayer modes that kept players busy fragging each other for hours at a time.

Most of Rare’s post-Nintendo triumphs came during the Xbox 360 era, but its earliest efforts on the original Xbox are solid games that hold up reasonably well today. They didn’t exactly set the world on fire, but they’re fun to revisit even now. You can still acquire them on the Xbox Store today, and they’re well worth a look.

Disc-to-digital is either a genuine players-first initiative or a swipe at Sony. Either way, I'll take it

#3366. The Rings of Power’ Officially Confirms a Major Season 3 Storyline Was Scrapped Because of One Actor

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has plenty of logistical challenges to overcome, and fortunately, its cast seems to have a pretty good understanding of what's expected of them. However, not every actor is capable, and during production on the show's third season, one particularly troublesome performer managed to cause enough problems that the creative team had to rethink its plans.

Speaking exclusively with Maggie Lovitt for Collider Behind the Scenes, co-showrunner Patrick McKay and director Charlotte Brändström revealed that a dog introduced in Season 3 was originally supposed to have a much larger role, but to be blunt, he was not a very good boy. McKay told Collider:

"We had this idea that Arondir had a dog, and there's this scene — I actually really love this scene. I love the way you put it together — where Galadriel returns home from the battle, and everyone else has a partner or a child waiting for them. Even Arondir has the dog, and she has no one. I find it very touching, and I love Morfydd's performance. But the idea that this dog would be in many scenes and be a source of humor and interact with the Orc, and I think we even had an idea of bringing the dog back later in the season. No, that dog was an absolute nightmare."

Brändström admitted that the animal certainly looked the part, but getting it to behave long enough to film anything was another matter entirely. She explained, "He looked great. He looked how we wanted, but we managed to get him to eat the bone at some point. It was very hard to keep him still. It was very hard to keep him still long enough to say, 'Camera, start rolling.'" McKay then revealed just how much unusable footage the production accumulated while attempting to work with the animal. "There's a hard drive filled with, like, bum takes and the dog whimpering and yelling and barking and going after the Orc. I mean, it was a nightmare," McKay laughed. "So we ended up with less dog. However, I think that a little bit of dog goes a long way."

While the dog's intended recurring storyline was scaled back, its introduction is part of a much larger effort to make Middle-earth feel more tangible in Season 3. The new episodes introduce Rivendell, the famous Elven sanctuary that audiences will recognize from Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings movies. McKay told Collider:

"We really like building things. We really want these fantastical worlds to feel real and tangible and immersive. You know, one example I think of in the first episode is we introduce Rivendell, right? And I think the move that you and Alex came up with is starting in a virtual world and then entering into a physical set all in one shot. We do that a lot because one makes the other feel more real, right? And I think we're constantly looking for something photographic to ground it in."

Brändström agreed, emphasizing the importance of giving the actors something real to interact with, even when their surroundings will eventually be expanded digitally. "For the actors, it's important to feel grounded. They need to touch stuff. They need to feel the world around them," she explained. "They don't really care about whether we extend it then and add some mountains in the background, because they don't look at that. But they need to have something to be grounded, to touch, to feel. I mean, we even brought in horses on the stages and had a road that they could come up."

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 is streaming on Prime Video. #3365. David O. Russell’s ‘Madden’ Biopic Is Out Next Week — Does Anybody Know or Care?

Once upon a time, a new David O. Russell movie would be a must-see cinematic event. The writer/director earned three consecutive Best Picture Oscar nominations with “The Fighter,” “Silver Linings Playbook,” and “American Hustle,” all of which scored at the box office and are roundly regarded as generational classics of their era and even holiday fare. But did you know Russell has a new movie opening next week from Amazon MGM Studios? That would be “Madden,” his biopic starring a physically distended and hair-pieced Nicolas Cage as the iconic NFL commentator. When I told an IndieWire colleague about this story, they had heard of “Madden” the movie, yes, but had no idea that Russell directed it. Doesn’t bode well. Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

The film co-stars Russell perennial collaborator Christian Bale, strapped back into the hair and makeup chair for another grotesque transformation, as Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis, receding bleach-blond hairline and all, plus a wigged-out Kathryn Hahn as Madden’s wife Virginia, and poor Sienna Miller as Davis’s wife Carol. Reports have claimed the sports biopic carries a $75 million budget, making it one of the “Spanking the Monkey” director’s most expensive movies next to the critically flayed COVID release “Amsterdam,” which, not adjusted for inflation, cost a reported $80 million and earned a paltry $14 million domestically. That’s a movie that entirely vaporized from the cultural imagination — though you may recall a much-memed excerpt of a blink-and-you’ll-miss-her Taylor Swift being thrown under a car to her doom.

The “Madden” release strategy does not inspire confidence, either, suggesting a classic case of bag-and-tag on the part of Amazon MGM Studios: a day-and-date release on Prime Video globally with a perfunctory, subterranean-level theatrical bow, both on Wednesday, November 18. The critics’ screening takes place Monday, November 16, with the embargo lifting about 15 hours later. Muted marketing only further intimates Amazon wants to take the latest Russell joint gently into that good night — but why? Is it that bad? The trailer has more than 8.6 million views and counting, though that’s largely explained by the prolific fanbase behind Madden, who died in 2021, and the NFL. Less so by any fanbase of Russell’s.

To be fair, the studio has its hands full trying to position “Project Hail Mary” in the Oscar race and back into voters’ consciousness after opening theatrically six months ago. Amazon MGM’s social media heist movie “How to Rob a Bank” opens in theaters this Friday, while another awards hopeful, “I Play Rocky,” is in limited release. While “Project Hail Mary” was a box office juggernaut for the company, the tech giant has yet to master juggling multiple tentpole-scale projects theatrically at once — though they’ve had a banner year with considerable successes “Verity” and “The Sheep Detectives” spread out throughout 2026.

Co-scripted by Russell and Cambron Clark, “Madden” centers on Madden’s Super Bowl-winning partnership with Al Davis and the Raiders that led to the “NFL Madden” games. The film wrapped production well over a year ago, in late spring 2025 in Atlanta. A TMZ report from May 21 claimed several actors walked off set after Russell allegedly used a racial epithet during a scene. A reputation for volatility has followed Russell across projects, from the widely seen behind-the-scenes footage of the filmmaker chewing out his “I Heart Huckabees” star Lily Tomlin, to Amy Adams’ confessional interviews in which she revealed the filmmaker made her cry throughout the “American Hustle” shoot. George Clooney has called Russell “a miserable fuck” and swore never to work with him again after his experience making “Three Kings.”

The five-time Oscar nominee has built a career on quirky, sprawling ensembles and pushing actors toward extreme physical performances, like Christian Bale, who went gaunt (again) to win an Academy Award for “The Fighter,” then put on the pounds for “American Hustle.” Back in October, Russell and producer Todd Black appeared at the Virginia Film Festival in Charlottesville to present four clips from “Madden” — which showcased Cage in prosthetic padding that’s more January Jones in “Mad Men” Season 5 than Kazu Hiro Oscar-level effort, plus an exasperatingly accented Bale with bleached eyebrows, and the women, including Hahn and Miller, in insane wigs. Clearly, this is Russell operating at an 11, with characters, based on these clips, squawking over each other like the most strident ensemble scenes out of “Silver Linings.”

During the panel, Russell described the casting process as “trippy,” noting that Cage gained weight for the role along with the prosthetics.

“We were scared because we weren’t telling a documentary, but we were honoring John Madden and honoring Al Davis,” Black said. “We were trying to make it an entertaining story without making it a documentary. So some stuff was inspired by, some stuff was true, and a lot of stuff we made up, not wildly, but just for entertainment value.”

The producer added, “I think when you see the movie, you’ll see it really is an incredibly positive film that when you watch it at Thanksgiving time, I think you’ll watch it with your family, hopefully, and you’ll walk out feeling really happy about it and telling people it’s such an inspiring film.”

He might be onto something. With three NFL games scheduled for Thanksgiving — including the Kansas City Chiefs at the Buffalo Bills on NBC and Peacock — “Madden” could prove apt counter-programming to sports spectacle. That’s if enough people know where to watch it, or that it’s available at all.

#3364. How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.

While phishing on the dark web works as it does on the clear web, scammers have a few unique advantages due to the secretive nature of the environment. Most importantly, you can’t just glance at an onion link to tell if the site is genuine. Normal website URLs tend to be short and memorable, while onion links are 56-character strings of alphanumeric text that look mostly like gibberish.

When you try to connect, Tor Browser verifies the URL against the originating website’s cryptographic key, which is how you know nobody has hijacked the address or tampered with it midway. But since this has the unwanted effect of making domains harder to recall, scammers have a much easier time generating lookalike addresses or creating website clones.

For example, many popular websites use “vanity prefixes” to make their onion addresses more easily identifiable or to add some branding appeal. That means their 56-character onion link starts with something like “facebook,” “bbcnews,” or “ciadotgov.” But scammers can use a free tool like mkp224o to generate lookalike addresses with the same vanity prefix as the legitimate website, which gives users a false sense of security.

Of course, most dark web users don’t type addresses directly into Tor Browser; they use dark web directories like the Hidden Wiki to find useful onion sites relevant to their search. Scammers will create fake search engines or link directories to point users to their fake websites, like when the Ahmia search engine discovered that a copy of its platform was directing users to 255 cloned services back in 2015.

Of course, it’s possible to orchestrate phishing attempts that don’t involve cloning sites at all. Researchers at Freie Universität Berlin describe a sophisticated technique where attackers serve the real website through their own reverse proxy, which lets them manipulate parts of the site or log your online activity without your awareness. In 2019, ESET even found a trojanized version of Tor Browser that replaced Bitcoin addresses on websites to direct payments to hackers. So both genuine websites and your browser itself are also vulnerable to manipulation if you download or access them from an unverified source.

There are a few best practices to avoid phishing attacks when using the dark web. None of them are foolproof on their own, but together, they considerably lower the risk of ending up on a fake or manipulated website.

On the desktop version of Tor Browser, you can access an onion site using a shortened version of its URL called an Onion Name. For now, this feature only works with SecureDrop, so newsrooms can establish tip lines with addresses like mysitename.securedrop.tor.onion, which would then redirect to the 56-character original onion address. This feature is in active development, so more platforms might support it in the future.

When you load up an onion site using the Tor Browser, you’ll see an onion icon on the address bar, which confirms that your connection is end-to-end encrypted. But you can also click on the onion icon to check if the site has an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, which tells you that its authenticity has been verified by a trusted certificate authority like DigiCert. While not every legitimate onion site will have an EV certificate, famous ones like Facebook tend to.

On the other hand, if you see a caution sign next to the onion icon, that means the site is using a self-signed or expired certificate that isn’t guaranteed by a trusted authority. It may also imply that the site is being served over an insecure URL. This doesn’t definitely tell you it’s a phishing site, but it’s a red flag to watch out for nevertheless.

Don’t rely on search engines, link directories, Reddit threads, or Telegram channels too heavily on the dark web. Once you’re sure you’ve found the onion address for a genuine site, bookmark it so you can access it directly the next time you want to visit.

If you realized that you’ve been the victim of a phishing attempt, the first step is to close the browser window with the fake site and access the real onion address to reset any account passwords you may have accidentally divulged.

Also, generally try to enable two-factor authentication and PGP logins on any dark web account that supports it for added security. And if you downloaded Tor Browser from anywhere other than the official Tor Project site, uninstall it now and grab a fresh copy from the official address.

#3363. Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go

The term that comes to mind most is “ambulance-chasing.” Earlier this week, just one week after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault and two days after he was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for his crimes, word spread that Netflix was prepping a documentary on the comedian-turned-criminal.

Olivia Isaacs’ documentary has been in the works for a while. Deadline’s initial story on the project even noted that it “was referenced during the trial” and that while “giving evidence at London’s Southwark Crown Court, Mark Pinheiro, a former friend of Brand, said he had been approached by a producer about the Netflix show.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

But that the project — “Russell Brand: Open Secret,” a slim and unfocused documentary feature that clocks in at just under 90 minutes — was being dropped on the streamer to ride the wave of interest after Brand’s conviction and sentencing felt distasteful. How essential, after all, could this be? And what could it tell us about Brand’s actual trial, sentencing, and conviction?

Turns out, not much. Isaacs’ film doesn’t get into the trial until its final five minutes (counting its end credits to boot), when it uses title cards to share the conviction news, note that all of the allegations contained in the film itself “pre-date” those that led to the conviction, and make clear that Brand’s legal team was contacted after the Monday conviction and chose not to respond. That’s perhaps the most interesting part of the film’s literally tacked-on final moments: a desire to show its work when it comes to the journalism and attendant standards behind Brand’s long-simmering takedown.

Other elements are far less successful, as Isaacs’ film leans hard on tired tropes and cloying conventions. Captions frequently mention “[unsettling music playing]” or “[dramatic music playing]” during the most benign moments. Old footage of Brand, from home video to early stand-up gigs, is played slowly, all the better to maximize the sense that something is wrong with this man. Far more effective are interviews with those who were allegedly victimized by Brand, but those are often drowned out by played-out techniques.

The film opens with a typical “rise and fall” style montage, charting Brand’s humble beginnings, meteoric rise to fame, profound injection into the cultural consciousness (he met the queen! and also Tom Cruise!), stumble into right-wing ideology, and eventual criminal convictions for horrific acts the film posits everyone knew about forever.

It is, after all, called “Russell Brand: Open Secret.”

Isaacs’ film lacks a thesis beyond the general idea that everyone knew Brand was a creep from the jump. She assembles a hodgepodge of talking heads to hammer that home, including fellow comedians, some genuinely freaked out ex-girlfriends, a handful of accusers (including one who, reticent to appear on camera, is replaced with an actress, one of the film’s most thoughtful choices), and some bizarrely starry-eyed commentators (journalist George Monbiot comes across particularly badly here, zipping from talking about his early delight in Brand and his now-held belief that Brand’s far-right switch is the most horrifying aspect of all of this, oof).

Most compelling are Times journalists Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace, who worked tirelessly to investigate myriad accusations against Brand for years (Urwin first began to look into Brand in January of 2019). Even smushed up against a herky-jerky timeline and a loose sense of purpose, the way that Urwin and Wace talk about the precise nature of their work, what they can and cannot report, the women they spoke to, and the ways in which they were nearly shut down (and, in fact, many other investigations of its ilk were allegedly turned off) is both gripping and necessary.

With more time and better access, the film could have focused more on the police and legal minds that helped build the case against Brand, but in the rush to get this out in the world, that was surely not a major aim.

By its midpoint, Isaacs’ film turns its lens on the culture that helped give rise to Brand, the wild “noughties” when “ladette culture” ruled and being overtly sexy and crude was de rigueur. Women were into Brand! Being ruthlessly unfunny and breathlessly boorish was hot! Also, his dad was mean to him! Diddy and David Walliams jump scares! These are some of the insights on offer in “Open Secret,” and the only thing truly revealing about them is how huge of a mistake it was to let someone as outwardly disgusting and deeply unwitty as Brand get into a place where he could pick and choose his “damsels” or his “whores,” depending on who is talking about them.

The film speed-runs through the last few years of Brand’s life and career, as he pivots into far-right shock politics and Christianity just as the walls are starting to close in on him. Brand may have alleged that his former cadre of famous friends and stalwarts won’t “touch him with a barge pole” these days, but the film’s distinct lack of bigger talking heads stands out. That could stand some further interrogation, too, but there’s simply no time for that. (Well, there is, but not if you want to be a part of this news cycle.)

The four-day gap between Brand’s conviction and the film’s release is zippy, even for Netflix, which has gotten progressively speedier with its true crime joints. In July of 2024, it was announced that Netflix would release a multi-part Karen Read documentary, just days after her first murder trial ended in a mistrial due to a hung jury on July 1, 2024. Three episodes dropped earlier this month.

In January of 2026, the streamer announced a Lucy Letby project with “unprecedented access” after the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) announced it would bring no further criminal charges against the former nurse, who was sentenced to life imprisonment for a slew of charges of murder and attempted murder of infants in her care following a review of additional allegations. “The Truth and Tragedy of Moriah Wilson” was first publicly announced in February of 2026, almost three years after Kaitlin Armstrong was convicted of first-degree murder of the cyclist in November of 2023.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” will surely capture lots of eyeballs as this part of the news cycle winds down, but what the film trades for immediacy, it more than loses in actual insight. Part two can’t be far behind. Let’s just hope it takes far more time to make and far more consideration to craft.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” is now streaming on Netflix.

#3361. 'The Martian' Meets 'Interstellar' in Netflix's 10-Episode Sci-Fi Drama Made for Your Next Binge

Amanda M. Castro is a Network TV writer at Collider and a New York–based journalist whose work has appeared in Newsweek, where she is an Associate Editor, and The U.S. Sun, where she previously served as a Senior Consumer Reporter.

She specializes in network television coverage, delivering sharp, thoughtful analysis of long-running procedural hits and ambitious new dramas across broadcast TV. At Collider, Amanda explores character arcs, storytelling trends, and the cultural impact of network series that keep audiences tuning in week after week.

Born and raised in Puerto Rico, Amanda is bilingual and holds a degree in Communication, Film, and Media Studies from the University of New Haven.

Getting to Mars is hard enough, but leaving everyone you love behind might be even harder. Netflix's Away takes the idea of a mission to the Red Planet and fleshes it out on a more personal level by following a crew of astronauts as they try to make history while managing their relationships and obligations at home. The 10-episode science-fiction series, which stars two-time Oscar winner Hilary Swank, will likely appeal to fans of The Martian's survival aspect and Interstellar's family-oriented storytelling. Plenty of complications arise aboard the spacecraft, but some of the show's hardest moments happen millions of miles away.

Created by Andrew Hinderaker, Away premiered on Netflix in September 2020. Although the series was canceled after its first season, its 10 episodes tell a largely self-contained story about the first crewed mission to Mars. The journey takes three years, and the people aboard have much to lose before they reach their destination, making for a different kind of space drama that draws as much interest from people watching from Earth as from the astronauts traveling through space.

Swank stars as Emma Green, a NASA astronaut selected to command the Atlas, a spacecraft carrying an international crew on humanity's first mission to Mars. Joining her are Indian pilot and medical officer Ram Arya (Ray Panthaki), Chinese chemist Lu Wang (Vivian Wu), Russian cosmonaut Misha Popov (Mark Ivanir), and British botanist Kwesi Weisberg-Abban (Ato Essandoh). They come from different backgrounds and have varying levels of experience, but they share the significant responsibility of getting to Mars alive.

Emma's appointment as commander is hardly straightforward, as some crew members question her leadership after an early emergency aboard the Atlas, leaving her to earn their confidence while managing the demands of an increasingly dangerous expedition. They also face the challenge of keeping everyone alive for three years in a confined spacecraft. Equipment malfunctions, medical emergencies, and problems with the ship's essential systems put the mission at risk, forcing the astronauts to rely on one another even when their personal differences get in the way.

One of the mission's most compelling aspects is its international nature. Every astronaut goes through a unique set of experiences that influence their relationships throughout the mission. Misha is a seasoned space traveler, with a lot of turbulence in his personal life as the price of his success. Kwesi is a newcomer to astronautics, with knowledge of botany and some faith beliefs that influence how he sees the mission.

Although this book has a central theme of the technological obstacles of space travel, much of the content focuses on events on Earth. Here, Matt Logan (Josh Charles), Emma's husband, and their daughter, Alexis “Lex” Logan (Talitha Bateman), must learn to cope without Emma. Matt is an ex-astronaut who was unable to join the expedition due to his medical problems and suffered a stroke shortly after Emma's departure. As a result, the family faces issues beyond the distance between Earth and Mars. Recovery includes both the difficult rehabilitation process for Matt while Lex is doing everything in her power to deal with the experiences of being a mother without her mother and caring for her father. All Emma can do is accept that, unfortunately, she cannot simply abandon the mission every time something goes wrong at home.

Christopher Nolan's Interstellar explores the emotional consequences of space exploration through a father and daughter separated by an extraordinary journey. Away approaches a similar idea from a different family dynamic, with a mother attempting to reconcile her professional ambitions with her responsibilities as a parent. The separation is difficult for everyone involved, and the series gives those feelings considerable room to develop.

Of course, viewers looking for the relentless action of The Martian should adjust their expectations. Away has its share of emergencies, including a damaged solar panel and a failing water reclamation system, but it often prioritizes the crew's emotional lives over the mechanics of survival. That's a deliberate choice, although it occasionally comes at the expense of the show's pacing.

One thing prospective viewers should know before settling in for all 10 episodes is that Away will not return for Season 2; Netflix canceled the series in October 2020, just weeks after its premiere. The decision was reportedly tied to production costs, with individual episodes costing about $6 million, despite the show's early streaming success.

The good news is that the first season does give a certain amount of closure. The Atlas arrives at Mars, and the crew manages to pull through with the main mission goals. Although some characters have unresolved issues and contradictions that could be developed in the second season, they still get enough closure related to the mission itself.

For anyone who is interested in a show about astronauts who spend as much time thinking about their loved ones as performing operations in outer space, Away is unsurprisingly worth watching. The show may struggle with pacing and its emotional core, and some of the emotional backstory may feel too sweet. Nevertheless, Swank and the other actors give the series a personality you can't help but appreciate.

#3360. GTA 6 Launch Times Confirm How You Can Play Early

With the Grand Theft Auto 6 launch just days away, players are already looking for ways to get into Vice City before everyone else. And while Rockstar isn’t offering an early-access period, its confirmed regional release schedule has given gamers a familiar workaround to consider: the New Zealand trick.

Rockstar Games has officially confirmed that GTA 6 will unlock at midnight local time on November 19, across all regions on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. This means players won’t all be getting access at the same moment. Instead, the game will slowly go live as the clock strikes midnight in each time zone, putting New Zealand among the first places to receive it.

For players in the US, GTA 6 will unlock at 12am local time on November 19. However, New Zealand players will get access much earlier, with the game going live at midnight on November 19 in their region. Depending on the US time zone, this could give players a head start of several hours by switching their console location to New Zealand.

The New Zealand trick is a popular workaround among Xbox players who want to access games before their local release time. It involves changing the console’s location to New Zealand, allowing players to potentially access a game when it becomes available in that region.

For GTA 6, Xbox Series X|S owners can find the location setting following these steps:

Now you can open your library when the clock strikes midnight in New Zealand on November 19, which is around 5am CT in the United States on November 18, and check if GTA 6 is available to play. If it works, it should give you a 19-hour headstart to the game access, which is huge and will help avoid spoilers.

There’s a catch, though. Neither Rockstar nor Microsoft has explicitly confirmed that this workaround will work for GTA 6. The regional release schedule is official, but that doesn’t automatically guarantee that changing your console location will unlock the game early.

There’s also a potential account risk worth considering before attempting the workaround. Microsoft’s Xbox Community Standards specifically prohibit attempts to circumvent regional content restrictions. Its guidance also recommends changing your country or region when you have actually moved to another country, rather than simply using a different location to access content.

Microsoft could take action against accounts found violating these restrictions. Possible consequences include warnings, suspensions or bans, although that does not mean every player attempting the trick will automatically face enforcement. So, do it at your own discretion.

Unfortunately, PS5 owners don’t have an equally simple option. PlayStation accounts are tied to the country selected when they are created, and Sony does not allow users to change that country later.

Accessing the New Zealand storefront would therefore require a separate account registered in that region, along with purchasing the game through that storefront. Simply changing the console's time or location won’t move an existing purchase to New Zealand.

For now, Xbox owners have a potentially easier route to an earlier Grand Theft Auto 6 session, but it remains unconfirmed whether it’d work as expected. With the November 19 launch approaching, players will have to decide whether a few extra hours in Vice City are worth the uncertainty.

The sixth installment in Rockstar Games' incomparable generational franchise, GTA VI's new Miami-flavored locale promises another violence-filled sandbox leveraged by cutting edge tech.

Black Friday is still a couple of weeks away, with the big shopping event falling on November 27, but Amazon's early Black Friday sale is already bringing some worthwhile discounts on Soundcore's Nebula projectors. There's quite a bit of variety here, too, from battery-powered projectors you can take camping or move between rooms to more powerful 4K models designed for a dedicated movie-night setup.

The Soundcore Nebula P1i is down to $299 from $399, while the Nebula P1 is $699.99, down from $799. Both offer 1080p resolution and Google TV, but their speaker setups are what make them interesting. The P1i has two 10W speakers that flip out and rotate to direct sound toward your seating area, while the P1's speakers detach completely and can run wirelessly for up to 20 hours. Small enough to slip into a bag, the Nebula Capsule 3 and Capsule 3 Laser are worth considering if you want something you can easily take on trips or move around the house. Both offer 1080p resolution, automatic image adjustments, and up to 2.5 hours of battery life, although the Laser model is a little brighter at 300 ANSI lumens compared with the standard model's 200.

The smaller Mars 3 Air is down to $519.99 from $599.99, offering 1080p resolution, 400 ANSI lumens of brightness, and up to 2.5 hours of playback. The larger Mars 3, now $899.99 from $999.99, steps things up with 1,000 ANSI lumens, up to five hours of battery life in Eco mode, and a more powerful 40W speaker. If you're ready to move beyond 1080p, the Nebula Cosmos 4K SE at $1,099.99 (originally $1,299.99) offers a more affordable way to get 4K resolution. Its hybrid LED and laser light source delivers up to 1,800 ANSI lumens, while its Dolby Vision support helps bring out more detail in compatible movies and shows. You also get Google TV and automatic image adjustments for easier setup, though it doesn't have a built-in battery, so you'll need a power outlet nearby.

At the premium end of Nebula's lineup, the X1 and newer X1S are designed for a more serious home theater setup. The X1 is down to $2,299 from $2,999, saving you $700, while the X1S is $2,799 from $3,299. Both use triple-laser technology with 4K resolution, Dolby Vision, and optical zoom, but the X1S has a considerable advantage in brightness, reaching up to 6,000 ANSI lumens compared with the X1's 3,500. That extra brightness is useful in rooms with some ambient light, but the tradeoff is louder fan noise.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). #3357. Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas?

Look, it’s only November, but we know we’re not the only people getting excited about Christmas already. In fact, we know that some studio executives have been thinking about the holiday season a lot for a while now. That’s because they know as well as anyone that they have two juggernauts to contend with: “Dune: Part Three” and “Avengers: Doomsday,” which open on Dec. 18 in true clash of the titans fashion.

There’s a question that if those movies take up so much oxygen, will there be room for anything else? The last “Dune” movie surpassed $700 million globally at the box office, and “Avengers: Doomsday” has already sold over $60 million in pre-sales. Those top two titles create enormous competition for everything opening on Christmas weekend itself. Those include the Dwayne Johnson threequel “Jumanji: Open World” from Sony, the football biopic “Mr. Irrelevant” from Paramount, Robert Eggers’ horror film “Werwulf” from Focus, and Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” from Neon. Paramount’s “The Angry Birds Movie 3” is also opening on December 23 just ahead of the rest. Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

Anyone will tell you the Christmas holiday is always crowded at the movies. And there’s usually room for multiple blockbusters to draw crowds. Despite the onslaught of new titles, U.S, distributors are confident they’ll be able to secure the screens they need to be successful. For instance, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” this year opened at the end of July to $360 million domestic, and “The Odyssey” in its third week in theaters still made $50 million. Even during the “Barbenheimer” weekend, “Sound of Freedom” in its third week managed to bring in another $19.8 million. There’s always opportunity if the demand is there.

Recent Christmases have been similarly crowded. Last year had “Avatar: Fire and Ash,” “The Housemaid,” a new “Spongebob,” and “Marty Supreme” open the weekend before Christmas, then “Anaconda” and “Song Sung Blue” over the holiday itself. 2024 had “Mufasa: The Lion King,” “Nosferatu,” “Sonic the Hedgehog 3,” “A Complete Unknown,” “Babygirl,” and “The Fire Inside” all in a short span just before Xmas.

But this Christmas does bring some unique challenges that studios are preemptively working around for their titles that are not “Dune” or “Avengers.” Both of those films have had tickets on sale for months, and both are locked in a fight for premium large format screens that distributors would be lying to say they didn’t want, even if it’s for a family film that doesn’t need it. Warner Bros. and Legendary’s “Dune: Part Three” specifically will exclusively be on IMAX screens, which has famously left “Doomsday” without them, leaving Disney to create its Infinity Vision certification to drum up excitement.

To compete, “Angry Birds 3” is still opening in 3D if on otherwise standard format screens. “Werwulf” won’t have IMAX as Focus did for “Nosferatu,” but it has pre-sold select 35mm screenings of the film that have already done quite well (they went on sale on the full moon last month). The hope, too, is that titles like “Jumanji” and “Mr. Irrelevant” appeal to crowds that are distinctive from the male, fanboy-heavy audiences for “Dunesday.”

One source IndieWire spoke with argued that even though this Christmas is top heavy, it’s arguably lighter in sheer quantity than we’ve seen in recent years. What we’re not seeing is a movie like “Marty Supreme” or “Uncut Gems” getting a run in a more mid-size or limited number of screens. Universal doesn’t have a movie opening in that window, nor does Amazon MGM. Other awards titles like “The Debut” from A24 are going earlier in the month and aren’t doing the limited, Christmas day, qualifying run before going wide in January (GKIDS’ “Look Back” may be an exception, opening December 30).

There are some potential holdovers that could generate money well into Christmas. Rival studio execs are keeping an eye on movies like Disney’s animated “Hexed” or Universal’s “Focker-in-Law,” and Focus’ “Elsinore” will also be going wider shortly before the holidays.

The hope now is that all of these films get their flowers and collectively put an exclamation point on a stellar 2026, with the box office now projected to finish far above $10 billion domestic, a number that might’ve been a pipe dream this time in 2025. That’s reason for holiday cheer, indeed.

#3356. 10 Best Shows Like The Mentalist On Netflix

One of the best procedural dramas of the 2010s is The Mentalist, which introduced the audience to Patrick Jane (Simon Baker), and for those looking for something similar to it, Netflix has some excellent options. Procedural drama is a popular genre on TV, bringing some of the best TV shows of all time, such as The Wire, Law & Order, Criminal Minds, and The X-Files, some of them adding elements from other genres. A procedural drama TV series follows professionals and/or specialized teams who investigate a new case every episode, with some shows having overarching plots.

These shows usually have a leading pair of characters with different yet complementary personalities, becoming the heart of the show. Procedural dramas don’t forget about depth, and their main characters often struggle with trauma and other personal issues that impact their careers, as is the case with The Mentalist’s Patrick Jane. Created by Bruno Heller, The Mentalist follows Patrick Jane, a former psychic and now consultant to the California Bureau of Investigation, but his career as a psychic was a fraud.

Jane is no psychic, but he uses his highly developed observational skills to “read” people’s minds, which allowed him to pose as a psychic medium. Jane now uses those skills to solve murders, but he carries a lot of trauma that led him to change his career. The Mentalist combines a charming but broken lead with engaging cases, and luckily, Netflix has some great TV shows to watch after The Mentalist to continue on that line, but with some twists.

Will Trent is a police procedural TV series based on the book series by Karin Slaughter. Will Trent follows the title character (played by Ramón Rodríguez), a Special Agent in the Georgia Bureau of Investigation who solves the highest number of cases thanks to his incredible observation skills. Like Patrick Jane, Trent carries a lot of trauma, having been abandoned as a child and growing up in foster homes, while also facing other challenges like severe dyslexia. Both characters use unconventional methods in their investigations, with their shows balancing their darkest parts with good doses of humor.

A Man on the Inside is a comedy TV series created by Michael Schur and based on Maite Alberdi’s 2020 documentary The Mole Agent. A Man on the Inside introduces viewers to Charles (Ted Danson), a retired college engineering professor and widower who is encouraged by his daughter, Emily (Mary Elizabeth Ellis), to break out of his routine and rejoin the world.

Charles then takes a job as an investigative assistant for a private detective at Kovalenko Investigations, and so his first case is that of a missing necklace at a Pacific View Retirement Community. Unlike The Mentalist, A Man on the Inside is a more comedic show, but both are led by charming investigators who use unconventional methods and who are grieving a loved one, with their new careers helping them find a new “family.”

Dead to Me is a black comedy-crime thriller TV series created by Liz Feldman. Dead to Me follows Jen Harding (Christina Applegate) and Judy Hale (Linda Cardellini), who meet at a grief support group after Jen’s husband was killed in a hit-and-run incident and Judy claims to have lost her fiancé. In reality, Judy’s fiancé broke up with her, and she’s the hit-and-run driver. The two women form a special and deep bond, but Jen becomes more unhinged as she learns more about her husband’s death and Judy’s secrets.

Dead to Me isn’t a procedural drama, but it’s a great companion to The Mentalist thanks to their characters struggling with trauma and loss, their partner dynamics that complement each other, and how they use humor to cope with truly difficult situations.

The Following is a crime thriller TV show created by Kevin Williamson. The Following centers on Ryan Hardy (Kevin Bacon), a disgraced former FBI agent working to recapture serial killer Joe Carroll (James Purefoy) after the latter’s escape from prison. Carroll has formed a cult of fanatical killers and has his own son abducted by his people, as part of a plan to escape custody, humiliate Hardy, and reunite with his ex-wife.

The Mentalist’s Patrick Jane has a mission: capture Red John, a serial killer who murdered his family. Like Jane, The Following’s Hardy is on a mission to find Carroll, with whom he also has a connection through personal tragedy.

Marcella is a British Nordic noir detective TV series created by Hans Rosenfeldt. Marcella follows Marcella Backland (Anna Friel), a former detective at the London Metropolitan Police who returns to work to investigate three unsolved murders from 11 years earlier. However, Marcella is struggling in her personal life, as her husband of 15 years abruptly leaves her, and her two children are in boarding school.

On top of that, Marcella is dealing with dissociative blackouts that are rooted in deep trauma, tied to one specific event so traumatic that she blocked it from her memory. Marcella, like Jane, has to battle her own demons while investigating crimes and uses unconventional methods in her work, but it must be noted that Marcella is a darker show than The Mentalist.

Lupin is a French mystery thriller TV series based on the character Arssène Lupin, created by Maurice Leblanc. Lupin introduces the audience to Assane Diop (Omar Sy), a professional thief who arrives in France from Senegal hoping to build a better life for himself. When Assane was young, his father was framed for the theft of a diamond by his employer, the wealthy Hubert Pellegrini, and killed himself in prison.

Years later, Assane sets out to clear his father’s name and avenge him, and with the help of his charisma and mastery as a thief, he looks to expose Pellegrini’s crimes and bring him down. Once more, Lupin is a show with a main character carrying a lot of trauma, and just like Patrick Jane, Assane uses psychological manipulation, misdirection, and his charm to get the information he needs.

Hannibal is a psychological horror-thriller TV show based on Thomas Harris’ novels Red Dragon, Hannibal, and Hannibal Rising. Hannibal follows Will Graham (Hugh Dancy), an FBI special investigator assigned to the case of a serial killer. When the investigation turns out to have a heavy impact on Graham, his boss has him supervised by forensic psychiatrist Dr. Hannibal Lecter (Mads Mikkelsen), who is secretly a serial killer and cannibal.

Graham and Jane have similar ways of “reading” their subjects – one through observation and body language, and the other through the reconstruction of crime scenes by placing himself as the killer. Both shows have a core dynamic of opposite but complementary pairs, though Hannibal is more horror-oriented and thus is darker than The Mentalist.

Based on the character from DC Comics, Lucifer follows Lucifer Morningstar (Tom Ellis), the fallen angel-turned-lord of Hell who, bored and tired of his life in Hell, decides to abdicate his throne and move to Los Angeles, where he runs his own nightclub. After finding himself involved in a murder case, Lucifer begins working as a police consultant for the Los Angeles Police Department alongside detective Chloe Decker (Lauren German), with whom he forms a strong bond.

Like Patrick Jane, Lucifer uses his charisma and charm to get the information he needs, though he also uses his very special power to make humans tell him their deepest desires. The pairing of Lucifer and Chloe is also reminiscent of that of Jane and Teresa Lisbon, but Lucifer has fantasy elements that give the show a very interesting twist.

The Blacklist is a crime thriller TV series created by Jon Bokenkamp. The Blacklist follows Raymond Reddington (James Spader), a criminal and one of the FBI’s Most Wanted fugitives who cooperates with the FBI to capture other criminals on his “blacklist.” Reddington doesn’t have the skills that Patrick Jane has, but like him, he has his own reasons to help the FBI find other criminals, and he’s as charismatic, observant, and manipulative as Jane.

Based on John Douglas and Mark Olshaker’s 1995 true-crime book of the same name, Mindhunter follows FBI agents Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff) and Bill Tench (Holt McCallany), who, along with psychologist Wendy Carr (Anna Torv), lead a research project to interview serial killers to understand their psychology and use that knowledge to solve other cases.

While Patrick Jane uses skills he has developed over the years, Mindhunter shows how those skills can be developed through deep research, and is a much deeper and more serious look into the minds of serial killers, making it a darker and more realistic complement to The Mentalist.

#3353. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon and Best Buy, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

On Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console. Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.99, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games. During this promotion, each of the following is $39.99:

Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. Games like Donkey Kong Bananza retail for upwards of $69.99, so you're saving as much as $30 on these games during this week-long promotion. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale.

Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Use price tracking tools to determine if the deals you're keeping tabs on are actually a deal. If you feel like that's too much work, we already do that for you, so follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. #3352. Over 720K BMW Vehicles Recalled Over Fire Risk

A whopping 720,796 BMWs have been recalled over the risk of a fire ... as officials urge owners to turn their cars off and leave them parked.

Apparently, the issue lies with an improperly sealed electrical connector located on the water pump ... according to a safety alert by the NHTSA.

If the connector gets exposed to water, it could short-circuit and cause a fire.

The NHTSA stressed ... "If you have one of these vehicles, you should park your vehicle outside and away from buildings and other vehicles until the vehicle is repaired."

So far, they've only experienced 10 incidents related to the issue ... but better safe than sorry!

2012-2016 3 Series, 2012-2016 5 Series, 2012–2015 X1, 2012-2016 Z4, 2013-2017 X3, 2014-2016 2 Series coupe, 2014–2016 3 Series sportswagon, 2014-2016 328xi Gran Turismo, 2014-2016 4 Series convertible, 2014-2016 4 Series coupe, 2015-2016 2 Series convertible, 2015-2016 4 Series gran coupe, 2015-2018 X4, and 2016-2018 X5 xDrive40e.

This isn't the first time these vehicles have been recalled either ... apparently they had another water pump issue back in 2024.
