#3332. Netflix's New Bestselling Adaptation Officially Sets Major Vampire Diaries Reunion

Netflix is hosting a major Vampire Diaries reunion.

The Vampire Diaries began as a book series written by L.J. Smith and was later adapted into a major supernatural series for The CW by Kevin Williamson and Julie Plec. The series ran for eight seasons and included two spinoff series titled The Originals and Legacies. The Vampire Diaries achieved major success across its run and has since become a huge phenomenon, thanks to finding new life on streaming, constantly returning as a top 10 series on the charts.

Now, the beloved supernatural series is getting a big reunion on Netflix. Paul Wesley, known for portraying Stefan Salvatore, and Sara Canning, known for portraying Jenna Sommers, will be reuniting for Netflix's new adaptation of the bestselling novel Icebreaker. Wesley has joined the cast as Coach Faulkner, with Canning on board as Coach Brady. The rest of the cast includes Daisy Jelley, Connor Simos, Gabriel Tierney, Auli'i Cravalho, Peter Berry, Chaneil Kular, Devin Craig, and Aidan Shaw.

Icebreaker is a viral sports romance novel written by British author Hannah Grace, which began as a self-published series on Wattpad before becoming a New York Times bestseller. Due to its success, Grace has launched the Maple Hills series, and the novels are heading to Netflix for a major adaptation. The plot follows Anastasia Allen (played by Jelley), a fiercely driven, competitive figure skater aiming for Team USA, and Nathan Hawkins (played by Simos), the easygoing captain of the college hockey team. When a mishap forces both teams to share a single ice rink, their worlds collide.

Gossip Girl's Amanda Lasher is the series' showrunner and writer, and shared her thoughts on the upcoming adaptation: "I have been a fan of steamy YA since the seventh grade, reading Judy Blume stealthily hidden behind a textbook. I love this genre, and it’s been a joy working with Jade, the team at Unwell, and Netflix to bring Hannah Grace’s beloved Icebreaker novel to the screen." Icebreaker's adaptation creator, Jade Halley Bartlett (known for Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness) stated:

"It’s been such a joy to play in Hannah Grace’s world of Icebreaker, a story filled with ambitious, talented, and undeniably sexy characters. But the real special sauce is that, above all, they are good, deeply compassionate people … and we cannot get enough of them. Hannah has created the kind of world you want to live in, and Amanda and I are having an absolute romp, with our incredible teams at Unwell and Netflix, bringing this cherished story to the screen."

The rise of adapting bestselling YA romances has become a major trend, especially with sports involved. Crave's adaptation of Heated Rivalry, which also landed on HBO Max, took the world by storm and is returning for multiple seasons and even a movie with special theatrical releases of season 1 being released worldwide. Netflix's decision to adapt Icebreaker is no surprise given its popularity and how viral the novel series has become.

At the time of writing, Netflix has yet to announce an official release date for Icebreaker, but filming is already underway and is expected to arrive on the streaming giant in late 2027.

#3329. ’Frozen’s Kristen Bell and Idina Menzel Officially Reunite for a New Disney Series

Disney's rich history of animation success continued earlier this year, as its latest collaboration with Pixar proved hugely popular. Toy Story 5, the latest installment in the groundbreaking animated series, scored more than $1 billion in a mammoth box office run, as audiences in their many millions booked tickets to see the return of Woody (Tom Hanks), Buzz (Tim Allen), Jessie (Joan Cusack), and the rest of the gang.

Called "a necessary response to how much the world has changed in the past three decades," in Taylor Gates' review for Collider, this timely animated favorite was considered a likely contender for the Best Animated Feature prize at the Academy Awards, only for LAIKA to return with the fantasy masterpiece Wildwood a few months later.

Either way, Disney struck gold once again with Toy Story 5, 13 years after producing another pop culture phenomenon with Frozen. Unable to let the IP go, the company is returning to the Frozen pool for a brand-new series that features several returning favorites. The Real Frozen (currently a working title) is the latest natural history series collaboration between National Geographic and Walt Disney Animation Studios.

Lion, based on The Lion King, Emmy-winner A Real Bug's Life, and the upcoming The Real Finding Nemo are the first three entries into the growing series, which expands with one of Disney's biggest IPs. Perhaps most excitingly, Kristen Bell, Idina Menzel, and Jonathan Groff will return as Anna, Elsa, and Kristoff, respectively, with it reported that Josh Gad will also appear as Olaf. This news comes following the first plot details for Frozen 3 being revealed at D23 in August. Frozen 4 is also in development.

According to a synopsis, The Real Frozen reimagines the characters of Frozen "as if they were inhabiting the real worlds depicted throughout the series." The synopsis continues:

"Set against the breathtaking icy landscapes of Iceland, Finland, Norway and Sweden, The Real Frozen follows real-life animals whose fortitude, loyalty, resilience and relationships echo the emotional heart of the Frozen franchise. These animals navigate the harshest winters, revealing extraordinary behaviors, survival strategies and bonds."

Ahead of the release of Frozen 3, which is scheduled to hit theaters on November 24, 2027, The Real Frozen ​​​​​​is on the way. For more of the latest news, make sure to stay tuned to Collider.

#3326. ‘The Violinist’ Composer Ricky Ho Took Two Months To Write The First Four Notes Of Central Sonata – Contenders L.A.

The Violinist is an animated film about a woman searching for her long-lost love after being separated during World War II. She was a violinist, so her music is a major piece of the story. Ricky Ho, one of two composers along with Isabel Latorre, said he toiled over the beginning of the film’s signature piece, “Sunset Sonata.”

“It’s not an easy piece to come up with,” Ho said. “It has to be very special, especially the first few notes. Maybe the first two months I write, put aside, take it back, change some notes. In the end, I find these four notes are the perfect notes for the film.”

Co-directors Ervin Han and Raúl García joined Ho on the panel at Deadline’s Contenders Film Los Angeles panel Saturday. While the score could be added to the film later, they actually needed to know what notes he was composing as a plot point. Watch on Deadline

“We had this back-and-forth because Ricky was composing his music,” García said. “There are scenes where characters write the notes of the sonata.”

RELATED: Deadline Launches Its Contenders London Streaming Site

“Sunset Sonata” connects the leads of the film as their lives drive them apart. Much of the film involves the Japanese occupation of Singapore.

“It represents their connection, their love together,” Ho said. “This piece of music is really important throughout the film.”

The epic story also encompasses epic emotions.

“We are melodrama, and we’re proud of it,” García said. “We need to cry from time to time, and this movie helps you.”

RELATED: Deadline Launches Its Sound & Screen Film Streaming Site

Han said he was influenced by the Hong Kong melodramas of the ’80s. He saw them with his parents in theaters and understood their catharsis looking back as an adult.

“They would quietly weep in the corner,” Han said. “We embrace that sincerity.”

Likewise, Han shared some frustrations with being questioned on animating the film. As a filmmaker, he just thinks of animation as a way to tell certain stories.

“Animation has a different contract with the audience,” Han said. “The fact that it’s not real, that it’s drawn, opens up a lot to personal memories, personal life experience, to bring it to the emotion. In many ways, you surrender emotion more readily to it.”

García said animation served The Violinist for both aesthetic and budgetary reasons.

“Animation and especially 2D animation, they have this quality of timelessness,” he said. “The movement is stylized. The artwork is beautiful and really takes you to the place much easier than you try to do this live action. There won’t be money in the world to actually make it in live action because of the scope of the story.”

#3322. The Greatest Led Zeppelin Lyrics Ever Written, Ranked

Led Zeppelin is one of the biggest rock bands of all time. The group has its genesis in London, 1968, taking form after the dissolution of The Yardbirds – a blues-rock band that launched the careers of multiple legendary guitarists, Jimmy Page included. Zeppelin quickly rose to fame. Boasting eight consecutive number one albums in the UK and a 1995 induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame (amongst many other accolades), their work has been appreciated and celebrated for decades.

Led Zeppelin's music is rooted in the blues and influenced by the British and American folk revival, giving their work immense depth and a unique texture. Their lyrics tackle all aspects of the human experience, from love and desire to the seemingly endless search for purpose. Emotional and introspective, frontman Robert Plant’s vivid storytelling played a key role in their massive success. While they have countless unforgettable lyrics, these five Led Zeppelin songs contain their very best.

“Over the Hills and Far Away” was written by Robert Plant and Jimmy Page during their time at Bron-Yr-Aur, a remote holiday cottage in Wales. After their North American tour wrapped, Plant and Page retreated to this peaceful oasis to recover, spend time in nature, and write. The cottage had no electricity or running water, so the pair spent many a cold evening making music by the roaring fire. This return to simplicity allowed them to create many beautiful pieces – the influence of the Welsh countryside can be heard throughout their discography.

“Over the Hills and Far Away,” the lead single from their 1973 album Houses of the Holy, is heavily influenced by Celtic folklore and Welsh mythology. The song’s title is a classic idiom from 17th century British folklore, referring to the romantic uncertainty of the future. It has a recurring role in English folk culture, a tradition that Zeppelin continued some 300 years later.

This song explores the ongoing search for purpose – the seemingly endless journey one must undertake in order to let go of the past and build the future. It is about breaking free, hitting the open road and living beyond the constraints of society. Most of all, it is about finding love. Plant writes about the toxic relationships of the past and dreams of a better future: “Many have I loved, and many times been bitten/ Many times I've gazed along the open road.” The cure for a broken heart? Adventure.

“Ramble On” is the seventh track on Led Zeppelin II, released in 1969. This song was heavily influenced by The Lord of the Rings trilogy, written by J.R.R. Tolkien. Tolkien and Page grew up in the same region in the West Midlands of England. Plant felt very connected to Tolkien and his literature, specifically his creation of Middle Earth, a fantasy land that romanticized the English countryside. This song directly references Tolkien characters and locales: “T'was in the darkest depths of Mordor/ I met a girl so fair/ But Gollum and the evil one/ Crept up and slipped away with her.”

This song follows the same classic monomyth structure as LOTR and The Hobbit – the main character must leave the comforts of home behind and journey into the unknown, a transformative experience necessary for personal growth. In Plant’s lyrics, this takes the form of leaving the fast-paced toxicity of urban living and returning to the natural world in order to find himself. His expedition is set up in the first verse: “The leaves are falling all around/ Time I was on my way/ Thanks to you, I'm much obliged/ For such a pleasant stay/ But now it's time for me to go/ The autumn moon lights my way/ For now, I smell the rain/ And with it pain/ And it's headed my way.”

“Stairway to Heaven” is widely regarded as one of the best rock songs of all time. It was also created during their stay at Bron-Yr-Aur, written mostly in a single night and then fleshed out through fragmented recordings. Plant initially improvised the lyrics on the spot, then refined them over time. This powerful progressive rock anthem is expansive and soaring, steeped in haunting folk magic.

The lyrics condemn the material greed and consumerism of the modern world. Plant ruminates upon society’s obsession with money: “There's a lady who's sure all that glitters is gold/ And she's buying a stairway to Heaven/ When she gets there she knows, if the stores are all closed/ With a word she can get what she came for.” Like much of his writing, the focus is on finding meaning in a seemingly meaningless existence. While he might not have all the answers, he knows that salvation and peace cannot be achieved through the accumulation of material things. The gently and poetically urges the listener to let go of ego and think beyond the self, to return to nature and discover inner peace. This song is Led Zeppelin’s pièce de résistance, and rightfully so.

You won't find "Stairway to Heaven" or "Kasmir" on this list.

“Kashmir” is perhaps the only other Zeppelin song in the same league (and on the same scale) as "Stairway." Plant was inspired not by the Indian region of Kashmir (as the title suggests), but instead by the vast emptiness of the deserts of Morocco: “Oh, all I see turns to brown/ As the sun burns the ground/ And my eyes fill with sand/ As I scan this wasted land/ Trying to find, trying to find where I've been.” The lyrics ruminate on the significance of the journey rather than the destination – the transformation itself is what is important, not the end result.

Every member of the band has songwriting credits on this track – except for multi-instrumentalist John Paul Jones, who was late for the recording session on the day it was written. Zeppelin considered this song one of their biggest musical accomplishments, often wishing they were known for “Kashmir” instead of “Stairway.” They performed constantly, gracing countless crowds with its magic and majesty. Plant is very proud of the lyrics, and deservedly so. His writing is abstract and poetic, capturing massive ideas and emotions in a handful of words: “Oh, let the sun beat down upon my face/ With stars to fill my dream/ I am a traveler of both time and space/ To be where I have been.”

Plant was only 22 when he wrote “Going to California.” The song is a lilting, melodic reflection upon the counterculture of the 1960s and the glamorization of the American West Coast. The track was initially about the earthquakes in California, which is still a theme in the lyrics: “Seems that the wrath of the Gods/ Got a punch on the nose and it started to flow/ I think I might be sinking.” As they worked on the song, earthquakes took on a metaphoric role: representing radical, transformative change in one’s life.

In continuity with much of his other work, the lyrics describe a search for a meaning through adventure and new experiences. Plant describes letting go of the toxicity of the past and the women who have scorned him: “Spent my days with a woman unkind/ Smoked my stuff and drank all my wine./ Made up my mind to make a new start/ Going To California with an aching in my heart.” California is framed as this fantasy world where anything is possible.

Plant describes the woman of his dreams: “To find a queen without a king/ They say she plays guitar and cries and sings/ Side a white mare in the footsteps of dawn/ Tryin' to find a woman who's never, never, never been born.” Plant has said that he finds these lyrics somewhat embarrassing in retrospect, but they captured how he was feeling at the time – which is exactly what songwriting should do. Some have posited that this mystical figure is inspired by Joni Mitchell, which may very well be the case. But more than anything, this song is a life-affirming love letter to California.

#3320. Danny Boyle Talks ‘Ink’, The Common Architecture Of His Movies And More ‘28 Years Later’ As He Receives The Deadline Legend Award

Danny Boyle says he used to believe that he that he never made the same film twice, thus a filmography that includes hit movies across genres like Shallow Grave, Trainspotting, 127 Hours, The Beach, 28 Days Later and of course Slumdog Millionaire, the 2009 Best Picture Oscar winner that also won him Best Director.

But Boyle, speaking onstage Saturday after receiving the Deadline Legend Award during Deadline’s Contenders Film Los Angeles awards-season event, said he was set straight on that idea long ago.

“I can’t remember if it was a press conference or a Q&A in Paris, and this French journalist stood up at the back and said, ‘This is nonsense, Mr. Boyle’,” he recalled. “And I said, ‘Excuse me, what?’ And she said, ‘All your films are exactly the same.’ She said, ‘They’re all about, and it’s usually a guy, who overcomes, who faces insurmountable odds and overcomes them.’ And with that she walked out.”

He continued, “Ever since then I’ve accepted that she’s absolutely right — they are all about the same thing, really. And you do realize, and you can see in other filmmakers as well. You’re desperately trying to make a different film, and they basically turn out the same in a way. They’re the skeleton or the the kind of architecture of them is the same somehow. I have to hold my hand up and admit that. So if you keep buying tickets to go and see the films, thank you.” Watch on Deadline

Boyle’s latest entry on his list is Ink, based on Hames Graham’s Tony-winning play about Rupert Murdoch and editor Larry Lamb’s efforts to revive the British newspaper The Sun, ushering in a new kind of tabloid journalism with lurid headlines and questionable tactics. Graham adapted the screenplay for the pic, which opened this year’s Venice Film Festival and is gearing for its December 11 release in theaters.

In Ink‘s case, the underdogs in question are Guy Pearce’s Murdoch and Jack O’Connell’s Lamb, who are faced with the daunting task to make inroads against a dozen UK paper including what Doyle called “the Real Madrid” of publications at the time, The Mirror.

“One of them from Australia, and the other one from Yorkshire in the north of England, with a plan to beat [The Mirror] in a year, in just one year, to overtake it in a year,” Boyle said in conversation with Deadline’s Mike Fleming Jr. “And what they did in order to do that was, in my contention and James’, is that they invented the tabloid vernacular, the language, the the vocabulary, the techniques of the tabloid, and they began to use it. And it connected with what people in Britain wanted, who were still in a dreary world of paternalism and postwar ‘we know what’s best for you’ kind of mentality, and they suddenly found a kind of liberation.”

That’s in the first half of the film, which he said “I hope is very very funny because it employs the tabloid techniques to to gain your trust really, but through your pleasure. Then it begins to change a little bit when you find out some of the things that they’re up to and some of the costs of what that approach entails.”

Boyle during the conversation also confirmed that headlines that appeared in the movie’s epilogue that have been redacted in UK versions of the film because of stringent libel laws will be shown in the U.S. versions.

He also said a difference from Graham’s play is Claire Foy’s character Jules Davies, a composite of several women who worked at The Sun including one that had an affair with Lamb. Lamb’s son objected to the inclusion, Boyle said, because he thought it disparaged the memory of his mother, “which is absolutely right,” the director says.

“The film’s about Larry Lamb and his reputation and his behavior. And he was a public figure. And it’s only right and proper that we have the right to investigate him,” Boyle said. “He changed British society significantly in many ways, as much as Margaret Thatcher changed British society.”

Thatcher also appears in the film. “We didn’t want an impersonator to play her, so we actually re-created her, the real Margaret Thatcher. But we didn’t ask Margaret Thatcher’s estate because these powerful people, we have to be able to investigate them, and provided you do it truthfully and responsibly …. I think it’s right to have that kind of artistic license. In fact, it’s crucial to freedom and artistic freedom that you do have that license with public figures.

Boyle also provided an update on a third installment of the 28 Years Later franchise, after he and Alex Garland brought back the franchise in 2025. A second movie, Nia DaCosta’s 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple also penned by Garland, hit theaters this past January.

“Alex has written a fantastic script. Seriously, he’s written a fantastic script, so we’ve got to raise the money to make it,” Boyle said. He also confirmed that Cillian Murphy, who appeared in the 2002 Boyle-directed franchise starter 28 Days Later, was game to return.

“I mean, he’s up for it, and it’s a fantastic part — Alex has written this fantastic part for him,” Boyle said. “Those of you who saw [Bone Temple], he’s teased at the end of that, and then the third film does complete the story in a beautiful, mathematically perfect way in which the circle is closed in a way that even Chris Nolan might admire, actually, because it’s perfect. So let’s hope it all comes together.”

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Upgrading your TV's sound doesn't necessarily mean spending a fortune on a full home theater setup, especially with early Black Friday deals bringing substantial discounts on soundbars and audio systems from Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG. Sony has some of the biggest price cuts, with savings of up to 32% across select Bravia Theater models, including more than $700 off its premium Theater Trio system.

Samsung's Dolby Atmos soundbars are also discounted by as much as $400, while Bose and LG have more affordable options for anyone looking to improve dialogue clarity, add some bass, or enjoy surround sound without a complicated setup. Whether you're shopping for a compact speaker for a bedroom TV or a more immersive system for movie nights, here are the deals worth considering.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

For smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

Samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

At just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3314. Microsoft Officially Apologized for Yesterday's Outages

If you were having trouble accessing certain services like Microsoft Teams or Outlook, you were not alone. Early Thursday afternoon, many of Microsoft's biggest apps and services were experiencing downtime. According to Downdetector, which tracks user reports of issues with websites and platforms, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Teams, and OneDrive were all experiencing issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft has restored service to many users, and has officially apologized for the outages.

When I first published this article on Thursday, I couldn't even load Microsoft 365's status page. (I've reported on many service outages, but I can't recall a time when a service's status page was also down.) Even as of Friday afternoon, the page still says "Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise)," and Microsoft says the following services may be affected: Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center, Microsoft 365 Education, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft Power Apps, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft To Do, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, and Windows 365.

Looking specifically at Outlook, Microsoft's email service had hundreds of thousands of user reports Thursday afternoon, signaling a major issue somewhere in Microsoft's pipeline. The reports did "slow down" throughout the day, but Downdetector still showed over 50,000 reports coming in every 15 minutes when I checked Thursday afternoon.

While the root cause of the issue was a mystery throughout Thursday's outage, Microsoft confirmed the problem in an apology on Friday. According to the company, "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI [or] agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions."

Microsoft says it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption to its customers and partners. The company says the fix rolled out slower than some might expect, since it wanted to restore service gradually to evaluate stability at each stage. It also says it will release a full post-incident report once it completes a review.

During the outage, the company had confirmed that some of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load, which it said was likely contributing to the issues. Microsoft then said it was pausing all deployments and moving traffic from affected infrastructure, and that it found that a number of its servers were unexpectedly unavailable after failing health checks. The company then thought a specific component responsible for processing server health may be the reason the system is failing health checks. Microsoft said an alternative service health check method successfully restarted some of the affected servers. The company was then actively restarting and validating affected servers to bring them back to service.

#3313. Carrie Coon & Lily James Humanized Cult Member And Leader In Guy Nattiv’s ‘The Liberation’ – Contenders L.A.

Carrie Coon and Lily James grew to understand their roles in the cult thriller The Liberation — compounded by the fact that director Guy Nattiv based the film on his own grandmother.

Coon plays Rita, an unhappy woman who finds a place she feels she belongs. Under the mentorship of Ricki King (James), Rita unburdens herself. Eventually, though, Ricki convinces Rita to give her money and divorce her husband. The trio spoke about the film at Deadline’s Contenders Film Los Angeles on Saturday.

“I just was so moved by Guy’s grandmother’s story and the way Guy has humanized every step,” Coon said. “We understand just how radical what she’s doing is. As a woman, I understand why she might want to cede all agency to someone else. I understand why a patriarchal structure wasn’t fulfilling to her.”

Coon also called The Liberation a love story between Rita and Ricki. Likewise, James did not want to make Ricki a caricature villain.

RELATED: ‘The Liberation’ Review: Carrie Coon, Lily James And Bella Ramsey Soar In Guy Nattiv’s Explosive Cult Thriller – Telluride Film Festival

“We really wanted to do that to find the total humanity in these women,” James said. “It’s not the villain. It’s so much more complicated. The fact that she could switch from generosity and empathy and love and kindness to savagery and annihilation. When you’re out, you’re out. Her motivations are so clear. She truly believes she’s saving these women. She truly believes she has this power. I could lead with strength.”

Nattiv remembered the changes in his grandmother when he was a child. After the real Rita’s death, he visited the cult leader and was able to ask some real questions before she expelled him.

“She was miserable and unhappy,” the writer-director said. “Then she became happy again. Then she started dancing and started to find herself again, which made sense to us as a family. It didn’t make sense when money started disappearing and she was advised to divorce my grandfather and live for good somewhere in America writing postcards. I didn’t see my grandmother until after she passed.”

Coon’s real-life husband, Tracy Letts, plays Rita’s husband, Reuben. They have two daughters, played by Bella Ramsey and Odessa Young.

RELATED: ‘The Liberation’ Trailer: Carrie Coon Stars In Guy Nattiv’s Complex Cult Thriller

“Who are we to say what someone needs to process their trauma?” Coon said. “We don’t get to decide for somebody else. The tragedy and the pain played out in Bella and Odessa and Tracy … you feel the loss. Bella is the cypher for the audience.”

The real Rita also was the sole survivor of her family in the Holocaust. Coon studied her testimonies about surviving.

“Speaking the unspeakable is a very challenging act and so many people have to brace themselves,” Coon said. “The video gets stopped very frequently. I wanted to dignify that experience because I’m not culturally Jewish. I would never want that to feel not lived in.”

The Liberation will have a Oscar-qualifying theatrical run this year and open January 8.

Most crime shows want viewers on the side of the law. The detectives are the stars of the show, and the criminal is only a vehicle for them to show off how clever they are. The bad guy usually gets a few scenes and a quick motive before disappearing. The formula obviously works, but it also means the most interesting person in the story barely gets a voice, and audiences rarely find out what actually pushed these characters to become who they are.

Only a few shows have done the exact opposite. They make the risky move of handing the story to the criminal and let viewers see every lie and every bad decision up close. The strange part is how quickly the audience starts rooting for them, even when they know they shouldn’t. That uncomfortable sense of loyalty is what keeps people glued to the screen. Here are the best crime shows told from the criminal’s perspective, ranked.

Ozark proves that a crime show doesn’t need a traditional big bad monster to feel dangerous. In fact, Marty Byrde (Jason Bateman) doesn’t even look like a criminal, but that’s exactly why he’s so good at being one. On paper, the show’s protagonist is a boring Chicago financial advisor with his wife Wendy (Laura Linney) and two kids. In reality, he has spent years quietly laundering money for a Mexican drug cartel. When his business partner gets caught stealing from them, Marty only survives by making a desperate promise. He tells the higher-ups that he will move his family to Missouri’s Lake of the Ozarks and clean even more money there. Unfortunately, the locals there turn out to be just as dangerous as the cartel.

Ozark works because viewers are never really asked to like Marty. All they have to do is watch him survive one impossible situation after the other. The real star, though, is Wendy, who starts as a reluctant passenger and slowly becomes the most ruthless person in the story. Ozark is equal parts family drama and equal parts crime thriller. That emotional grounding really raises its stakes. The longer the Byrdes stay in the Ozarks, the more the question becomes whether they can make it out alive without losing who they used to be. A must-watch for anyone who can appreciate morally gray TV characters.

Dexter pulls off the impossible task of making a serial killer the guy viewers cheer for. The show follows Dexter Morgan (Michael C. Hall), who works as a blood spatter analyst for the Miami police by day. By night, though, he hunts down murderers who have escaped justice. His adoptive father, Harry (James Remar), noticed Dexter’s violent urges when he was a child and taught him a strict set of rules, so he only kills people who seem to deserve it. Of course, keeping that secret gets harder as Dexter builds a family and a life that look completely normal from the outside.

The secret weapon in Dexter is the show’s narration. Viewers hear Dexter’s thoughts in every scene, and his dry, deadpan jokes make him feel more like a friend than a monster. That closeness between him and the audience is the whole point, because they end up making the same excuses for him that he makes for himself, and the show occasionally snaps them back to reality with a reminder of just how cold he can be. Dexter Season 4, where the protagonist faces John Lithgow’s terrifying Trinity Killer, is the series at its peak. The ending may have disappointed fans, but Dexter paved the way for every killer that viewers have rooted for since.

Anyone who watched Breaking Bad already knows how Jimmy McGill’s (Bob Odenkirk) story ends, and Better Call Saul turns that into its greatest strength. Before he became Saul Goodman, the sleazy lawyer for drug dealers, Jimmy was a struggling attorney in Albuquerque trying to leave his past as a small-time con man behind. In the spinoff, he wants nothing more than to be taken seriously, especially by his successful older brother, Chuck (Michael McKean). Unfortunately, though, Jimmy just can’t stop cutting corners, and every shortcut pulls him a little closer to the cartel. Watching Better Call Saul feels like watching a slow-motion car crash, because viewers can see the danger long before Jimmy does.

The show makes it easy to understand him, since so many of his worst moments come from pure desperation. His relationship with Kim Wexler (Rhea Seehorn), a brilliant lawyer who secretly loves a good scheme as much as he does, is the emotional heart of the series, and their story is the show’s most heartbreaking part. Plenty of fans agree that the show is even better than the original, and that is primarily because it helps them understand the man behind the ruthless, larger-than-life Saul Goodman persona, who ends up becoming one of the most tragic characters in TV history.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

The Sopranos begins with a mob boss in a therapist’s office, and that one idea changed TV forever. Tony Soprano (James Gandolfini) runs a New Jersey crime family, but he’s also a husband and father who suddenly starts having panic attacks. Desperate to make them stop, he secretly begins seeing a psychiatrist, Dr. Jennifer Melfi (Lorraine Bracco). Their sessions give the audience a front-row seat to the mind of a man who has spent his whole life hiding his feelings behind anger.

The therapy sessions are the most fascinating part of The Sopranos. Tony is often charming and funny, and it’s easy to feel for him when he talks about his difficult mother or his fears about his kids. Then he walks out of Dr. Melfi’s office and does something horrifying, and viewers are reminded that understanding someone isn’t the same as excusing them. Gandolfini makes both sides of Tony feel completely real, which is why the character still feels so alive today. The show refuses to give him a neat redemption, and its famously abrupt ending is still polarizing fans decades later. The Sopranos is the show that taught TV how to take its antiheroes seriously, and every other crime show since then has tried to live up to its legacy.

Breaking Bad opens with Walter White (Bryan Cranston) being a harmless chemistry teacher, desperate to ensure his family’s financial security after he is diagnosed with terminal lung cancer. To do so, he partners up with his former student, Jesse Pinkman (Aaron Paul), to cook and sell meth so his family will be taken care of after he’s gone. Walter’s chemistry skills make their product the best on the market, and soon enough, Walter starts transforming into Heisenberg, the cold alter ego he invents to do business in the drug world.

Now, the brilliance of Breaking Bad is how it plays with the audience’s sympathy. Early on, it’s easy to cheer for Walt as an underdog finally standing up for himself. Then, little by little, the show reveals that he was never really doing it for his family, and viewers are left wondering why they rooted for him in the first place. Cranston’s slow evolution into an entirely different character is one of the greatest performances in TV history, and Walt’s relationship with Jesse gives the series some of its most memorable villains. Breaking Bad is a near-perfect series from beginning to end, and it’s the ultimate example of how to tell a story from the bad guy’s side.

Saturday Night Live opened with host John Mulaney instructing a naive group of tech leaders how to tell whether a woman is genuinely interested in them or is a spy trying to extract valuable information from them, as may be the case with ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Mulaney, as a CIA officer, summons Peter Thiel (James Austin Johnson), Sam Altman (Ben Marshall), Dario Amodei (Jane Wickline), Mark Zuckerberg (Andrew Dismukes) and Elon Musk (Jeremy Culhane) to agency headquarters to brief them on a matter of national security.

“America needs you to learn the difference between a woman who would actually want to have sex with you, and a woman who is clearly a spy,” Mulaney says. He then asks the group what the lesson in Huang’s downfall is.

“Never date a Chinese woman,” Amodei says.

“Never date a human woman,” Zuckerberg answers.

“Never date anyone, lest they become the antichrist,” Thiel says.

Mulaney then tries using a Venn diagram to get his point across. The diagram shows two circles that do not overlap one bit: “beautiful women” and “your interests and opinions.”

“So,” he asks the group, “if someone is both of these things, then they are a what?”

The script — and actress Olivia Colman’s attachment to the project – was the ultimate draw for star Alexander Skarsgård to undergo quite a transformation into the straw-plaited husband of Ursula Wills’ short story-based film Wicker from Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson.

“From the first page, I was just immersed in this fantasy, in this fable, in this saga, and I thought it was so funny and romantic and sexy and irreverent with a lot of interesting social commentary on patriarchy and the institution of marriage and jealousy in society and that hierarchy that we that we have in our society and how hard it is to break that,” Skarsgård said Saturday during the panel for the film at Deadline Contenders Film Los Angeles event. “But I thought these guys had done it so beautifully, where it never felt too preachy or annoying. ‘Oh, this is the message of the movie.’ It was so subtly inserted into the story. At no point was it not entertaining and sweet and funny and crazy.”

The wicker-suit getup was “horrible” to wear, Skarsgård joked.

#3308. Liam Neeson’s New Action Thriller Officially Finds Redemption on Streaming

Liam Neeson and action movies go hand in hand. The star of the genre's modern masterpiece Taken is never far from another actioner, even bringing back one of the genre's funniest franchises in 2025. Neeson joined forces with Pamela Anderson (The Last Showgirl) and Paul Walter Hauser (The Fantastic Four: First Steps) in The Naked Gun, earning rave reviews for his lead performance that Leslie Nielsen would've been proud of.

"If this is the start of a new rebooted franchise's legacy, it'd be difficult to complain," wrote Aidan Kelley in his review of The Naked Gun for Collider, one of many full of praise. This sort of praise is the stuff of dreams for Neeson's latest project, which has been widely panned by critics. The Mongoose, a high-octane thriller directed by Neeson's long-time stunt double Mark Vanselow in his feature debut, was released late last month and was met with some of the worst reviews in Neeson's career.

"How long can Liam Neeson keep doing this?" said ScreenRant's Alex Harrison in a 3/10 review, in which he also called the film "a lazy mess" that is "only made enjoyable by how unintentionally funny it is." The additions of Marisa Tomei (Spider-Man: Brand New Day), Ving Rhames (Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning), Michael Chiklis (The Senior), and Maurice Marvel Meredith (Monarch: Legacy of Monsters) couldn't save the film from critical destruction, but its fortunes on the small screen are proving much better. At the time of writing, The Mongoose is one of the ten most-watched movies on Prime Video in the world.

Although the film was never intended to be this season's big new action blockbuster, there's no doubt that those in charge of The Mongoose will be bitterly disappointed by its box office performance. The film debuted on the big screen two weeks ago, only managing just over $400,000 from 1,014 theaters. In its second weekend, The Mongoose dropped by a staggering 83% in ticket sales, no doubt due to being removed from almost all of its locations.

The Mongoose is one of the ten most-watched movies on Prime Video in the world. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3307. 10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

If Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

If you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

If you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae shows up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

Looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

Love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

If you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.

#3305. ‘SNL’ Weekend Update Roasts Trump Admin Over Grounded Flights, Jensen Huang Affairs

Saturday Night Live‘s Weekend Update took aim at the Trump administration’s explanation for grounding all flights for hours on Friday, and questioned what the president knew about ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“The scariest part about all these flights getting grounded was the messaging from the normally dependable Trump administration,” Colin Jost began. “First, they said it was a ‘telecommunications outage, as of now.’ Why add ‘as of now?’ No one wants to hear: ‘Your child is safe, as of now.'”

“Then, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said the whole situation was the result of a contractor upgrading copper wire to fiberoptic cable. So, one guy switched out one wire and took out all planes? I think that’s literally a scene from the movie, ‘Airplane!'” Jost joked.

Co-anchor Michael Che turned to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin telling reporters in the early stage of the incident that it was not a 9/11-type situation.

“Which he knew, because Rudy Giuliani didn’t see his shadow,” he joked.

Jost then addressed ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affairs, some reportedly with his subordinates and one with a suspected Chinese spy. The news has caused stocks to fall, since the company’s A.I. chips are shouldering a large part of the U.S. economy.

“Jensen Huang had a midlife crisis so bad, you might lose your house in his divorce,” he joked.

Jost then addressed the uncertainty about what Donald Trump knew about Huang potentially being taken advantage of and when he knew it.

“Insiders are also saying that despite Trump’s claim that he didn’t know about the Nvidia CEO’s relationship with a Chinese spy, he was actually briefed about it on a trip to China in May,” Jost said. “So this concludes yet another game of ‘Dementia or Lying?’

#3296. These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.)

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

Updates are generally good for your devices. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

#3286. Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know

The latest Apple Watches have a lot of new features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

The Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps.

You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is currently in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

It's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter.

To finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own important details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind.

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time.

First, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at.

The double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details.

If you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri.

A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the new AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri launches into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop.

If you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

Getting the family together is one of the best parts of the holiday season, but it can also be one of the most stressful parts — whether you’re visiting family or hosting the gathering yourself. However, there are ways to make holiday get-togethers not only run smoother but also be fun and memorable for the whole family.

As a jumping-off point, we’ve put together four product ideas to help make your holiday gatherings great: a single-serve coffee machine, karaoke microphones, AI glasses, and a dependable printer. Together, these check off some key needs for any family rendezvous, including keeping everyone satiated, providing a fun activity, and recording memories.

All of these products (and more) are available at Best Buy, where you’ll also find many of them at a discount. The best bet: Sign up for the My Best Buy Membership, which gets you member pricing, 1% rewards, extended returns/exchanges, and free one-day savings for just $29.99 a year.

Making sure everyone can get their caffeine fix is crucial. A good single-serve machine is the way to go, letting everyone get their coffee when they want it (instead of waiting for a shared pot). This Nespresso Vertuo Next Premium by Breville is an excellent option with six pour size options, automatic adjustments depending on the pod, and a sleek design that fits on almost any counter. Plus, it comes with a Nespresso Aeroccino3 milk frother.

Need a good post-dinner activity for the whole family? Karaoke is a great option. And thanks to portable options like these EasySing microphones from JBL, it’s also easy to set up anywhere. The wireless mics include a dongle that you connect to your speaker to amplify your voice (sweet or otherwise).

A novel way to capture family gatherings — and blow the older family members’ minds — is a pair of Meta AI glasses. The glasses’ built-in camera captures POV videos in crisp 3K resolution, creating unique (and often funny) videos. They have a ton of other features outside video/photo, like built-in speakers and Meta AI for hands-free controls.

Chances are someone will need a printer, be it for some remote work during the holidays or printing a gift card. For a printer that can handle it all, check out this INKvestment 1365 from Brother. The compact printer features an easy-to-use interface and a companion app, and can crank out up to 16 pages per minute.

#3283. Cornelis launches CN6000 800G networking to rival Nvidia InfiniBand

Its new 800G network cards aim to stop costly AI chips from sitting idle while they wait for data.

Cornelis’s CN6000 network card and switch, which partner systems will use from early 2027.

Cornelis, which Intel spun out in 2020, has launched CN6000, a family of 800G network cards and switches for AI and supercomputers. It claims lower latency than Nvidia’s InfiniBand, based on its own tests. Partner systems arrive in early 2027.

Cornelis, a networking company spun out of Intel, has launched CN6000, a family of 800G network cards and switches for AI clusters and supercomputers, it announced this week. It is pitching them as a rival to Nvidia’s InfiniBand.

In large AI systems, thousands of chips must constantly swap data. If the network is slow, expensive chips sit idle. “Every minute an accelerator waits on the network is capacity our customers paid for and didn’t use,” said CEO Lisa Spelman.

The main card uses Omni-Path, a networking technology Intel dropped in 2019 before spinning the business off as Cornelis in 2020. Cornelis says the card can handle 1.6 billion messages a second. It also says it is 21% faster than Nvidia’s InfiniBand at passing a small message, though that comes from its own tests.

A faster single message does not mean jobs finish 21% sooner, since that depends on the workload. Cornelis also launched a card for standard Ethernet networks, which most AI data centres use, with support for the newer Ultra Ethernet standard due later.

The cards work with chips from AMD, Intel, Nvidia and Qualcomm. Dell, Lenovo and Supermicro are among the server makers planning to support them, with systems due in early 2027.

Networking has become a hot spot in AI. Nvidia has spent billions on optical links, Huawei is betting on wiring over chips, and startups such as Upscale AI are building ways to connect rival chips. AMD, a Cornelis partner, is also building rack-scale systems to compete with Nvidia.
